blocks.html: Introduction

In this exposé the formalism of cohomology with proper support is developed. The variance questions have been treated with a fair amount of care, whereas in the oral seminar they were merely made plausible. This accounts for the length of the exposé, whose paragraphs 1 to 4 are devoted to categories and to general topology. The reader is very strongly urged to read only paragraphs 5 and 6, where the geometric substance of the exposé is concentrated (§ 5: construction and variance of cohomology with proper support, base change, finiteness, finite Tor-dimension and comparison theorems; § 6: theory of the trace morphism for a quasi-finite flat morphism).

In paragraphs 1 and 2, we "recall" a few results on derived categories. § 1 no. 1 is devoted to the formalism of signs. In § 3, we treat the problem of gluing two variance formalisms. In § 4, we introduce flat resolutions and study the special properties of GODEMENT's flasque resolutions.

In this exposé, the functors \(R^q f_!\), higher direct images with proper support, and the functor \(Rf_!\) which gives rise to them, are defined only for \(f\) a compactifiable morphism (3.2.1). In the appendix, written by B. SAINT-DONAT, it is shown how to extend the definition to separated morphisms of finite type with quasi-compact quasi-separated target.
§ 5 no. 5 (cohomology of a symmetric product) will not be used again in this seminar. It will be used in SGA 5 to refine the rationality theorem for L-functions.

§ 6 no. 3 (theory of the trace for continuous coefficients) will be used in Exposé XVIII only in the relatively easy case of smooth groups; the reader interested in the Poincaré duality theorem (global duality), and willing to accept a transcendental argument, may even dispense entirely with reading this § 6 no. 3, as well as the greater part of § 1 of XVIII.
0. Terminological preliminaries.

0.1. The sign \(=\) placed between two groups of symbols denoting objects of a category will sometimes mean (by abuse of notation) that these objects are canonically isomorphic. The category and the canonical isomorphism should in principle have been defined beforehand. In a diagram, the sign \(=\) will then denote the isomorphism itself.

0.2.0. Let \(f : S \longrightarrow S'\) be a morphism of sites (IV 4.9.3). If \(U\) and \(U'\) are objects of \(S\) and \(S'\), an \(f\)-morphism from \(U\) to \(U'\) will by definition be a morphism from \(U\) to \(f^*U'\). For the étale sites of schemes, one recovers the usual notion.
0.2.1. If \(\mathfrak{F}\) and \(\mathfrak{F}'\) are sheaves on \(S\) and \(S'\), an \(f\)-morphism from \(\mathfrak{F}\) to \(\mathfrak{F}'\) will be, indifferently,

1. (i) a morphism from \(f^*\mathfrak{F}'\) to \(\mathfrak{F}\)
  2. (ii) a morphism from \(\mathfrak{F}'\) to \(f_*\mathfrak{F}\)
  3. (iii) a function which, to each \(f\)-morphism \(\varphi\) from an object \(U\) of \(S\) to an object \(U'\) of \(S'\), assigns a function from \(\mathfrak{F}'(U')\) to \(\mathfrak{F}(U)\), and this in a way compatible with the composition of \(\varphi\) with an arrow of \(S\) or \(S'\) (∗).
One sees from (i), (ii) and (iii) that the sheaves of sets form a fibred and cofibred category over the category of sites.

Likewise for the sheaves of left modules on ringed sites. Likewise for the étale sheaves on schemes; this is not immediately a special case of what precedes, for the sites in fact form a 2-category and "étale site of \(X\)" is only a pseudo-functor in \(X\) (VII 1.4).

The preceding definition makes the sheaves of sets (resp. ...) on variable sites a fibred category over that of sites, having as fibre categories the categories opposite to the usual categories of sheaves of sets (resp. ...).

0.3. Let \(I\) be a finite set, \(\varepsilon\) a function on \(I\) with values in \(\{+1, -1\}\), \((\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}\) a family of additive categories graded by translation functors \(T_i\) (CD I 1.10) and \(F\) a multiadditive multifunctor from the categories \(\mathcal{A}_i\) to an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\) graded by the translation functor \(T\). Assume \(F\) covariant (resp. contravariant) in the \(i\) such that \(\varepsilon_i = 1\) (resp. \(\varepsilon_i = -1\)). Modifying and completing ([CD] I 1.11), we shall say that \(F\) is a graded functor if one is given a family \((\varphi_i)_{i \in I}\) of isomorphisms of functors between \(T \circ F\) and \(F \circ T_i^{\varepsilon_i}\), such that the following diagrams are anticommutative, for \(i \neq j\) in \(I\),

\[\xymatrix{ F \circ (T_i^{\varepsilon_i}, T_j^{\varepsilon_j}) \ar[rr]^-{\varphi_j * T_i^{\varepsilon_i}} \ar[d]_-{\varphi_i * T_j^{\varepsilon_j}} & & T \circ F \circ T_i^{\varepsilon_i} \ar[d]^-{T * \varphi_i} \\ T \circ F \circ T_j^{\varepsilon_j} \ar[rr]_-{T * \varphi_j} & & T \circ T \circ F }\]
We leave to the reader the task of defining the composite of two graded functors and of verifying that it is again a graded functor.

0.4. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category and \(I\) a finite set. For \(i \in I\), we denote by \(1_i\) the \(i\)-th basis vector of \(\mathbb{Z}^I\). An \(I\)-fold complex (resp. a naive \(I\)-fold complex) of \(\mathcal{A}\) consists of

1. (a) a family \((K^k)_{k \in \mathbb{Z}^I}\) of objects of \(\mathcal{A}\);
  2. (b) for each \(i \in I\) and each \(k \in \mathbb{Z}^I\), an arrow \(d_i^k : K^k \longrightarrow K^{k+1_i}\), these arrows satisfying \(d_i^{k+1_i} d_i^k = 0\), and, for \(i \neq j\), \(d_i^{k+1_j} d_j^k + d_j^{k+1_i} d_i^k = 0\) (resp. \(d_i^{k+1_j} d_j^k = d_j^{k+1_i} d_i^k\)).

0.5. By a pro-object of a category \(C\) we shall mean a functor from \(C\) to (Ens) which is a filtered inductive limit (along a small filtered category) of representable functors (cf. I 8.10). Every pro-object is an inductive limit along a small filtered ordered set of representable functors. If \(X_i\) is a projective system of objects of \(C\), indexed by a small filtered category, we denote by "\(\varprojlim\)" \(X_i\) the pro-object \(\varinjlim h^{X_i}\).
0.6. The reader will dualize 0.5 to the case of ind-objects (Cf. I 8.2).
0.7. In accordance with the new terminology, we call scheme what was formerly called prescheme, and we call separated scheme what was formerly called scheme.

0.8. The category of ringed schemes is the category whose objects are the schemes whose étale site is equipped with a sheaf of rings, an arrow from \((S, \mathcal{A})\) to \((T, \mathcal{B})\) being a pair consisting of a morphism of schemes \(f\) from \(S\) to \(T\), and a homomorphism \(\omega\) of sheaves of rings from \(f^*\mathcal{B}\) to \(\mathcal{A}\). The morphism of schemes \(f\) is said to be induced by \((f, \omega)\).
0.9. If \(X\) is a scheme over \(Y\), we denote by \((X/Y)^n\) the \(n\)-fold fibre product of \(X\) over \(Y\).

0.10. Let \(S\) be a scheme. We call big étale site (resp. big fppf site, resp. big fpqc site) of \(S\) the site \(\mathrm{Sch}_{/S}\), equipped with the étale (resp. fppf, resp. fpqc) topology (SGA 3 IV 6.3). One should be careful that this is not a \(U\)-site (\(U\) being the fixed universe, \(\mathrm{Sch}_{/S}\) consisting of the schemes \(\in U\)).

We call small fpqc site (resp. small fppf site) of \(S\) the site of schemes flat over \(S\) (resp. flat of finite presentation) equipped with the fpqc (resp. fppf) topology. When a confusion must be avoided, we shall call small étale site of \(S\) the site \(S_{\mathrm{et}}\) (VII 1.2).

0.11. In many cases, the author has taken the liberty of speaking of commutative diagrams of morphisms of sites where one should have spoken of essentially commutative diagrams, i.e. commutative up to isomorphism (cf. IV 3.2.2). The reader may verify that the arguments we give apply also to the general situation.
0.12. The terminology "coherent scheme" for "quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme" has been surreptitiously introduced in places by A. Grothendieck.

0.13. A torsion sheaf \(F\) on a scheme \(S\) will be said to be prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\) if it is the inductive limit of its subsheaves annihilated by integers \(n\) invertible on \(S\).

footnotes.html: (∗) These terminologies are not compatible with the identification of the objects of \(S\) with the associated sheaves.

blocks.html: 1. The derived categories.
1.1. Exact functors (the sign rules).
1.1.1. For the fundamental theorems concerning derived categories, I refer to VERDIER [CD] and [2]. In this no., quite special attention has been paid to the problems of signs.
Recall that if \(f : X \longrightarrow Y\) is a morphism of complexes (in an additive category, understood in what follows), its cone \(C(f)\) is defined by
When \(X = 0\) (resp. \(Y = 0\)), one has \(C(f) = Y\) (resp. \(C(f) = X[1]\)), so that the commutative diagram
\[\xymatrix{ 0 \ar@{=}[r] \ar[d] & 0 \ar[r] \ar[d] & X \ar@{=}[r] \ar[d]^{f} & X \ar[d] \\ X \ar[r]_{f} & Y \ar@{=}[r] & Y \ar[r] & 0 }\]
defines a "triangle"
\[X \xrightarrow{\;f\;} Y \longrightarrow C(f) \xrightarrow{\;j\;} X[1] \, .\]

In the category of complexes up to homotopy, we call distinguished a triangle isomorphic to a triangle of this type, and antidistinguished a triangle which becomes distinguished when one changes the sign of its arrows. One verifies that the triangle defined by an exact sequence of complexes split in each degree ([CD] p. 10, cf. the proof of 1.1.5.4) is antidistinguished and that, up to isomorphism, every antidistinguished triangle is obtained in this way.

∗ 1.1.2. The computations of signs are carried out most easily by means of the following "formal rules". One writes an element of \(C(f)^n\) in the form \(1 \otimes x + y\) (\(x \in X^{n+1}\), \(y \in Y^n\)), \(1\) being a "cell" of dimension \(1\), and one sets \(d(1) \otimes x = f(x)\). One thus has
\[d(1 \otimes x + y) = d1 \otimes x - 1 \otimes dx + dy = -1 \otimes dx + f(x) + dy. \quad ∗\]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1.3

(i) A graded functor (0.3) from a triangulated category \(\mathcal{A}\) to a triangulated category \(\mathcal{B}\) is said to be exact if it transforms distinguished triangles into distinguished triangles.

(ii) A contravariant graded functor from a triangulated category \(\mathcal{A}\) to a triangulated category \(\mathcal{B}\) is said to be exact if for every distinguished triangle \((X,Y,Z,u,v,w)\) of \(\mathcal{A}\), the triangle \((F(Z), F(Y), F(X), F(v), F(u), TF(w))\) is distinguished (in this definition, one identifies \(F X\) with \(T F T X\) by means of the grading of \(F\)).

(iii) Let \((\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}\) be a finite family of triangulated categories, \(\varepsilon\) a function from \(I\) to \(\{+1, -1\}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) a triangulated category. A graded functor \(F\) from the product of the \(\mathcal{A}_i\) to \(\mathcal{A}\), covariant in the \(i\) such that \(\varepsilon(i) = 1\) and contravariant in the \(i\) such that \(\varepsilon(i) = -1\), is said to be exact if, whatever \(i \in I\), the functors from \(\mathcal{A}_i\) to \(\mathcal{A}\) deduced from \(F\) by fixing all the variables except the \(i\)-th are exact functors.
A composite of exact functors is again an exact functor.
1.1.4. If \((K^{n_1 \ldots n_p}, d_1, \ldots, d_p)\) is a multiple complex (0.4), the associated simple complex is defined by
\[(1.1.4.0)\qquad K^n = \prod_{\sum n_i = n} K^{(n_i)} \, , \qquad d = \sum d_i \, .\]
When, exceptionally, it is defined by a sum rather than by a product, this fact will be explicitly indicated.
Let \(I\) be a finite set. Following CARTAN-EILENBERG and J.P. SERRE, we propose to explain how to every naive \(I\)-fold complex \(K\) there is canonically associated an \(I\)-fold complex (0.4).
For every total order \(<\) on \(I\), let \(K(<)\) be the following \(I\)-fold complex:
\[(1.1.4.1)\qquad \begin{cases} K(<)^k = K^k \\[4pt] d(<)_i^k = (-1)^{\sum_{j<i} k_j}\, d_i^k \, . \end{cases}\]
If \(<_1\) and \(<_2\) are two total orders on \(I\), the canonical isomorphism \(\tau\) between \(K(<_1)\) and \(K(<_2)\) is by definition the one given by
\[(1.1.4.2)\qquad \tau^k = (-1)^{\varepsilon(<_1, <_2)} \, , \quad \text{where } \varepsilon(<_1, <_2) = \sum_{\substack{i <_1 j \\ i >_2 j}} k_i k_j \, .\]

1.1.4.2.1. One verifies that these canonical isomorphisms establish a transitive system of isomorphisms between the \(K(<)\) for \(<\) a total order on \(I\); these \(K(<)\) therefore form a single \(I\)-fold complex, unique up to unique isomorphism, which we shall denote in this no. by the notation \(K(*)\) and which we call the \(I\)-fold complex associated with the naive \(I\)-fold complex \(K\). One should be careful that \(K(*)\) is not canonically isomorphic to \(K\): only the choice of a total order on \(I\) allows one to identify these two objects.
If \(K\) is a naive \(I\)-fold complex, and if \(i \in I\), we denote by \(K[1_i]\) the following naive complex, with differentials denoted \(d_j[1_i]\):
\[(1.1.4.3)\qquad \begin{cases} K[1_i]^k = K^{k+1_i} \\[4pt] d_j[1_i]^k = d_j^{k+1_i} & \text{if } i \neq j \\[4pt] d_i[1_i]^k = -d_i^{k+1_i} \, . \end{cases}\]
If \(K\) is an \(I\)-fold complex, one sets
\[(1.1.4.4)\qquad \begin{cases} K[1_i]^k = K^{k+1_i} \\[4pt] d_j[1_i]^k = -d_j^{k+1_i} \, . \end{cases}\]

If \(K\) is a naive \(I\)-fold complex and \(<\) a total order on \(I\), so that \(K(*)\) is given by (1.1.4.1), one defines an isomorphism \(\sigma\) between \(K[1_i](*)\) and \(K(*)[1_i]\) by the formula
1.1.4.6. One verifies that this isomorphism does not depend on the choice of the total order \(<\); it therefore defines an isomorphism, called canonical, between \(K[1_i](*)\) and \(K(*)[1_i]\).

Lemma 1.1.5.4

(i) For every additive contravariant functor \(F : \mathcal{A} \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\), the formulas 1.1.5.1, 1.1.5.2 define an exact contravariant functor from \(K(\mathcal{A})\) to \(K(\mathcal{B})\).

(ii) For every pair \((G,F)\) of composable additive contravariant functors, the formula (1.1.5.3) defines an isomorphism of graded functors between the extension to complexes of \(GF\) and the composite of the extensions to complexes of \(G\) and \(F\).
Proof. A morphism of degree \(i\): \(f : K \longrightarrow L\) is, at will,

1. (a) a morphism from \(K\) to \(L[i]\)
  2. (b) a morphism from \(K[-i]\) to \(L\)
  3. (c) a family \(f^n : K^n \longrightarrow L^{n+i}\) which commutes or anticommutes with the differentials according to the parity of \(i\).
If \(f : K \longrightarrow L[i]\) is a morphism of degree \(i\), then \(F(f) : F(L)[-i] \longrightarrow K\) is again a morphism of degree \(i\); for \(i=1\), one has

If \(0 \longrightarrow K \xrightarrow{u} L \xrightarrow{v} M \longrightarrow 0\) is an exact sequence of complexes split degree by degree, the choice of a splitting allows one to write the differential of \(L\) in the form
where \(f\) is a morphism of degree one from \(M\) to \(K\). Likewise, the dual exact sequence
\[0 \longrightarrow F(M) \longrightarrow F(L) \longrightarrow F(K) \longrightarrow 0\]

1.1.6. Let \(s = +\), or \(s = -\); let \(I\) be a finite set, \(\varepsilon : I \longrightarrow \{+,-\}\) a function, \((\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) additive categories, and \(F\) a multiadditive multifunctor from the categories \(\mathcal{A}_i\) to \(\mathcal{A}\), covariant in the arguments of index \(i\) such that \(\varepsilon(i) = +\) and contravariant in the others. We propose to define the extension \(K^s(F)\) (or simply \(F\)) of \(F\) to complexes as an exact multifunctor from the categories \(K^{s\varepsilon(i)}(\mathcal{A}_i)\) (\(s\varepsilon(i) = \pm\), according to the rule of signs) to \(K^s(\mathcal{A})\) having the same variance as \(F\) (∗). We shall then explain in what sense this construction is compatible with the composition of functors. Other conventions of degrees are possible, and will be used; this point is independent of the questions of sign considered here.
1.1.6.1. If \(F\) is contravariant in one variable, one defines \(K^s(F)\) by the formulas (1.1.5).

1.1.6.2. If \(F\) is covariant, one defines the functor \(K^s(F)\) by passage to the quotient from the composite of the obvious functor from the product of the categories \(C^s(\mathcal{A}_i)\) to the category of naive \(I\)-fold complexes, of the functor (1.1.4) from the category of naive \(I\)-fold complexes to that of \(I\)-fold complexes (1.1.4.2.1), and of the associated simple complex functor (1.1.4.0):
Let \(K_j \in K^s(\mathcal{A}_j)\) be complexes, and \(i \in I\); one sets \(K_j[1_i] = K_j\) for \(j \neq i\), and \(K_i[1_i] = K_i[1]\). One then has obvious isomorphisms:

1.1.6.3. In the general case, \(F\) is the product of canonical contravariant functors \(\mathcal{A}_i \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}_i^o\) (for \(\varepsilon(i) = -\)) and of a covariant functor \(F^+\); one defines the functor \(K^s(F)\) by composition from 1.1.6.1 and 1.1.6.2.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.1.7

Under the preceding hypotheses, the functor \(K^s(F)\) is an exact multiadditive functor.

It suffices to verify 1.1.7 under the hypotheses of 1.1.6.1 (where the proposition is 1.1.5.4 (i)) or of 1.1.6.2. To verify that the functors deduced from \(K^s(F)\) by fixing all the variables except the \(i\)-th are exact, one may make \(K^s(F)\) explicit in terms of an order on \(I\) for which \(i\) is the smallest element; a distinguished triangle of type (1.1.1.1) is then transformed into a distinguished triangle of that type.

1.1.8. Let \(I\) and \(J\) be two finite sets, \(\psi : I \longrightarrow J\) a surjective map, \(\varepsilon_I : I \longrightarrow \{+,-\}\) and \(\varepsilon_J : J \longrightarrow \{+,-\}\) functions, and multiadditive multifunctors, covariant in the arguments for which \(\varepsilon = +\) and contravariant in the others:
\[G_j : \prod_{\psi(i)=j} \mathcal{A}_i \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}_j \qquad (j \in J)\] \[F : \prod_{j \in J} \mathcal{B}_j \longrightarrow \mathcal{C}\]

Let us choose total orders on \(I\) and \(J\), in such a way that \(\psi\) is an increasing map. One then defines the canonical isomorphism \(\rho\) between the extension to complexes of \(F \circ (G_j)\) and the composite of the extensions to complexes of \(F\) and of the \(G_j\) by the formula
\[(1.1.8.1)\qquad \rho^k = \prod_i \eta_i^{k_i} \; : \; \text{automorphism of } F \circ (G_j)\big(K_i^{k_i}\big)^{\varepsilon(i)\,\varepsilon(\psi(i))}\]
with \(\eta_i = -1\) if \(\varepsilon_I(i) = \varepsilon_J(\psi(i)) = -\), \(\eta_i = 1\) otherwise.
This formula generalizes (1.1.5.3); one verifies that \(\rho\) does not depend on the orders chosen on \(I\) and \(J\), and is an isomorphism of graded functors (cf. 1.1.5.4 (ii)).
These isomorphisms \(\rho\) satisfy the obvious cocycle condition for a triple composite.

1.1.9. Let \(I\) be a finite set, \(i\) and \(j\) two distinct elements of \(I\), \(I' = I \smallsetminus \{i,j\}\), \((\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) additive categories and \(F : (\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I} \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}\) and \(G : (\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I'} \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}\) multiadditive multifunctors. Assume that \(\mathcal{A}_i = \mathcal{A}_j\) and that \(F\) is contravariant in the \(i\)-th variable and covariant in the \(j\)-th. For \(X, Y \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}_i\), we shall denote by \(F_{X,Y}\) the multifunctor from the \((\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I'}\) to \(\mathcal{A}\) obtained by fixing the \(i\)-th and \(j\)-th arguments:
\[F_{X,Y}(\ldots) = F(\ldots X, \ldots, Y, \ldots) \, .\]
We call contraction morphism \(c : F \longrightarrow G\) the datum, for every \(X \in \mathcal{A}_i\), of a morphism of functors
\[c_X : F_{X,X} \longrightarrow G \, ,\]
such that for every arrow \(f: X \longrightarrow Y\) of \(\mathcal{A}_i\), the diagram
\[\xymatrix{ F_{Y,X} \ar[r] \ar[d] & F_{X,X} \ar[d]^{c_X} \\ F_{Y,Y} \ar[r]_{c_Y} & G }\]
is commutative.
The conventions 1.1.6 are motivated by the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.1.9.1

Let \(c : F \longrightarrow G\) be a contraction morphism and \((K_\ell)_{\ell \in I}\) complexes in the \(\mathcal{A}_\ell\), with \(K_i = K_j\). Let \(<\) be a total order on \(I\) for which \(i\) is the predecessor of \(j\). Let, with the notation of 1.1.6, for \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\),

\[c^k : K^s(F)(K_\ell)^k \longrightarrow K^s(G)(K_\ell)^k\]

be the morphism whose restriction to \(F(\ldots K_i^{k_i}\, K_j^{k_j} \ldots)\) equals \(0\) if \(k_i \neq k_j\), and equals \(c_{K_i^{k_i}}\) if \(k_i = k_j\). Then \((c^k)_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}\) is a morphism of complexes.
We leave to the reader the task of verifying this lemma, and the fact that the contraction morphism \((c^k)\) does not depend on the order chosen on \(I\).
The standard example of a contraction morphism is that of the composition law
\[\operatorname{Hom}(Y,Z) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}(X,Y) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(X,Z)\]

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.html:
Examples 1.1.10

(i) If one applies the definitions of 1.1.6 to the tensor product functor, one recovers the usual notion of tensor product of two complexes, the differential being given by

\[d(x \otimes y) = dx \otimes y + (-1)^{\deg x} x \otimes dy \, .\]

(ii) If one applies the definitions of 1.1.6 to the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\), considering \(Y\) as the first variable and \(X\) as the second variable, a convention we shall always follow, this convention allows one to identify, for two complexes \(X,Y\), the \(k\)-th component of the complex \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\) defined in 1.1.6 with \(\prod_n \operatorname{Hom}(X^n, Y^{n+k})\), and one recovers the usual differential; for \(f \in \operatorname{Hom}(X^n, Y^{n+k})\), one has

\[df = d \circ f - (-1)^k f \circ d \, .\]

(iii) The preceding conventions have the virtue that the following systems of arrows are morphisms of complexes, without one having to perturb them by any sign (1.1.9):

\[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(L,M) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(K,L) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(K,M) : f \otimes g \mapsto f \circ g\]

\[\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(L,M) \otimes L \longrightarrow M : f \otimes x \mapsto f(x) \, .\]

∗ 1.1.10.1. The convention (1.1.4.5)-(1.1.6.2) is justified as follows, for \(F = \otimes\): an element of \(((K \otimes L)[1])^n\) is written in the form (1.1.2) (recalling that \((K \otimes L)[1] = C(K \otimes L \longrightarrow 0)\) (1.1.1.1)) \(\sum 1 \otimes (x^p \otimes y^q)\), an element of \((K[1] \otimes L)^n\) in the form \(\sum (1 \otimes x^p) \otimes y^q\) and an element of \((K \otimes L[1])^n\) in the form \(\sum x^p \otimes (1 \otimes y^q)\); the sign appears when one interchanges \(x^p\) and \(1\). For \(F = \text{dual}\), the convention (1.1.5.2) is justified thus: an element of \(K^*[1]\) is written \(1 \otimes \omega\); its value on an element \(1' \otimes x\) of \(K[-1]\) (\(1'\) a cell of dimension \(-1\)) is \(\langle 1 \otimes \omega, 1' \otimes x \rangle = (-1)^{\deg \omega} \langle 1, 1' \rangle \cdot \langle \omega, x \rangle = (-1)^{\deg \omega} \langle \omega, x \rangle\); this is the convention adopted. ∗

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.1.11

"Recall" that a sub-additive category is a category whose sets of arrows \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\) are equipped with abelian group laws, the composition of morphisms being biadditive. An additive functor \(F\) between sub-additive categories is a functor which satisfies the formula

\[F(f + g) = F(f) + F(g)\]

for \(f,g \in \operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\). The additive functors from a sub-additive category \(\mathcal{A}\) to another \(\mathcal{B}\) form a category, denoted \(\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathrm{add}}(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B})\).
Let \((D)\) be the unique sub-additive category, with set of objects indexed by \(\mathbb{Z}\), \((X^n)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\), with

\[(1.1.11.1)\qquad \begin{cases} \operatorname{Hom}(X^n, X^n) = \mathbb{Z} \, , \text{ generated by the identity} \\[4pt] \operatorname{Hom}(X^n, X^{n+1}) = \mathbb{Z} \, , \text{ generated by an arrow denoted } d_n \\[4pt] \operatorname{Hom}(X^i, X^j) = 0 \text{ if } j - i \neq 0 \text{ or } 1 \, . \end{cases}\]
Let \(D\) be the complex of \((D)\) defined by \(D^n = X^n\) and \(d^n = d_n\).
For every sub-additive category \(\mathcal{A}\), the functor \(G \mapsto G(D)\) from \(\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathrm{add}}((D), \mathcal{A})\) to \(C(\mathcal{A})\) is an isomorphism.
The construction 1.1.6 extends to the case of a multiadditive functor from sub-additive categories \(\mathcal{A}_i\) to an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\).
Let
\[F^\bullet = (F^n, d^n)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\]

be a complex of multiadditive functors from additive categories \(\mathcal{A}_i\) to an additive category \(\mathcal{A}\). One may regard \(F^\bullet\) as a functor from \((D)\) to a category of multifunctors, or again as a multiadditive functor
\[F_1 : \textstyle\prod \mathcal{A}_i \times (D) \longrightarrow \mathcal{A} \, .\]
One defines the extension of \(F\) to complexes by the formula
\[(1.1.11.2)\qquad F^\bullet(K_1 \ldots K_n) = F_1(K_1 \ldots K_n, D) \, .\]
1.1.12. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) be two additive categories and
\[F^\bullet = (F^n, d^n)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\]

a complex of additive functors from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\). Suppose that the functors \(F^i\) admit right adjoints \(F_i\); if \({}^t d^i : F_{i+1} \longrightarrow F_i\) is the transpose of \(d^i\), let \(F_\bullet\) be the complex of additive functors from \(\mathcal{B}\) to \(\mathcal{A}\), with components the \(F_i\), and with differential operator
\[(d_\bullet)^i = (-1)^{i+1}\, {}^t d^{-i-1} : F_{-i} \longrightarrow F_{-i-1}\]
Let \({}^t\) be the contravariant functor from \((D)\) to \((D)\) given by
\[{}^t X^n = X^{-n} \quad \text{and} \quad {}^t d^n = d^{-n-1} \, .\]
The following diagram is commutative up to canonical isomorphism

\[(1.1.12.1)\qquad \xymatrix@C=3em{ \mathcal{A} \times (D) \times \mathcal{B} \ar[r]^-{(F^n(A), \mathrm{Id})} \ar[d]_-{(\mathrm{Id}, {}^t, \mathrm{Id})} & \mathcal{B} \times \mathcal{B} \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{B}}} & (\mathrm{Ab}) \ar@{=}[d] \\ \mathcal{A} \times (D) \times \mathcal{B} \ar[r]_-{(\mathrm{Id}, (F_\bullet)^n(B))} & \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{A} \ar[r]_-{\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}} & (\mathrm{Ab}) }\]
This expresses the adjunction formula
\[(1.1.12.2)\qquad \operatorname{Hom}(F^n(A), B) \; \overset{\sim}{\longleftrightarrow} \; \operatorname{Hom}(A, F_n(B)) \, .\]
The general conventions 1.1.3 therefore furnish an isomorphism
\[(1.1.12.3)\qquad \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(F^\bullet(K), L) \; \overset{\sim}{\longleftrightarrow} \; \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(K, F_\bullet(L)) \, .\]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1.13

If \(K\) is a complex of an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\), we call right (resp. left) truncation of \(K\) in dimension \(n\), and denote by \(\tau_{\leqslant n}(K)\) (resp. \(\tau_{\geqslant n}(K)\)) the following complexes

\[\tau_{\leqslant n}(K) : \; \ldots K^{n-2} \longrightarrow K^{n-1} \longrightarrow \operatorname{Ker}(d^n) \longrightarrow 0\]

\[\tau_{\geqslant n}(K) : \; 0 \longrightarrow \operatorname{coker}(d^{n-1}) \longrightarrow K^{n+1} \longrightarrow K^{n+2} \ldots \, .\]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.1.14

(i) \(H^i(\tau_{\leqslant n}(K)) = 0\) for \(i > n\) and \(H^i(\tau_{\geqslant n}(K)) = 0\) for \(i < n\).

(ii) The canonical morphism \(\tau_{\leqslant n}(K) \longrightarrow K\) (resp. \(K \longrightarrow \tau_{\geqslant n} K\)) induces isomorphisms on the \(H^i\) for \(i \leqslant n\) (resp. \(i \geqslant n\)).

The functor \(\tau_{\leqslant n}\) (resp. \(\tau_{\geqslant n}\)) transforms homotopic morphisms into homotopic morphisms. Consequently, it follows from 1.1.4 that the functor 1.1.13 keeps a meaning in the derived category.
1.1.15. If \(K\) is a double complex, with first (resp. second) differential \(d'\) (resp. \(d''\)), we denote by \(\tau''_{\leqslant n}(K)\) the double subcomplex of \(K\) such that
\[\tau''_{\leqslant n}(K)^{pq} = \begin{cases} K^{pq} & \text{if } q < n \\[4pt] \operatorname{Ker}(d'') & \text{if } q = n \\[4pt] 0 & \text{if } q > n \end{cases}\]
one defines in the same way \(\tau''_{\geqslant n}(K)\), \(\tau'_{\leqslant n}(K)\) and \(\tau'_{\geqslant n}(K)\).
1.1.16. We shall also have to consider the "stupid truncations" of a complex \(K\), defined by

\[\sigma_{\leqslant n}(K)^i = \begin{cases} K^i & \text{if } i \leqslant n \\[4pt] 0 & \text{if } i > n \end{cases} \qquad\qquad \sigma_{\geqslant n}(K)^i = \begin{cases} K^i & \text{if } i \geqslant n \\[4pt] 0 & \text{if } i < n \end{cases}\]
1.2. Derived functors.

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a triangulated category and \(S\) a saturated multiplicative system (CD 2.1.2). If \(A \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}\), we shall denote by \(A^+\) and \(A^-\) the ind- and pro-objects ((0.5) and (0.6))
\[A^+ = \underset{A \xrightarrow{s} A'}{\text{"}\varinjlim\text{"}}\, A' \qquad\qquad A^- = \underset{A' \xrightarrow{s} A}{\text{"}\varprojlim\text{"}}\, A' \, ,\]
where \(s\) runs through the filtered category of arrows of \(S\) with source or target \(A\).

The functors \(A \mapsto A^+\) and \(A \longrightarrow A^-\) make the elements of \(S\) invertible and define fully faithful functors from \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) to the categories of Ind- and pro-objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) respectively.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.2.1

Let \(F\) be a covariant exact multifunctor from the triangulated categories \((\mathcal{A}_i)_{0 \leqslant i \leqslant n}\) to the triangulated category \(\mathcal{A}\) and let \(S_i\) and \(S\) be saturated multiplicative systems of the categories \(\mathcal{A}_i\) and \(\mathcal{A}\).

(i) The right derived functor \(RF\) of \(F\) (relative to the \(S_i\) and to \(S\)) is the functor from the categories \(\mathcal{A}_i(S_i^{-1})\) to the category of Ind-objects of \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) which makes the following diagram commutative

\[\xymatrix{ (\mathcal{A}_i) \ar[r]^-{(A_i) \,\mapsto\, F(A_i^+)} \ar[d] & \operatorname{Ind} \mathcal{A} \ar[d] \\ \mathcal{A}_i(S_i^{-1}) \ar[r]_-{RF} & \operatorname{Ind} \mathcal{A}(S^{-1}) \, . }\]

(ii) We say that \(RF\) is defined at \((A_i)\) if the Ind-object \(RF(A_i)\) of \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) is "essentially constant", i.e. comes from an object of \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\); this object is called the value of \(RF\) at \((A_i)\).

(iii) We say that \(F\) is right derivable if \(RF\) is everywhere defined; we shall then again denote by \(RF\) the functor from the \(\mathcal{A}_i(S_i^{-1})\) to \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) which it defines.

(iv) A family \((A_i)\) of objects of the \(\mathcal{A}_i\) is said to be split for \(RF\) if the canonical morphism from \(F(A_i)\) to \(RF(A_i)\) is an isomorphism.

We leave to the reader the task of defining by duality the left derived functor \(LF\) of \(F\) (with values in Pro \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\)) and of extending the preceding definitions to the cases where \(F\) is covariant in certain arguments and contravariant in others.
When \(RF\) is everywhere defined, the definition we have given of it here coincides with that of Verdier (CD p.39), as one verifies easily.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2.2

Let \((A_1', A_1, A_1'')\) be a distinguished triangle in \(\mathcal{A}_1\), and \(A_i \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}_i\) (\(i \neq 1\)).

(i) If \((A_1',(A_i))\) and \((A_1'',(A_i))\) are split for \(RF\), then the family \((A_1,(A_i))\) is so too.

(ii) If \(RF\) is defined at \((A_1',(A_i))\) and at \((A_1'',(A_i))\), it is so also at \((A_1,(A_i))\) and the triangle \((RF(A_1',(A_i)), RF(A_1,(A_i)), RF(A_1'',(A_i)))\) is distinguished in \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\).
Let us prove that (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i). Since \(F\) is exact, the arrow
is a morphism of distinguished triangles. By hypothesis, this arrow is an isomorphism at two vertices; it is therefore one at the third, as was wanted.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.2.2.1

If \(\Delta = (X,Y,Z)\) is a distinguished triangle of a triangulated category \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(S\) a saturated multiplicative system of \(\mathcal{A}\), then the triangle \(\Delta^+ = (X^+, Y^+, Z^+)\) of Ind \(\mathcal{A}\) is a limit of distinguished triangles of \(\mathcal{A}\).
Let us denote by \(\mathcal{L}\) the category of morphisms of distinguished triangles with source \(\Delta\) whose arrows belong to \(S\).

(a) If \(\Delta = (X,Y,Z)\) and \(\Delta' = (X',Y',Z')\) are two distinguished triangles of \(\mathcal{A}\) and if \(f : \Delta \longrightarrow \Delta'\) is an \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\)-morphism of triangles, there exist in \(\mathcal{A}\) morphisms of triangles \(s : \Delta' \longrightarrow \Delta''\) and \(f_1 : \Delta \longrightarrow \Delta''\) such that the components of \(s\) are in \(S\) and such that the diagram
\[(1)\qquad \xymatrix{ \Delta \ar[d]_{f} \ar[dr]^{f_1} & \\ \Delta' \ar[r]_{s} & \Delta'' }\]
is commutative in \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\).
There exists a commutative diagram
\[(2)\qquad \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]_{f} \ar[dr]^{f_1} & \\ X' \ar[r]_{s} & X'' } \qquad\qquad (s \in S, \; f_1 \in \operatorname{Fl} \mathcal{A})\]

and a morphism \(\Delta' \xrightarrow{s_1} \Delta_1''\) in \(S\), admitting \(s\) as component. Arguing likewise at the other vertices: one obtains a diagram of type (1), in which, however, \(f_1\) is not yet a morphism of triangles in \(\mathcal{A}\), the diagrams
\[(3)\qquad \xymatrix{ Z \ar[r]^{f} \ar[d]_{w} & Z_o'' \ar[d]^{w'} \\ X \ar[r]_{f} & X_o'' }\]

for example possibly failing to be commutative in \(\mathcal{A}\), only in \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\). There exists \(t_o : X_o'' \longrightarrow X_1''\) in \(S\) such that \(t_o\, w' f = t_o\, f w\) and \(t : \Delta_o'' \longrightarrow \Delta_1''\) admitting \(t_o\) as component. Let us replace \(\Delta_o''\) by \(\Delta_1''\), \(s\) by \(ts\) and \(f_1\) by \(tf_1\); in the diagram of type (1) obtained, (3) is this time commutative; proceeding likewise at the other vertices, one obtains (1). We leave to the reader the task of verifying likewise:

(b) If \(f,g : \Delta \rightrightarrows \Delta'\) are two morphisms of distinguished triangles in \(\mathcal{A}\), equal in \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\), then there exists a morphism of distinguished triangles with arrows in \(S\), \(s : \Delta' \longrightarrow \Delta''\), such that \(Sf = Sg\).
(c) The category \(\mathcal{L}\) is right filtered.
(d) One completes the proof of the lemma by noting that
\[\Delta^+ = \underset{s \in \mathcal{L}}{\text{"}\varinjlim\text{"}} (\text{target of } s) \, .\]

Let us prove 1.2.2 (ii). Let \(X'\) and \(X''\) be objects of \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) representing \(RF(A_1',(A_i))\) and \(RF(A_1'',(A_i))\), and let us complete the morphism of degree 1 from \(X''\) to \(X'\) into a distinguished triangle \((X',X,X'')\). Replacing the \(A_i\), \(A_1'\), \(A_1\) and \(A_1''\) by the target of an arrow of \(S\) with source \(A_i\), \(A_1'\), \(A_1\) or \(A_1''\), one reduces to the case where there exists a commutative diagram

where \(a''\) and \(a'\) are sections of arrows from \(F(A_1'',(A_i))\) to \(X''\) and from \(F(A_1',(A_i))\) to \(X'\). By virtue of axiom TR 3 of [C.D] one may complete this diagram into a morphism of triangles

The composite arrow is a morphism of triangles, whose source is a distinguished triangle and whose target is a limit (in Ind \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\)) of distinguished triangles (1.2.2.1). For every \(Y\) in \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\), the following diagram is commutative and its rows are exact

\[\xymatrix@C=1em@R=2.5em{ \operatorname{Hom}(Y,X''[1]) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \operatorname{Hom}(Y,X') \ar[r] \ar[d] & \operatorname{Hom}(Y,X) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \operatorname{Hom}(Y,X'') \ar[r] \ar[d] & \operatorname{Hom}(Y,X'[1]) \ar[d] \\ \operatorname{Hom}(Y,RF(A_1'',(A_i))[1]) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}(Y,RF(A_1',(A_i))) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}(Y,RF(A_1,(A_i))) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}(Y,RF(A_1'',(A_i))) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}(Y,RF(A_1',(A_i))[1]) }\]

By hypothesis, the arrows other than the central arrow are isomorphisms. The five lemma shows that the central arrow is also an isomorphism, for every \(Y\), hence that the distinguished triangle \((X',X,X'')\) is isomorphic to the triangle \((RF(A_1',(A_i)), RF(A_1,(A_i)), RF(A_1'',(A_i)))\). This completes the proof.

If \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) are two abelian categories and \(F\) is an additive covariant functor from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\), then \(F\) defines exact functors from \(K(\mathcal{A})\) to \(K(\mathcal{B})\), from \(K^+(\mathcal{A})\) to \(K^+(\mathcal{B})\), and from \(K^-(\mathcal{A})\) to \(K^-(\mathcal{B})\) (1.1.7).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.2.3

(i) We call right derived functors of \(F\) the functors from \(D^+(\mathcal{A})\) to Ind \(D^+(\mathcal{B})\) and from \(D(\mathcal{A})\) to Ind \(D(\mathcal{B})\) that are the right derived functors of the extensions of \(F\) to the complexes \(K^+(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow K^+(\mathcal{B})\) and \(K(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow K(\mathcal{B})\).

(ii) An object \(A\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) is said to be right-acyclic for \(F\), or, by abuse of language, acyclic for \(RF\), if the complex reduced to \(A\) in degree \(0\) is split for \(RF\).

We shall be interested chiefly in the case where \(RF\) is everywhere defined; one can then regard it as a functor from \(D^+(\mathcal{A})\) to \(D^+(\mathcal{B})\), or from \(D(\mathcal{A})\) to \(D(\mathcal{B})\), as the case may be.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2.4

The following diagram is commutative.

\[\xymatrix{ D^+(\mathcal{A}) \ar[r] \ar[d]_{RF} & D(\mathcal{A}) \ar[d]^{RF} \\ \operatorname{Ind} D^+(\mathcal{B}) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Ind} D(\mathcal{B}) \, . }\]

If \(K\) is a complex that is zero in degrees \(< n\) and if \(s : K \longrightarrow L\) is a quasi-isomorphism, then the composite morphism \(K \xrightarrow{s} L \longrightarrow \sigma_{\geqslant n}(L)\) (1.1.16) is again a quasi-isomorphism. The quasi-isomorphisms from \(K\) to a bounded-below complex thus form a (full) cofinal subcategory of the category of all quasi-isomorphisms with source \(K\). The proposition follows formally.

In particular, if the functor \(RF\) is everywhere defined on \(D(\mathcal{A})\), then it is everywhere defined on \(D^+(\mathcal{A})\), and the derived functor \(RF : D^+(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D^+(\mathcal{B})\) is the restriction of the derived functor \(RF : D(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D(\mathcal{B})\).
(1.2.5) We leave to the reader the task of:
(i) generalizing Definition 1.2.3 to the case of a complex of multifunctors, covariant in certain variables and contravariant in others;
(ii) dualizing Definition 1.2.5 (i) to define the left derived functors;
(iii) extending Proposition 1.2.4 to the case of a bounded complex of multifunctors;
(iv) dualizing Proposition 1.2.5 (iii) by considering left derived functors and the inclusion of \(D^-(\mathcal{B})\) into \(D(\mathcal{B})\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2.6

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) be two abelian categories, \(P\) a subset of \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A})\) and \(F\) an additive functor from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\). Suppose that

(a) every object of \(\mathcal{A}\) is a quotient of an element of \(P\)

(b) for every short exact sequence

\[0 \longrightarrow P \longrightarrow Q \longrightarrow R \longrightarrow 0 \, ,\]

where \(Q\) and \(R\) are in \(P\), \(P\) also belongs to \(P\) and the \(0\)-sequence

\[0 \longrightarrow FP \longrightarrow FQ \longrightarrow FR \longrightarrow 0 \quad \underline{\text{is exact}}.\]

Then every object of \(P\) is acyclic for \(LF\).

If \(A \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}\), the left resolutions of \(A\) by objects of \(P\) form a cofinal system in the filtered category of left resolutions of \(A_o\). It therefore suffices to prove that if a complex
\[\ldots \longrightarrow A_2 \longrightarrow A_1 \longrightarrow A_o \longrightarrow A \longrightarrow 0\]
is acyclic and has its objects in \(P\), then its image is acyclic. Cutting it into short exact sequences
\[0 \longrightarrow \operatorname{Im}(d_{i-1}) \longrightarrow A_i \longrightarrow \operatorname{Im}(d_i) \longrightarrow 0 \qquad (1.2.6.\text{ i})\quad (i \geqslant 0)\]
one sees by induction on \(i\) that \(\operatorname{Im}(d_i) \in P\) and that the image of (1.2.6 i) under \(F\) is a short exact sequence. The image of the complex is therefore acyclic.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2.7

Let \(F\) be an additive functor from an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) to an abelian category \(\mathcal{B}\). If every object of \(\mathcal{A}\) is a quotient (resp. subobject) of an object acyclic for \(LF\) (resp. \(RF\)) (1.2.3), then the derived functor \(LF : D^-(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D^-(\mathcal{B})\) (resp. \(RF : D^+(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D^+(\mathcal{B})\)) is everywhere defined, and every complex bounded above (resp. below) of objects acyclic for \(LF\) (resp. \(RF\)) is split.

It suffices to consider the left derived functor \(LF\). If \(K\) is a bounded-above complex, the quasi-isomorphisms \(s : L \longrightarrow K\) with \(L\) bounded above and having acyclic objects form a cofinal system in the category of quasi-isomorphisms with target \(K\). It suffices to show that for \(K\) with acyclic objects, \(F(s) : F(L) \longrightarrow F(K)\) is a quasi-isomorphism; one will then have, in the general case, \(F(L) = LF(K)\). Let \(M\) be the cone of \(s\). The complex has acyclic objects and \(H^*(M) = 0\); we must prove that \(H^*(F(M)) = 0\).

Let \(i\) be an integer. The split complexes form a triangulated subcategory, so that every bounded complex of acyclic objects, in particular \(\tau_{\geqslant i}(M)\), is split. Since \(H^j(\tau_{\geqslant i}(L)) = 0\) for \(j > i\), we have, for \(j > i\), \(H^j(F(M)) = H^j(F(\tau_{\geqslant i}(M))) = H^j LF(\tau_{\geqslant i}(M)) = 0\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2.8

Let \(F^\bullet\) be a bounded-below complex of functors from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\). If for every \(K \in K^+(\mathcal{A})\) there exists a quasi-isomorphism \(L \xrightarrow{s} K\), where \(L \in K^+(\mathcal{A})\) is split for all the \(RF^i\), then the derived functor \(RF^\bullet : D^+(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D^+(\mathcal{B})\) exists, and every bounded-below complex split for all the \(RF^i\) is split for \(RF\).

The proof is left to the reader, as is that of the dual statement, or of the variants obtained by taking \(F\) contravariant, or by taking a bounded complex of functors and working in \(D(\mathcal{A})\) and \(D(\mathcal{B})\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.2.9

Let \(F\) be a functor from \(D^b(\mathcal{A})\) to \(D(\mathcal{B})\) and \(d\) an interval of \(\mathbb{Z}\). We say that \(F\) is of cohomological amplitude \(\subset d\) if for every \(A \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}\), \(H^i F(A) = 0\) for \(i \notin d\).

Very often, \(d\) will be an interval of the form \([0,x]\) or \([-x,0]\), and one then says that \(F\) is of cohomological, resp. homological, dimension \(\leqslant x\). One says that \(F\) is of finite dimension if there exists a finite interval \(d\) of \(\mathbb{Z}\) such that \(F\) is of amplitude \(\subset d\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2.10

Suppose the hypotheses of 1.2.7 are satisfied, and that the functor \(RF : D^+(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D^+(\mathcal{B})\) (resp. \(LF : D^-(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D^-(\mathcal{B})\)) is of finite dimension. Then every complex of objects acyclic for \(RF\) (resp. \(LF\)) is split, and the functor \(RF : D(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D(\mathcal{B})\) (resp. \(LF : D(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D(\mathcal{B})\)) is everywhere defined.
For the proof, we refer to Verdier [CD]. There is an analogous statement for bounded complexes of functors. One may again replace the exponent \(+\) (resp. \(-\)) by \(b\).

footnotes.html: (∗) The construction also provides an extension of \(F\) to a multifunctor from the categories \(C^{s\varepsilon(i)}(\mathcal{A}_i)\) to \(C^s(\mathcal{A})\).

blocks.html: 2. Categories fibred in derived categories.
2.1. Introduction.
The author insists that the reader refrain from reading this §. In it we give the formalism of the trivial duality theorem, and resolve the perplexity raised by Artin in XII 4.

For the notions of a category over another, of fibred category, of cofibred category, and of cleavage, we refer to SGA 1 VI. Among other things, we establish in this exposé an equivalence between the notions of normalized cleaved fibred categories over a category \(C\), and of pseudo-functor from \(C^o\) to (Cat).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.1.1

If \(X\) is a ringed site, we denote by \(D(X)\) the derived category of the abelian category of sheaves of left modules on \(X\).
When it is necessary to avoid confusion, we write instead \(D(X, \mathcal{A})\), where \(\mathcal{A}\) denotes the sheaf of rings.
If \(f : X \longrightarrow Y\) is a morphism of ringed sites, then \(f\) defines derived functors
\[(1)\qquad Rf_* : D^+(X) \longrightarrow D^+(Y)\] \[(2)\qquad Lf^* : D^-(Y) \longrightarrow D^-(X) \, ,\]
and, by passing to the opposite categories, functors
\[(1^o)\qquad Rf_* : D^+(X)^o \longrightarrow D^+(Y)^o\] \[(2^o)\qquad Lf^* : D^-(Y)^o \longrightarrow D^-(X)^o \, ,\]

"functorial" in \(f\). More precisely, (1°) and (2°) define two pseudo-functors from the category of sites to that of triangulated categories, one covariant and the other contravariant. One thus obtains two categories over that of sites: one cofibred, with fibres the \(D^+(X)^o\) and with direct-image functors the \(Rf_*\); the other fibred, with fibres the \(D^-(X)^o\) and with inverse-image functors the \(Lf^*\). If the functor \(f^*\) is of finite homological dimension (i.e. of "finite Tor-dimension"), one may in (2) replace the exponent by an exponent \(+\). One thus obtains two categories over the category \(\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{tdf}}\) of ringed sites and morphisms of ringed sites of finite Tor-dimension, categories whose fibres are the categories \(D^+(X)^o\). VERDIER's "trivial duality theorem" ([CD] p. 48) expresses that these two categories are canonically isomorphic; they are therefore fibred and cofibred; the "direct-image" functors are the functors \(Rf_*\)(sic), and the "inverse-image" functors are the functors \(Lf^*\)(sic).

2.1.2. The language of fibred categories allows one to resolve easily the perplexity raised by ARTIN in XII 4: it suffices to apply the following proposition to the category, fibred and cofibred over that of sites, whose fibres are the opposites of the categories of sheaves on the corresponding sites (cf. 0.2).

Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a category over \(\mathcal{B}\), \(f: y \longrightarrow x\) an arrow of \(\mathcal{B}\), and \(F \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{E}_x)\). Recall that a pair \((G,\varphi)\) (\(G \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{E}_y\), \(\varphi \in \operatorname{Hom}_f(G,F)\)) is an inverse image in the strict sense of \(F\) by \(f\) if, for all \(g: Z \longrightarrow y\) and \(H \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{E}_Z\), one has
\[\operatorname{Hom}_g(H,G) \xrightarrow[\;\sim\;]{\varphi} \operatorname{Hom}_{fg}(H,F) \, .\]
Likewise for direct images. If \(\mathcal{E}\) is fibred or cofibred over \(\mathcal{B}\), this notion reduces to that of inverse image.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.1.3

Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a category over \(\mathcal{B}\), \(y \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{B}\), \(F \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{E}_y\) and a commutative diagram in \(\mathcal{B}\) :

\[(2.1.3.1)\qquad \xymatrix{ y' \ar[r]^{g'} \ar[d]_{f'} & y \ar[d]^{f} \\ x' \ar[r] & x \, . }\]

Suppose that the direct and inverse images \(f_*F\), \(g^*f_*F\), \(g'^*F\) and \(f'_* g'^*F\) exist in the strict sense. Then there exists one and only one arrow \(\varphi \in \operatorname{Fl} \mathcal{E}_{x'}\), called the base-change arrow, making the following diagram commutative

\[(2.1.3.2)\qquad \xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=1.5em{ g'^*F \ar[rr] \ar[d] & & F \ar[d] \\ f'_* g'^*F \ar[dr]_{\varphi} & & f_*F \\ & g^*f_*F \ar[ur] & }\]

If moreover the direct images \(g'_*g'^*F\) and \(g'_*f'_*g'^*F\) exist in the strict sense, then the arrow \(\varphi\) coincides with the one defined in XII 4. If \(f'^*f_*g'^*F\) and \(f'^*f'_*F\) exist in the strict sense, it again coincides with the second arrow defined in XII 4.
In particular, the two base-change arrows of XII 4 coincide.
By hypothesis, the arrows of the diagram (2.1.3.2) induce bijections

\[\operatorname{Hom}_y(F,F) = \operatorname{Hom}_{g'}(g'^*F,F) = \operatorname{Hom}_{g'}(g'^*F, f_*F) \quad \text{and}\] \[\operatorname{Hom}_{x'}(f'_*g'^*F, g^*f_*F) = \operatorname{Hom}_{f'}(g'^*F, g^*f_*F) = \operatorname{Hom}_{gf'}(g'^*F, f_*F) \, .\]
Since \(fg' = gf'\), \(\operatorname{Hom}_{fg'}(g'^*F, f_*F)\) is identical to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{gf'}(g'^*F, f_*F)\), and the arrows of the diagram (2.1.3.2) induce bijections
\[\operatorname{Hom}_y(F,F) = \operatorname{Hom}_{fg'}(g'^*F, f_*F) = \operatorname{Hom}_{x'}(f'_*g'^*F, g^*f_*F),\]
and the image of \(1_F\) is the only arrow of \(\mathcal{E}_{x'}\) making (2.1.3.2) commutative.
By definition, in XII 4, the base-change arrow \(\psi\) was the one making the following diagram commutative

\[(2.1.3.3)\quad \xymatrix@C=1.3em@R=3em{ f'_*g'^*F \ar[d]_{\psi} & g'^*F \ar[l] \ar@{=}[r] \ar[d]|-{u_4} & g'^*F \ar[r] \ar[d]|-{u_3} & F \ar@{=}[r] \ar[d]|-{u_2} & F \ar[d]^{u_1} \\ g^*f_*F & f'^*g^*f_*F \ar[l] & g^*f_*f^*F \ar[l] & f'^*f_*F \ar[l] \ar[r] & f_*F }\]

The horizontal arrows and \(u_1\) are the canonical arrows; \(u_2\) is thus the adjunction arrow, \(u_3 = g^*(u_2)\), \(u_4\) is deduced from the isomorphism between \(f'^*g^*\) and \(g'^*f^*\), and the arrow \(\psi\) is deduced from \(u_4\) by adjunction.

The composite map with source \(g'^*F\) and target \(f_*F\) is the one appearing in (2.1.3.2), and it is therefore the same in the following commutative diagram, whose left-hand square is extracted from (2.1.3.3)
\[\xymatrix{ g'^*F \ar[r]^-{u_4} \ar[d] & f'^*g^*f_*F \ar[r] \ar[d] & f_*F \ar@{=}[d] \\ f'_*g'^*F \ar[r]_-{\psi} & g^*f_*F \ar[r] & f_*F }\]
This means that \(\psi\) satisfies the characteristic property of \(\varphi\).
The definition of \(\varphi\) is self-dual, which dispenses with proving the second part of 2.1.3.
2.2. Categories fibred in triangulated categories.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.2.1

By an "additive category over a category \(\mathcal{B}\)" we mean a category \(\mathcal{A}\) over \(\mathcal{B}\) whose sets of arrows \(\operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y)\) (for \(f \in \operatorname{Fl}(\mathcal{B})\), \(X\) (resp. \(Y\)) lying above the source (resp. the target) of \(f\)) have been endowed with abelian group laws, in such a way that:

(i) For all \(x \xrightarrow{f} y \xrightarrow{g} z\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) and \(X, Y, Z\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) above \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) respectively, the composition law

\[\operatorname{Hom}_g(Y,Z) \times \operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y) \xrightarrow{\;\circ\;} \operatorname{Hom}_{gf}(X,Z) \quad \text{is biadditive.}\]

(ii) The fibre categories are additive.

We shall not need to use here that these abelian group laws, when they do exist, are uniquely determined by \(\mathcal{A}\), \(\mathcal{B}\) and \(\rho\). A \(\mathcal{B}\)-functor \(F : \mathcal{A}_1 \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}_2\) between additive categories over \(\mathcal{B}\) is said to be additive if it induces homomorphisms
\[F : \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}_1, f}(X,Y) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}_2, f}(X,Y) \, .\]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.2.2

By an "abelian category over a category \(\mathcal{B}\)" we mean a category \(\mathcal{A}\) additive over \(\mathcal{B}\), whose fibres are abelian, and such that for every arrow \(f: x \longrightarrow y\) of \(\mathcal{B}\) the bifunctor

\[\operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y) : \mathcal{A}_x^o \times \mathcal{A}_y \longrightarrow (\mathrm{Ab})\]

is left exact in \(X\) and \(Y\).

We shall not need to use here that if \(\mathcal{A}\) is a fibred and cofibred category over \(\mathcal{B}\) (SGA 1 VI 6), then it is abelian over \(\mathcal{B}\) as soon as its fibres are abelian categories.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.2.3

By a "triangulated category over a category \(\mathcal{B}\)" we mean a category \(\mathcal{A}\) additive over \(\mathcal{B}\), equipped with a functor \(T : \mathcal{A} \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}\) and whose fibres \(\mathcal{A}_x\) for \(x \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{B}\) are equipped with sets \(\Delta_x\) of triangles, in such a way that:

(i) \(T\) is an additive \(\mathcal{B}\)-automorphism of \(\mathcal{A}\)

(ii) each fibre category \(\mathcal{A}_x\), equipped with the functor \(T_x\) induced by \(T\) and with the set \(\Delta_x\), is a triangulated category (CD 1.1),

(iii) if the triangles \((X,Y,Z,u,v,w)\) and \((X',Y',Z',u',v',w')\) belong to \(\Delta_x\) and \(\Delta_{x'}\), respectively, then every diagram

\[\xymatrix@R=1.8em@C=1.6em{ X \ar[r]^{u} \ar[d]_{f} & Y \ar[r]^{v} \ar[d]^{g} & Z \ar[r]^{w} \ar@{-->}[d]^{h} & X[1] \ar[d]^{f[1]} \\ X' \ar[r]_{u'} & Y' \ar[r]_{v'} & Z' \ar[r]_{w'} & X'[1] }\]

where \(u'f = gu\) can be extended to a morphism of triangles \((f,g,h) : (X,Y,Z) \longrightarrow (X',Y',Z')\).
\(T\) will be called the translation functor; one will often write \(A[1]\) rather than \(T(A)\), \(A[n]\) then denoting \(T^n(A)\) (\(n \in \mathbb{Z}\)).
The triangles belonging to the sets \(\Delta_x\) will be called distinguished or exact.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.2.4

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a triangulated category over \(\mathcal{B}\), \(x\) an object of \(\mathcal{B}\), \((X,Y,Z,u,v,w)\) a distinguished triangle of \(\mathcal{A}_x\). For all \(f: y \longrightarrow x\) and the object \(A \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}_y\), the following infinite sequence is exact

\[\ldots \to \operatorname{Hom}_f(A,X) \to \operatorname{Hom}_f(A,Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}_f(A,Z) \to \operatorname{Hom}_f(A,X[1]) \to \operatorname{Hom}_f(A,Y[1]) \to \ldots\]
Analogous statement for \(f : x \longrightarrow y\) and \(A \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}_y\).
We leave to the reader the task of proving this proposition by paraphrasing VERDIER [CD] p. 4. We also leave to the reader the task of giving a meaning to the following proposition and verifying it:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.2.5

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category (resp. abelian, resp. triangulated) over \(\mathcal{B}\). For every functor \(\mathcal{B}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) with target \(\mathcal{B}\), the category \(\mathcal{A}' = \mathcal{A} \times_{\mathcal{B}} \mathcal{B}'\) is additive (resp. abelian, resp. triangulated) over \(\mathcal{B}'\).

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 2.2.6

The category of sheaves of modules over varying ringed sites is abelian over the category of ringed sites.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 2.2.7

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category over \(\mathcal{B}\). The category \(C(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\) of complexes of \(\mathcal{A}\) over \(\mathcal{B}\) has as objects the complexes of the fibre categories. An arrow \(f\) from \((X^n,d)\) to \((Y^n,d)\) is a system of arrows \(f^n : X^n \longrightarrow Y^n\) such that \(fd^n = f^{n+1} d\). We set \(p(f) = p(f^n)\) (this arrow does not depend on \(n\), since the \(p(d)\) are identities). \(C(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\) is an additive category over \(\mathcal{B}\). We define a "translation" functor by setting

\[(K[1])^n = K^{n+1} \, , \quad (d[1])_n = -d_{n+1} \, .\]

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 2.2.8

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category over \(\mathcal{B}\). The category \(K(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\) of complexes of \(\mathcal{A}\) over \(\mathcal{B}\) up to homotopy has the same objects as \(C(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\). One obtains it by declaring null, in \(C(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\), the arrows homotopic to zero; in other words, for \(f : x \longrightarrow y\) in \(\mathcal{B}\), \(X^\bullet \in \operatorname{Ob} C(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})_x\) and \(Y^\bullet \in \operatorname{Ob} C(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})_y\), we set

\[\operatorname{Hom}_f(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) = H^0 \operatorname{Hom}_f^\bullet(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet)\]

The translation functor passes to the quotient.

If \(F : \mathcal{B}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) is a functor with target \(\mathcal{B}\), and if \(\mathcal{A}' = \mathcal{A} \times_{\mathcal{B}} \mathcal{B}'\), we leave to the reader the task of identifying \(C(\mathcal{A}'/\mathcal{B}')\) with \(C(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B}) \times_{\mathcal{B}} \mathcal{B}'\) and \(K(\mathcal{A}'/\mathcal{B}')\) with \(K(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B}) \times_{\mathcal{B}} \mathcal{B}'\). In particular, the fibres of the category \(K(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\) are the categories \(K(\mathcal{A}_x)\) and, as such, are triangulated.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.2.9

(i) For the additional structures defined in 2.2.8, the category \(K(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\) is triangulated over \(\mathcal{B}\).

(ii) The formation of the additive category (resp. triangulated) \(C(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\) (resp. \(K(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\)) is compatible with any change of base category \(\mathcal{B}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\).
Conditions (i) and (ii) of Definition 2.2.3 are verified fibre by fibre. (iii) is verified by paraphrasing VERDIER [CD] p.4.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.2.10

What precedes applies also to the categories \(K^+(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\), \(K^-(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\) and \(K^b(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B})\) obtained by restricting respectively to complexes bounded below, bounded above, or bounded.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.2.11

Taking for \(\mathcal{B}\) the final category, one recovers the usual categories of complexes.

2.2.12. Let \(F\) be a pseudo-functor from a category \(\mathcal{B}^o\) to (Cat). It is known (SGA 1 VI) that \(F\) defines a fibred category over \(\mathcal{B}\), with fibres the categories \(F(x)\). For all \(f: x \longrightarrow y\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) and \(X \in \operatorname{Ob} F(x)\), \(Y \in \operatorname{Ob} F(y)\), one has by definition
\[(2.2.12.1)\qquad \operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y) = \operatorname{Hom}_{F(x)}(X, F(f)(Y)) \, .\]

It is known (ibidem) that the preceding construction defines an equivalence between the 2-category of pseudo-functors from \(\mathcal{B}^o\) to (Cat) and the 2-category of fibred categories over \(\mathcal{B}\).

Let us start from a pseudo-functor from \(\mathcal{B}^o\) to the 2-category whose objects are the additive (resp. abelian, resp. triangulated) categories and whose 1-arrows are the additive (resp. left exact, resp. triangulated) functors. One checks at once that the category defined by (2.2.12.1) is additive (resp. abelian, resp. triangulated). Conversely:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.2.13

The preceding construction establishes an equivalence between

(a) The 2-category of pseudo-functors from \(\mathcal{B}^o\) to the 2-category whose objects are the additive categories (resp. abelian, resp. triangulated), and whose 1-arrows are the additive functors (resp. left exact, resp. triangulated).

(b) The 2-category of additive categories (resp. abelian, resp. triangulated) over \(\mathcal{B}\), which are fibred over \(\mathcal{B}\).
The theory developed in SGA 1 VI allows one to verify only the following point:

2.2.13.1. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive (resp. abelian, resp. triangulated) category over \(\mathcal{B}\), \(f : x \longrightarrow y\) an arrow of \(\mathcal{B}\), and suppose that an inverse-image functor \(f^* : \mathcal{A}_y \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}_x\) exists; then \(f^*\) is additive (resp. left exact, resp. triangulated).
The functor \(f^*\) gives rise to isomorphisms
\[\operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,f^*(Y)) \, .\]
In the triangulated case, we must prove that \(f^*\) is triangulated for the isomorphism \(Tf^* = f^* T\) (\(T\) the translation functor) which makes the following diagrams commutative

\[(2.2.13.2)\quad \xymatrix@C=2.5em@R=2.5em{ \operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y) \ar@{=}[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,f^*Y) \ar[dr] & \\ \operatorname{Hom}_f(TX,TY) \ar@{=}[r] & \operatorname{Hom}_x(TX, f^*TY) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}_x(TX, Tf^*Y) }\]
Additive case: Consider a diagram
\[(2.2.13.3)\quad \xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ f^*X \ar[r]^{p} \ar@<0.5ex>[d]^{f^*(u)} \ar@<-0.5ex>[d]_{f^*(v)} & X \ar@<0.5ex>[d]^{u} \ar@<-0.5ex>[d]_{v} \\ f^*X' \ar[r]_{p'} & X' }\]
We have \(p'f^*(u+v) = (u+v)p = up+vp = p'f^*(u)+p'f^*(v) = p'(f^*(u) + f^*(v))\), and therefore \(f^*(u+v) = f^*(u) + f^*(v)\).
Abelian case: by definition (2.2), the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,f^*Y) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y)\) is left exact in \(Y\), for every \(X\), hence \(f^*\) is left exact.

Triangulated case: let \((Y',Y,Y'')\) be a distinguished triangle in \(\mathcal{A}_y\) and consider \((f^*Y', f^*Y)\). By virtue of 2.2.3, the canonical morphism between the bases of these triangles can be extended to a morphism of triangles, giving rise to the following diagram
\[\xymatrix@C=1.8em@R=1.8em{ f^*Y' \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & f^*Y \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & X'' \ar[r] \ar[d]^{s} & f^*Y'[1] \ar@{=}[d] \\ f^*Y' \ar[r] & f^*Y \ar[r] & f^*Y'' \ar[r] & f^*Y'[1] }\]
Let us prove that \(s\) is an isomorphism, which will complete the proof. For every \(X\) in \(\operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}_x\), we have the commutative diagram:

\[\xymatrix@C=0.7em@R=2em{ \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,f^*Y') \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,f^*Y) \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,X'') \ar[r] \ar[d] & \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,f^*Y'[1]) \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,f^*Y[1]) \ar@{=}[d] \\ \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,f^*Y') \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,f^*Y) \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,f^*Y'') \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,f^*Y'[1]) \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \operatorname{Hom}_x(X,f^*Y[1]) \ar@{=}[d] \\ \operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y') \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y'') \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y'[1]) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}_f(X,Y[1]) }\]

The first and last rows are exact by virtue of 2.2.4. By virtue of the five lemma, the map induced by \(s\) from \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,X'')\) to \(\operatorname{Hom}(X,f^*Y'')\) is always bijective, and \(s\) is therefore an isomorphism.
One obviously has dual results for cofibred categories.
2.3. Trivial duality formula.

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a category over a base category \(\mathcal{B}\), and let \(S\) be a set of arrows of \(\mathcal{A}\), each projecting onto an identity of \(\mathcal{B}\). The category \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) obtained from \(\mathcal{A}\) by calculus of fractions is a category over \(\mathcal{B}\) (in view of the universal property).

Let \(\mathcal{B}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) be a functor; we denote by \(\mathcal{A}'\) the fibre product \(\mathcal{A} \times_{\mathcal{B}} \mathcal{B}'\) and by \(S'\) the inverse image of \(S\) in \(\mathcal{A}'\). The composite functor \(\mathcal{A}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{A} \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) makes the arrows of \(S'\) invertible, hence factors through \(\mathcal{A}'(S'^{-1})\). One thus obtains a canonical \(\mathcal{B}'\)-functor
\[(2.3.1)\qquad \mathcal{A}'(S'^{-1}) \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}' \times_{\mathcal{B}} \mathcal{A}(S^{-1}) \, .\]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3.2

If \(\mathcal{B}'\) is a subcategory of \(\mathcal{B}\), and if, whenever a composite arrow \(h = f \circ g\) of \(\mathcal{B}\) belongs to \(\mathcal{B}'\), \(f\) and \(g\) belong to \(\mathcal{B}'\), then the functor (2.3.1) is an isomorphism.
Note that (2.3.1) always induces a bijection on objects, and that, in the present case, \(\mathcal{B}' \times_{\mathcal{B}} \mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) is a subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\).

Let us recall the "explicit" construction of \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) [1, Chap. I]. Given two objects \(X\) and \(Y\) of \(\mathcal{A}\), one considers the "formal composites" \(f_1 \ldots f_n\) where each \(f_i\) is either an arrow of \(\mathcal{A}\) or the inverse of an arrow of \(S\). The set \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})}(X,Y)\) is the quotient of the set of these "formal composites" by the equivalence relation generated by the relations

\[\begin{aligned} & f_1 \ldots uv \ldots f_n \equiv f_1 \ldots (u \circ v) \ldots f_n && \text{for } u,v \text{ in } \operatorname{Fl}(\mathcal{A}) \\ & f_1 \ldots ss^{-1} \ldots f_n \equiv f_1 \ldots f_n && \text{for } s \in S \\ & f_1 \ldots s^{-1}s \ldots f_n \equiv f_1 \ldots f_n && \text{for } s \in S \, . \end{aligned}\]

If one applies these constructions to \(\mathcal{A}\) and to the subcategory \(\mathcal{A}'\), one checks that \(\mathcal{A}'(S'^{-1})\) is identical to the subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) that is the inverse image of \(\mathcal{B}'\), by the fact that if a "formal composite" \(f_1 \ldots f_n\) has as its composite in \(\mathcal{B}\) an arrow of \(\mathcal{B}'\), then the image of each \(f_i\) is also an arrow of \(\mathcal{B}'\).

Suppose now that \(\mathcal{A}\) is a triangulated category over \(\mathcal{B}\), and that the sets \(S_x = S \cap \operatorname{Fl}(\mathcal{A}_x)\) for \(x \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\) are saturated multiplicative systems (CD Ch.1 §2.1).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.3.3

Under the preceding hypotheses, the category \(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B}\) will be said to be almost derivable (resp. derivable, resp. coderivable) relative to \(S\) if, for every functor \(F : \mathcal{B}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\), the functor (2.3.1) is an isomorphism (resp. and if \(\mathcal{A}'(S'^{-1})\) is fibred, resp. cofibred over \(\mathcal{B}'\)).
We shall denote by \(I\) the category of the following diagram
\[(2.3.4)\qquad I : \quad x_o \xrightarrow{\;F\;} x_1 \, .\]

By 2.2.13, it amounts to the same thing to give a triangulated category \(\mathcal{A}\) over \(I\), fibred (resp. cofibred) over \(I\), or to give its fibres \(\mathcal{A}_o\) and \(\mathcal{A}_1\) together with the triangulated inverse-image functor \(F^* : \mathcal{A}_1 \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}_o\) (resp. and the triangulated direct-image functor \(F_* : \mathcal{A}_o \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}_1\)). If \(A_o \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}_o\) and \(A_1 \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}_1\), one has (2.2.12.1)
\[\operatorname{Hom}_F(A_o, A_1) = \operatorname{Hom}(A_o, F^*A_1)\]
(resp. \(\operatorname{Hom}_F(A_o, A_1) = \operatorname{Hom}(F_*A_o, A_1)\)).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.3.5

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a triangulated category over \(I\) and \(S\) as in (2.3.3).

(i) \(\mathcal{A}\) is almost derivable relative to \(S\), and \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) is triangulated over \(I\).

(ii) If \(\mathcal{A}\) is fibred (resp. cofibred), then the functor \(F^*\) (resp. \(F_*\)) is right derivable (resp. left) relative to \(S_o\) and \(S_1\) (1.2.1) if and only if \(\mathcal{A}\) is derivable (resp. coderivable) over \(I\).

By virtue of 2.3.2, the fibre categories of \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) are the categories \(\mathcal{A}_o(S_o^{-1})\) and \(\mathcal{A}_1(S_1^{-1})\), where \(S_i = S \cap \operatorname{Fl}(\mathcal{A}_i)\) (\(i = 0,1\)). With the notation of § 1 no. 2, the functors \(A_o \longrightarrow A_o^-\) and \(A_1 \longrightarrow A_1^+\) identify \(\mathcal{A}_o(S_o^{-1})\) and \(\mathcal{A}_1(S_1^{-1})\) with categories of pro- and ind-objects of \(\mathcal{A}_o\) and \(\mathcal{A}_1\). This allows one to define a category over \(I\), with fibres \(\mathcal{A}_o(S_o^{-1})\) and \(\mathcal{A}_1(S_1^{-1})\), by setting, for \(A_o \in \mathcal{A}_o\) and \(A_1 \in \mathcal{A}_1\):
\[\operatorname{Hom}_F(A_o, A_1) = \operatorname{Hom}_F(A_o^-, A_1^+) = \varinjlim_{A_o \xrightarrow{s} A_o'} \; \varprojlim_{A_1 \xrightarrow{t} A_1'} \operatorname{Hom}(A_o', A_1') \, ,\]

where \(s\) and \(t\) range over the elements of \(S_o\) and \(S_1\) with target (with source) \(A_o\) (\(A_1\)). The category \(\mathcal{A}\) maps into this category, and one checks at once that it satisfies the universal property of \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\), over \(I\) and after any base change.

To verify (i), it suffices to prove that this category, namely \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\), is triangulated, and it suffices to verify condition 2.2.3 (iii). Let then \((X_o,Y_o,Z_o)\) and \((X_1,Y_1,Z_1)\) be distinguished triangles of \(\mathcal{A}_o\) and \(\mathcal{A}_1\), giving rise to the distinguished triangles \((X_o^-,Y_o^-,Z_o^-)\) and \((X_1^+,Y_1^+,Z_1^+)\) of \(\mathcal{A}_o(S_o^{-1})\) and \(\mathcal{A}_1(S_1^{-1})\).
By virtue of Lemma 1.2.2.1, the triangles \((X_o^-,Y_o^-,Z_o^-)\) and \((X_1^+,Y_1^+,Z_1^+)\) are limits of distinguished triangles; there therefore exist morphisms of distinguished triangles
\[(2.3.5.2)\qquad \begin{aligned} (X_o^-, Y_o^-, Z_o^-) & \longrightarrow (X_o', Y_o', Z_o') \\ (X_1', Y_1', Z_1') & \longrightarrow (X_1^+, Y_1^+, Z_1^+) \, , \end{aligned}\]
and a diagram
\[\xymatrix{ X_o' \ar[r]^{u'} \ar[d] & X_1' \ar[d] \\ Y_o' \ar[r]_{v'} & Y_1' \, , }\]
compatible with (2.3.5.1). Since the category \(\mathcal{A}\) is triangulated over \(I\), this diagram can be extended to a morphism of triangles
\[(X_o', Y_o', Z_o') \longrightarrow (X_1', Y_1', Z_1') \, .\]
Composing the latter with the morphisms (2.3.5.2), one sees that the diagram (2.3.5.1) can be extended to a morphism of triangles, which establishes 2.2.3 (iii).

Let us verify (ii), supposing for example that \(\mathcal{A}\) is fibred over \(I\). If \(A_1 \in \operatorname{Ob} (\mathcal{A}_1(S_1^{-1}))\), an inverse image of \(A_1\) in \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) is an object \(B\) of \(\mathcal{A}_o(S_o^{-1})\) such that, in \(\mathcal{A}_o(S_o^{-1})\), one has
\[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}_o(S_o^{-1})}(A_o,B) = \operatorname{Hom}_F(A_o^-, A_1) = \operatorname{Hom}(A_o^-, F^*(A_1)) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}_o(S_o^{-1})}(A_o, F^*(A_1^+)).\]

Such an object \(B\) exists if and only if the Ind-object \(F^*(A_1^+)\) of \(\mathcal{A}_o(S_o^{-1})\) is essentially constant (i.e. representable), and \(B\) then represents this ind-object, which is none other than \(RF(A_1)\) (1.2.1), whence the assertion.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3.6

With the notation of 2.3.3, if \(\mathcal{A}\) is almost derivable over \(\mathcal{B}\), then \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) is a triangulated category over \(\mathcal{B}\).

First of all, the fibre category \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})_x\) can be identified with \(\mathcal{A}_x(S_x^{-1})\): one applies the hypothesis to the base change \(\{x\} \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\). This category is triangulated, equipped with a set \(\Delta_x\) of triangles, which gives a meaning to the preceding statement. To verify condition 2.2.3 (iii), it suffices to do so after any base change \(I \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\), and the assertion follows from 2.3.5 (i).
It follows at once from the proof of 2.3.5 (ii) that:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.3.7

(trivial duality formula).

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a triangulated category fibred and cofibred over \(I\), and denote by \(F_*\) and \(F^*\) the direct-image and inverse-image functors. Let \(S = S_o \cup S_1\) be a multiplicative system as in 2.3.3. Suppose that \(LF_*\) is defined at \(A_o \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}_o(S_o^{-1})\) and that \(RF^*\) is defined at \(A_1 \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}_1(S_1^{-1})\). One then has

\[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}_o(S_o^{-1})}(A_o, RF^*A_1) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})}(A_o, A_1) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}_1(S_1^{-1})}(LF_* A_o, A_1) \, .\]

The position of the symbols \(R\), \(L\), \(*\) and \({}_*\) in 2.3.7 is only apparently aberrant; indeed, in the fibred and cofibred category 0.2 of sheaves over varying sites, the fibre categories are the opposite categories of the usual categories of sheaves.
2.4. Categories fibred in derived categories.

2.4.0. In this no., we denote by \(\mathcal{A}\) a triangulated category cofibred over \(\mathcal{B}\) and by \(S\) a multiplicative system of morphisms of \(\mathcal{A}\), all lying above an identity, and such that \(S_x = S \cap \operatorname{Fl}(\mathcal{A}_x)\) is a saturated multiplicative system of \(\mathcal{A}_x\) [CD 1.2.1] for every \(x \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\).

We seek a criterion for \(\mathcal{A}\) to be coderivable relative to \(S\) (2.3.3), which implies that \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) is triangulated over \(\mathcal{B}\) when one endows it with the set of triangles isomorphic to the image of a distinguished triangle of \(\mathcal{A}\) (2.3.5).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.4.1

Let \(\mathcal{A}\), \(\mathcal{B}\) and \(S\) be as above. For \(\mathcal{A}\) to be coderivable relative to \(S\), it suffices that the following condition be satisfied:

(*) \(\forall x \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{B}, \forall A \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}_x), \exists\, s : A' \longrightarrow A\) in \(S\) \(\forall g,f : x \xrightarrow{f} y \xrightarrow{g} z\), \(f_*A'\) is split on the left for the functor \(g_*\).

Let us denote by \(\mathcal{A}^1\) the full subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\) formed by the objects all of whose direct images are split relative to all the direct-image functors. Then 1.2.2 shows that \(\mathcal{A}^1\) is a triangulated subcategory of \(\mathcal{A}\), obviously cofibred. We set \(S^1 = S \cap \operatorname{Fl}(\mathcal{A}^1)\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.4.1.1

Suppose that \(S\) is stable under direct images. Then \(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{B}\) is coderivable and \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) can be computed by a right calculus of fractions.
Let us verify condition c) of [1, I 2.2], which is possibly less trivial than the others. We are given \(f\) and \(s\) (\(s \in S\)) and must find
\[(2.4.1.2)\qquad \xymatrix{ A' \ar@{-->}[r] & B' \\ A \ar[r] \ar[u]^{s} & B \ar[u]_{t} }\]

a commutative diagram (2.4.1.2) with \(t \in S\). Let \(F\) be the image of \(f\) in \(\mathcal{B}\). By hypothesis, \(F_*(s)\) is again in \(S\), so that, by VERDIER, there exists a commutative diagram
\[\xymatrix{ F_*(A') \ar[r] & B' \\ F_*(A) \ar[r]_{f} \ar[u]^{s} & B \ar[u]_{t} }\]
hence also a diagram (2.4.1.2).

From the fact that \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) is computed by a right calculus of fractions, it is trivial that its formation commutes with the base change \(c : \mathcal{B}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\).
This lemma applies in particular to \(\mathcal{A}^1\) and \(S^1\); the following lemma therefore implies 2.4.1:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.4.1.3

Over \(\mathcal{B}\) and after any base change \(c : \mathcal{B}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\), the canonical functor \(\varphi : \mathcal{A}^1(S^{1-1}) \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) is an equivalence of categories.

Let us construct a quasi-inverse functor to the functor \(\varphi\). For every \(A \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}\), let us choose \(s_A \in S\) with target \(A\) and source \(A^1 \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}^1\), with \(s_A = \operatorname{Id}_A\) for \(A \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}^1\). Let \(f\) be an arrow of \(\mathcal{A}\), with target \(A\), source \(B\), and image \(F\) in \(\mathcal{B}\). Since \(s_B \in S\) and \(F_*A^1 \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}^1\), one can find \(B^1\), \(v\) and \(s \in S^1\) making the following diagram commutative
\[(2.4.1.4)\qquad \xymatrix{ A \ar[r]^{f} & B \ar[r]^{s_B} & B_1 \\ A_1 \ar[r]_{a} \ar[u]^{s_A} & F_*A_1 \ar[u] & B' \ar[l]^{s} \ar[u]_{u} }\]
The arrow \(f^1 = us^{-1}a\) of \(\mathcal{A}^1(S^{1-1})\) then depends only on \(f\).

Let \(f\) and \(g\) be two composable arrows, with images \(F\) and \(G\) in \(\mathcal{B}\). To prove that \((g \circ f)^1 = g^1 \circ f^1\), let us contemplate the following diagram, in which diagrams (2.4.1.4) for \(f\) and \(g\) appear:

\[\xymatrix@C=1.5em@R=2.4em{ A \ar[r]^{f} & B \ar[r]^{g} & C & & & C^1 \ar[dd]^{v} \\ A^1 \ar[u]^{s_A} \ar[r]^{a} & F_*A^1 \ar[u] \ar[r]^{a'} & G_*F_*A^1 \ar[u] & & & \\ B \ar[u]^{u} \ar[r]_{b'} & B^1 \ar[u]_{s} \ar[r]_{b} & G_*B^1 \ar[u] & G_*B' \ar[l]^{G_*s} & C'' \ar[l]_{r} \ar[r]_{w} & C' }\]

Since \(t \in S\), there exist \(C''\), \(r \in S^1\) and \(w\) making it commutative. By definition, \(g^1 \circ f^1 = vt^{-1} b u s^{-1}a\) and \((g \circ f)^1 = vw\, (G_*(s)r)^{-1} s'a\), and one concludes by the commutativity of the diagram.

We have thus defined a functor from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{A}^1(S^{1-1})\); it factors as \(\psi : \mathcal{A}(S^{-1}) \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}^1(S^{1-1})\), by the universal property of \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\). The composite \(\varphi\, \psi\) is isomorphic to the identity, since its composite with the functor \(J : \mathcal{A} \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\) is isomorphic to \(J\). One verifies likewise that \(\psi\, \varphi\) is isomorphic to the identity.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.4.2

With the notation of 2.4.1, \(\mathcal{A}\) is coderivable relative to \(S\) as soon as, for every finite set \(B\) of arrows of \(\mathcal{B}\), condition (*) is satisfied when one restricts to considering only the direct images by the arrows of \(B\).

For every category \(\mathcal{B}'\) with a finite set of arrows, Prop. 2.4.1 will be applicable after any change of base category \(\mathcal{B}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\). We take for \(\mathcal{B}'\) the categories of the following diagrams:
\[(0)\; * \qquad\quad (1)\; * \to * \qquad\quad (2)\; * \to * \to * \qquad\quad (3)\; * \to * \to * \to * \, .\]

Consider the categories \(\mathcal{A}_x(S_x^{-1})\) (\(x \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{B}\)). Given \(f \in \operatorname{Fl}(\mathcal{B})\) and \(A_1, A_2\) in these categories above the source and the target of \(f\), one defines \(\operatorname{Hom}_f(A_1,A_2)\) as the analogous set defined after the base-category change of type (1) determined by \(f\). One defines the composition of morphisms by means of base-category changes of type (3). One thus constructs a category \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})^*\) over \(\mathcal{B}\), whose formation is compatible with any base change; one checks that it is a solution of the universal problem defining \(\mathcal{A}(S^{-1})\), using the base changes of types (0), (1) and (2).
The following result is the dual of 2.4.2.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.4.3

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a triangulated category fibred over \(\mathcal{B}\) and \(S\) as in 2.4.1. For \(\mathcal{A}\) to be derivable relative to \(S\), it suffices that for every finite set \(B\) of arrows of \(\mathcal{B}\), one has

(*') \(\forall x \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{B}), \forall A \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{A}_x), \exists\, s : A \longrightarrow A'\) in \(S\), \(\forall g,f : Z \xrightarrow{g} Y \xrightarrow{f} X\) in \(B\), \(f^*A'\) is split on the right for the functor \(g^*\).

pages.title: 3. Gluing of fibred or cofibred categories.

blocks.html: 3. Gluing of fibred or cofibred categories.
3.1. Introduction.

Let \(f : Y \longrightarrow X\) be a separated morphism of finite type from a scheme \(Y\) to a scheme \(X\), or a continuous map from a locally compact space to a locally compact space.
