One then knows how to define a "direct image with proper support" functor, denoted \(f_!\), from the category of abelian sheaves on \(Y\) to the category of abelian sheaves on \(X\) (cf. 5.3 in the case of schemes, and VERDIER [3] for the case of separated locally compact spaces). When \(Y\) and \(X\) are schemes of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\), these two definitions are compatible in an obvious sense. Unfortunately, in the case of schemes, contrary to what happens in the case of locally compact spaces, the derived functors of the functor \(f_!\) are pathological; one can, however, define a reasonable "direct image with proper support" functor, directly from the category \(D^+(Y)\) to \(D^+(X)\). To define it, one factors the morphism \(f\) into an open immersion and a proper morphism: \(f = \bar{f} j\). The desired functor \(Rf_!\) is then defined as the composite of the "extension by 0" \(j_!\) and the functor \(R\bar{f}_*\), derived from the direct-image functor by \(\bar{f}\).
These functors \(Rf_!\), "direct image with proper support", are usable only if one verifies for them a "variance formalism" including, for a composite \(f = gh\), a formula

which is best expressed in terms of cofibred categories. One has such a formalism separately for the "extensions by zero" and for the direct images by a proper morphism, and the problem is to glue these formalisms together. In order to avoid being bogged down later by silly computations, we propose in this § to draw up the list of the elementary verifications required to carry out such a gluing. We shall do so in a slightly more abstract setting than is indispensable, in the hope that the result may be reused.

The construction of the functor \(Rf_!\) sketched above requires that the morphism \(f\) can be factored into an open immersion and a proper morphism. Following the model of HARTSHORNE [RD III 8 p.189], we introduce in no. 2 the appropriate notion of compactifiable morphism.
3.2. Compactifiable morphisms.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.2.1

A morphism \(f\) from an \(S\)-scheme \(X\) to a quasi-compact, quasi-separated \(S\)-scheme \(Y\) is said to be \(S\)-compactifiable if there exist an \(S\)-scheme \(P\) proper over \(S\) and a factorization of \(f\) into a separated quasi-finite morphism \(j\) from \(X\) to \(P \times_S Y\) followed by the projection from \(P \times_S Y\) to \(Y\)

\[\xymatrix@C=1.4em@R=1.8em{ & & P \times_S Y \ar[ddl] \ar[drr] & & \\ X \ar[urr]^{j} \ar[dr]_{f} & & & & P \ar[dl] \\ & Y \ar[rr] & & S & }\]
When \(S = Y\), one speaks simply of a compactifiable morphism.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2.2

(i) An \(S\)-compactifiable morphism is separated and of finite type.

(ii) If \(Y\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, a separated quasi-finite morphism with target \(Y\) is compactifiable.

(iii) The composite of two \(S\)-compactifiable morphisms is again \(S\)-compactifiable.

(iv) Consider a diagram of \(S\)-schemes, quasi-compact and quasi-separated,

\[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=2em{ X \times_Y Y' \ar[r] \ar[d]_{f'} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ Y' \ar[r] & Y \, . }\]

If \(f\) is \(S\)-compactifiable, then \(f'\) is \(S\)-compactifiable.

(v) Let \(g\) be an \(S\)-compactifiable morphism; in order that a composite morphism \(g \circ h\) be \(S\)-compactifiable, it is necessary that \(h\) be so.
Assertions (i), (ii) and (iv) are trivial. To prove (iii) and (v), consider a composite \(f = gh\), with \(g\) compactifiable.
Suppose \(gh\) compactifiable, whence a diagram
\[\xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ & P \times_S Y \ar[r]^{v} \ar[d] & P \times_S Z \ar[d] \\ X \ar[ur]^{u} \ar[r]_{h} & Y \ar[r]_{g} & Z \, . }\]
The composite \(vu\) is quasi-finite; hence \(u\) is quasi-finite, and (v) is proved.
If \(h\) is compactifiable, one has a diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=1em@R=1.5em{ & & (Q \times_S P) \times_S Z \ar[dr] & & \\ Q \times_S Y \ar[ur] \ar[d] \ar[drrr] & & & P \times_S Z \ar[dl] \ar[dr] & \\ X \ar[u] \ar[r]_-{h} & Y \ar[rr]_-{g} \ar[dr] & & Z \ar[d] & P \ar[dl] \\ & & Q \ar[r] & S & }\]
and \(f = gh\) factors through a separated quasi-finite morphism into \((Q \times_S P) \times_S Z\).
Nagata asserts in [5] that every morphism of finite type between separated integral noetherian schemes is compactifiable. The author confesses that he has not understood the proof.

Let us now fix a scheme \(S\) and denote by \((S)\) the subcategory of the category of \(S\)-schemes whose objects are the quasi-compact, quasi-separated \(S\)-schemes and whose arrows are the \(S\)-compactifiable \(S\)-morphisms.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2.3

In the category \((S)\) :

(i) The open immersions (resp. the proper morphisms) define a subcategory \((S,i)\) (resp. \((S,p)\)) of \((S)\) having the same objects as \((S)\).

(ii) Fibre products exist in \((S,p)\) and are fibre products in \((S)\).

(iii) Every morphism \(f\) is the composite \(f = pj\) of a proper morphism \(p\) and an open immersion.

By 3.2.2 (iii), (iv) and (v), fibre products exist in \((S)\) and are fibre products in the category of all schemes. Since the fibre product \(X = X_1 \times_Y X_2\) of two schemes proper over \(Y\) is again proper over \(Y\), and since a scheme is proper over \(X\) if and only if it is proper over \(X_1\) and \(X_2\), condition (ii) is satisfied.

If \(f\) is a morphism of \((S)\), then by hypothesis it admits, in \((S)\), a factorization \(f = pj'\), where \(p\) is proper and \(j\) quasi-finite separated. By EGA IV 18.12.13, \(j'\) admits a factorization \(j' = qj\), where \(q\) is finite and \(j\) an open immersion; moreover, by 3.2.2 (ii), \(q\) and \(j\) lie in \((S)\). One then has \(f = (pq)j\), which proves (iii). Assertion (i) follows from 3.2.2 (iii).
3.2.4. In the remainder of this §, one supposes given a category \((S)\), equipped with two subcategories \((S,i)\) and \((S,p)\), such that
(i) \(\operatorname{Ob}(S) = \operatorname{Ob}(S,i) = \operatorname{Ob}(S,p)\) ;
(ii) fibre products exist in \((S,p)\) and are fibre products in \((S)\) ;
(iii) \(\forall f \in \operatorname{Fl}(S), \exists\, p \in \operatorname{Fl}(S,p), \exists\, j \in \operatorname{Fl}(S,i), \; f = pj\).
The arrows of \((S,i)\) (resp. of \((S,p)\)) will be called the open immersions (resp. the proper morphisms).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.2.5

(i) A compactification of a morphism \(f\) of \((S)\) (resp. of a pair \((f,g)\), resp. of a triple \((f,g,h)\) of composable morphisms) is a commutative diagram (3.2.5.1) (resp. (3.2.5.2), resp. (3.2.5.3)) whose horizontal arrows are open immersions and whose oblique arrows are proper.

(ii) A morphism of compactifications is a morphism of diagrams (3.2.5.1) (resp. ...) which is the identity on the 1st vertical line and proper at all vertices

\[(3.2.5.1) \qquad \xymatrix@C=1.6em@R=1.8em{ Y \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{i} \ar[d]_{f} & \bar{Y} \ar[dl]^{\bar{f}} \\ X & }\]

\[(3.2.5.2) \qquad \xymatrix@C=1.6em@R=1.8em{ Z \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{j} \ar[d]_{g} & \bar{Z} \ar[dl]_{\bar{g}} \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{j'} & \bar{\bar{Z}} \ar[dll]^{\bar{\bar{g}}} \\ Y \ar@{^{(}->}[r]_{i} \ar[d]_{f} & \bar{Y} \ar[dl]^{\bar{f}} & \\ X & & }\]

\[(3.2.5.3) \qquad \xymatrix@C=1.4em@R=1.6em{ T \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{h} \ar[d]_{k} & \bar{T} \ar[dl]_{\bar{h}} \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{h'} & \bar{\bar{T}} \ar[dll]|(0.4){\bar{\bar{h}}} \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{h''} & \bar{\bar{\bar{T}}} \ar[dlll]^{\bar{\bar{\bar{h}}}} \\ Z \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{j} \ar[d]_{g} & \bar{Z} \ar[dl]_{\bar{g}} \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{j'} & \bar{\bar{Z}} \ar[dll]^{\bar{\bar{g}}} & \\ Y \ar@{^{(}->}[r]_{i} \ar[d]_{f} & \bar{Y} \ar[dl]^{\bar{f}} & & \\ X & & & }\]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2.6

(i) Every morphism (resp. every pair \((f,g)\), resp. every triple \((f,g,h)\), of composable morphisms) admits a compactification.

(ii) The category of compactifications of \(f\) is left filtering.

(iii) If diagrams \((3.2.4.2)_i\) \((i=1,2)\) are compactifications of \((f,g)\), there exists a compactification \((3.2.4.2)_3\) of \((f,g)\) and morphisms of compactifications from \((3.2.4.2)_3\) into the compactifications \((3.2.4.2)_i\).

(i) The case of a morphism is nothing other than 3.2.4 (iii). Let us treat the case of a triple; with the notation of (3.2.5.3), it suffices to construct successively compactifications of \(f\), \(g\) and \(h\), of \(i\bar{g}\) and \(j\bar{h}\), and finally of \(j'\bar{\bar{h}}\).

(ii) Let \((3.2.5.1)_1\) and \((3.2.5.1)_2\) be two compactifications of \(f\). The projection \(\rho\) of \(\bar{Y}_1 \times_X \bar{Y}_2\) into \(X\) is proper, and \(Y\) maps into it by \((i_1,i_2)\), which (3.2.4 (iii)) can be compactified as \((i_1,i_2) = qj\). The compactification \(f = (\rho \cdot q) j\) dominates \((3.2.4.1)_1\) and \((3.2.4.1)_2\).

If \(r\) and \(s\) are two morphisms from \((3.2.4.1)_1\) to \((3.2.4.1)_2\), the kernel \(K\) of the double arrow \(\bar{Y}_1 \xrightarrow[s]{\;r\;} \bar{Y}_2\) maps by a proper morphism into \(\bar{Y}_1\), and \(i_1\) factors through \(K\): say \(i_1 = k\, i\). If \(i = p\, i_3\) is a compactification of \(i\), the existence of the compactification \(f = (\bar{f}_1\, k\, p) i_3\) shows that axiom \(L_2\) is satisfied.

(iii) Let us apply axiom \(L_1\) of filtering categories to the compactifications of \(f\) and \(g\) deduced from the \((3.2.4.2)_i\) \((i = 1,2)\). One thereby finds \(\bar{Y}_3\) and \(\bar{Z}_3\) giving rise to commutative diagrams \((3.2.5.1)_i\) \((i=1,2)\)

\[(3.2.5.1)_i \qquad \xymatrix@C=1.6em@R=1.6em{ & \bar{Z}_i \ar@{^{(}->}[r] \ar[d] & \bar{\bar{Z}}_i \ar[d] \\ \bar{Z}_3 \ar[ur] \ar[dr]_{\bar{g}_3} & Y \ar[r] & \bar{Y}_i \\ & Y \ar[r]_{i_3} & \bar{Y}_3 \ar[u] }\]

and it remains to find a compactification of \(i_3\, \bar{g}_3\) by \(\bar{Z}_3\), such that \(\bar{Z}_3\) can be mapped by a proper morphism into \(\bar{Z}_i\), so as to give rise to a commutative cube \((i = 1,2)\). If the target of a morphism between compactifications of \(i_3\bar{g}_3\) has this property, so too does the source, and by (ii) it will suffice to deal separately with the cases \(i = 1\) and \(i = 2\).

Let \(T\) be the fibre product of \(\bar{Y}_3\) and \(\bar{\bar{Z}}_i\) over \(\bar{Y}_i\): then \(T\) fits into a commutative cube analogous to the one sought, except that the arrow \(k\) from \(\bar{Z}_3\) into \(T\) might not be an open immersion. Setting \(k = pj\) (\(p\) proper, \(j\) an open immersion) and replacing \(T\) by the source \(\bar{Z}_3\) of \(p\), one finds the desired cube.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.2.7

Proposition 3.2.3 would still have been valid if, in Definition 3.2.1 of compactifiable morphisms, one had omitted the requirement that \(Y\) be quasi-compact and quasi-separated and asked in compensation that \(j\) be a quasi-compact open immersion and not merely a quasi-finite morphism.
3.3. Gluing.
Let us recall that hypotheses 3.2.4 are satisfied.
3.3.1. Suppose given:
\(\alpha\)) for each \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(S)\), a category \(F(X)\),
\(\beta\)) an \((S,i)\)-cofibred category \(F_i\) and an \((S,p)\)-cofibred category \(F_p\),
\(\gamma\)) for each \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(S)\), isomorphisms between \(F(X)\), \((F_i)_X\) and \((F_p)_X\),
\(\delta\)) a normalized splitting of \(F_i\) and a normalized splitting of \(F_p\).
By (SGA 1 VI), it "amounts to the same thing" to give instead \(\alpha\)) and:
(i) for every proper morphism \(p : X \longrightarrow Y\), a functor \(p_* : F(X) \longrightarrow F(Y)\),
(ii) for every composable pair \((p,q)\) of proper morphisms, an isomorphism of functors \(c_{p,q} : p_* q_* \longleftrightarrow (pq)_*\),
(i)' and (ii)', analogous data for \((S,i)\),
these data satisfying the following conditions:
(a) if \(p\) is an identity, then \(p_*\), \(c_{p,q}\) and \(c_{q,p}\) are identities,
(b) for every composable triple of proper morphisms, one has
\[c_{p,qr} \bullet (p_* \ast c_{q,r}) = c_{pq,r} \circ (c_{p,q} \ast r_*) \, ,\]
(a)' and (b)', conditions analogous for \((S,i)\).
Suppose given moreover,
(iii) for every commutative diagram \(D\)
\[\xymatrix@C=2em@R=2em{ X \ar[r]^{j'} \ar[d]_{p'} & Y \ar[d]^{p} \\ Z \ar[r]_{j} & T } \qquad j,j' \in \operatorname{Fl}(S,i) \; ; \; p,p' \in \operatorname{Fl}(S,p),\]
an isomorphism of functors \(d(D) : p_* j'_* \longleftrightarrow j_* p'_*\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.3.2

If data (i) (ii) (i') (ii') (iii) satisfy conditions (a) (b) (a') (b') as well as (c) and (c') stated below, then there exists one and "essentially" only one category \(F\) cofibred over \(S\), equipped with isomorphisms \(F \times_S (S,i) = F_i\) and \(F \times_S (S,p) = F_p\), compatible with the datum 3.3.1 \(\gamma\)) and such that the isomorphisms \(d(D)\) of (iii) are the composite isomorphisms \(j_* p'_* = (jp')_* = (pj')_* = p_* j'_*\).
(c) For every commutative diagram of the following type
whose horizontal arrows are open immersions and whose vertical arrows are proper, the following triangle of isomorphisms \(d\) of (iii) is commutative:
\[\xymatrix@C=1.5em@R=2.2em{ p_{3*} i'_* i_* \ar[rr] \ar[dr] & & j'_* j_* p_{1*} \ar[dl] \\ & j'_* p_{2*} i_* & } \qquad .\]
(c') For every commutative diagram of the following type
whose horizontal arrows are proper and whose vertical arrows are open immersions, the following triangle of isomorphisms \(d\) of (iii) is commutative:
\[\xymatrix@C=1.5em@R=2.2em{ i_{3*} p'_* p_* \ar[rr] \ar[dr] & & q'_* q_* i_{1*} \ar[dl] \\ & q'_* i_{2*} p_* & } \qquad .\]
3.3.2.1. Definition of \(f_*\).

Let \(f\) be a morphism from \(Y\) to \(X\). Each compactification of \(f\), with diagram (3.2.5(i)), defines a composite functor \(\bar{f}_* i_*\) from \(F(Y)\) to \(F(X)\). A morphism of compactifications defines a commutative diagram
The datum (iii) thus provides us with an isomorphism

Axiom (c') guarantees moreover that the isomorphism associated with a composite of morphisms of compactifications is the composite of the isomorphisms associated with each of them. Since the category of morphisms of compactifications is filtering (3.2.6 (ii)), one thus obtains a transitive system of isomorphisms between the functors associated with the various compactifications of \(f\). Choosing one of them, one defines the functor \(f_*\).
3.3.2.3. Transitivity homomorphisms.

Every compactification of a pair \((f,g)\) of composable morphisms (diagram (3.2.5.2)) defines a compactification of \(f\), one of \(g\), one of \(f \circ g = (\bar{f}\,\bar{\bar{g}})(j'j)\), and an isomorphism \(c_{f,g} : (fg)_* \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} f_* g_*\), the composite of the isomorphisms
(where the middle isomorphism comes from (iii)).

Let us prove that this isomorphism does not depend on the chosen compactification of \((f,g)\). By 3.2.6 (iii), it will suffice to compare the isomorphisms \(c_{f,g}\) obtained from two compactifications \((3.2.4.2)_i\) \((i=1,2)\) such that there exists a morphism of compactifications from the first into the second. The arrows of these morphisms will be denoted by \(p\).
Consider the following diagram of isomorphisms of functors. To ease its reading, the \(\ast\)'s have been omitted.

\[\xymatrix@C=0.5em@R=2.4em{ \bar{f}_2\bar{\bar{g}}_2 j'_2 j_2 \ar[rr] \ar[dd] & & \bar{f}_2\bar{\bar{g}}_2\, p\, j'_1 j_1 \ar[rr] \ar[dd] & & \bar{f}_1\bar{\bar{g}}_1 j'_1 j_1 \ar[dd] \\ & \bar{f}_2\bar{\bar{g}}_2 j'_2\, p\, j_1 \ar[dl] & (4) & \bar{f}_2\, p\, \bar{g}_1 j'_1 j_1 \ar[dr] & \\ \bar{f}_2 i_2 \bar{g}_2 j_2 \ar[r] & \bar{f}_2 i_2 \bar{g}_2\, p\, j_1 \ar[drr] & (3)\quad(5) & \bar{f}_2\, p\, i_1 \bar{g}_1 j_1 \ar[r] & \bar{f}_1 i_1 \bar{g}_1 j_1 \\ & & \bar{f}_2 i_2 1_Y \bar{g}_1 j_1 \ar[u] & & }\]
a) The composite isomorphism of the 1st row is the isomorphism 3.3.2.1 between two definitions of \((fg)_*\).
b) The composite isomorphism of the last row is the isomorphism 3.3.2.1 between two definitions of \(f_* g_*\).
c) The outermost vertical isomorphisms are the isomorphisms \(c_{f,g}\) between \((fg)_*\) and \(f_* g_*\) deduced from one or the other compactification.

The problem is therefore to prove that the outer boundary of the diagram is commutative. A commutative diagram of functors remains commutative when one composes each of them with one and the same functor. This being recalled, the commutativity of (i) follows from (c) applied to the diagram
The commutativity of (3) and (5) is trivial, as is that of (2), which concerns essentially proper morphisms. It remains to consider the hexagon (4).
Consider the following commutative cube

\[\xymatrix@!0@C=4em@R=3.2em{ & \bar{Z}_2 \ar[rr]^{j'_2} \ar[dd]_(0.6){\bar{g}_2} & & \bar{\bar{Z}}_2 \ar[dd]^{\bar{\bar{g}}_2} \\ \bar{Z}_1 \ar[ur] \ar[rr]^(0.7){j'_1} \ar[dd]_{\bar{g}_1} & & \bar{\bar{Z}}_1 \ar[ur] \ar[dd]^(0.3){\bar{\bar{g}}_1} & \\ & Y \ar@{=}[dl] \ar'[r][rr] & & \bar{Y}_2 \\ Y \ar[rr]_{i_1} & & \bar{Y}_1 \ar[ur]_{i_2} & }\]

There are six ways of traversing the edges of this cube from \(\bar{Z}_1\) to \(\bar{Y}_2\), each "adjacent" to two others; one has an isomorphism between the composite functors associated with two adjacent paths (i.e. separated by a single face), and the commutativity of (4) will follow from the commutativity of the hexagon thus obtained.

The moral of this kind of diagram is that an edge represents a functor, a face an isomorphism between composite functors, and a volume a compatibility condition (between the faces that form its boundary). One decomposes the cube into two prisms with triangular base (by the "plane" \(\bar{Z}_1\, \bar{\bar{Z}}_1\, Y\, \bar{Y}_2\)) so as to reduce to hypotheses (c').
More precisely, one completes the hexagon into the following diagram of isomorphisms (to ease its reading, the \(\ast\)'s have been omitted):

\[\xymatrix@C=1.4em@R=1.8em{ & & \bar{\bar{g}}_2 j'_2\, p \ar[dll] \ar[drr] & & \\ i_2 \bar{g}_2\, p \ar[dd] & & & & \bar{\bar{g}}_2\, p\, j'_1 \ar[dd] \\ & i_2 (\bar{g}_2 p) \ar@{-}[rr] & & (\bar{\bar{g}}_2 p) j'_1 & \\ i_2 1_Y \bar{g}_1 \ar[drr] & & & & p\, \bar{g}_1 j'_1 \ar[dll] \\ & & p\, i_1 \bar{g}_1 & & }\]
The triangles are trivially commutative, and the pentagons are so by (c').
3.3.2.4. Cocycle condition.

Let us verify that the isomorphisms \(c_{f,g}\) constructed in 3.3.2.3 satisfy a cocycle condition for a triple \((f, g, h)\) of composable morphisms. Let us introduce a compactification of \((f, g, h)\), with diagram (3.2.4.3), and consider the following diagram of isomorphisms of functors:

\[\xymatrix@C=2.2em@R=2.4em{ \bar{f} i \bar{g} j \bar{h} k \ar[rr] \ar[dd] & & \bar{f} \bar{g} j' j \bar{h} k \ar[dd] \\ & \bar{f} \bar{\bar{g}} j' \bar{\bar{h}} k' k \ar[ul] \ar[dr] & \\ \bar{f} i \bar{g} \bar{h} k' k \ar[rr] & & \bar{f} \bar{g} \bar{h} k'' k' k \, . }\]
The commutativity of the square is trivial, that of the triangles follows from (c) and (c'). Since the commutativity of the outer boundary is what was to be proved, this completes the proof of 3.3.2.

3.3.3. Suppose given, on \((S,i)\) and \((S,p)\) respectively, fibred categories \(F_i\) and \(F_p\) equipped with a normalized splitting, and suppose that \(F_i\) and \(F_p\) have the same fibre \(F(X)\) at every \(X \in \operatorname{Ob} S\).
By SGA 1 VI, it "amounts to the same thing" to give instead:
(i bis) for every proper morphism \(p : X \longrightarrow Y\), a functor \(p^* : F(Y) \longrightarrow F(X)\),
(ii bis) for every composable pair \((p,q)\) of proper morphisms, an isomorphism of functors \(c_{p,q} : q^* p^* \longleftrightarrow (pq)^*\),
(i' bis) and (ii' bis), analogous data for \((S,i)\),
these data satisfying conditions (a bis) (b bis) (a' bis) (b' bis) dual to 3.3.1 (a)(b)(a')(b').
Suppose given moreover,
(iii bis) for every commutative diagram \(D\)
\[\xymatrix@C=2em@R=2em{ X \ar[r]^{j'} \ar[d]_{p'} & Y \ar[d]^{p} \\ Z \ar[r]_{j} & T } \qquad j,j' \in \operatorname{Fl}(S,i) \; ; \; p\, p' \in \operatorname{Fl}(S,p)\]
an isomorphism of functors \(d(D) : j'^* p^* \longleftrightarrow p'^* j^*\).
We leave it to the reader to state conditions (c bis) and (c' bis) dual to 3.3.2 (c) and (c').
Arguments parallel to those above then prove the following proposition.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.3.4

If data (i bis)(ii bis)(i' bis)(ii' bis)(iii bis) satisfy conditions (a bis)(b bis)(a' bis)(b' bis)(c bis)(c' bis), there exists one and essentially one category \(F\) fibred over \(S\) and equipped with isomorphisms \(F \times_S (S,i) = F_i\), \(F \times_S (S,p) = F_p\), these isomorphisms being compatible with the identifications \(F_{iX} = F_{pX}\) \((X \in \operatorname{Ob} S)\) and such that the isomorphisms \(d(D)\) of (iii bis) become the composite isomorphisms \(p'^* j^* = (jp')^* = (pj')^* = j'^* p^*\).
It should be noted, however, that 3.3.4 is not dual to 3.3.2, since the hypotheses made on \((S,i)\) and \((S,p)\) are not self-dual.

pages.title: 4. Resolutions. Application to the base change arrow.

blocks.html: 4. Resolutions. Application to the base change arrow.
4.1. Flat resolutions.

Let us recall that if \(f : (X, \mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow (Y, \mathcal{B})\) is a morphism of ringed sites (or topoi), the inverse image under \(f\) of a sheaf of left \(\mathcal{B}\)-modules \(\mathcal{M}\) is the sheaf of left \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules \(\mathcal{A} \otimes_{f^*\mathcal{B}} f^*\mathcal{M}\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.1.1

Let \(f : (X, \mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow (Y, \mathcal{B})\) be a morphism of ringed sites, \(K\) a sheaf of right \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules, and \(0 \longrightarrow L \longrightarrow M \longrightarrow N \longrightarrow 0\) an exact sequence of sheaves of left \(\mathcal{B}\)-modules. If \(M\) and \(N\) are flat, then

(i) \(L\) is flat,

(ii) the following sequence is exact :

\[0 \longrightarrow K \otimes_{\mathcal{A}} f^*L \longrightarrow K \otimes_{\mathcal{A}} f^*M \longrightarrow K \otimes_{\mathcal{A}} f^*N \longrightarrow 0 \, .\]

Let us factor \(f\) into the arrows \((X, \mathcal{A}) \xrightarrow{\;u\;} (X, f^*\mathcal{B}) \xrightarrow{\;v\;} (Y, \mathcal{B})\). The functor \(v^*\) is exact and carries flat Modules to flat Modules (IV 15), so that it suffices to prove 4.1.1 for \(u\). The isomorphism
\[(4.1.1.1) \qquad K \otimes_{\mathcal{A}} (\mathcal{A} \otimes_{f^*\mathcal{B}} P) = K \otimes_{f^*\mathcal{B}} P\]
then reduces us to the case where \(f\) is the identity.
Let \(0 \longrightarrow R \longrightarrow P \longrightarrow K \longrightarrow 0\) be an exact sequence with \(P\) flat (4.1.2). The rows and columns of the following diagram are exact:

\[\xymatrix@C=1.6em@R=1.6em{ & & 0 \ar[d] & & \\ & R \otimes L \ar[r] \ar[d] & P \otimes L \ar[r] \ar[d] & K \otimes L \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & R \otimes M \ar[r] \ar[d] & P \otimes M \ar[r] \ar[d] & K \otimes M \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & R \otimes N \ar[r] \ar[d] & P \otimes N \ar[r] \ar[d] & K \otimes N \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ & 0 & 0 & 0 & }\]
Applying the snake diagram to the first two columns, one finds
\[0 \longrightarrow K \otimes L \longrightarrow K \otimes M \, ,\]

which proves (ii). Without further supposing \(P\) flat, one knows that in the preceding diagram the three columns and two rows are short exact sequences; the first row is therefore exact, i.e. \(L\) is flat.

4.1.2. Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a subcategory of the category of ringed sites. The sheaves of modules on the ringed sites of \(\mathcal{S}\) form a category \(\mathcal{M}\), abelian over \(\mathcal{S}\) (2.2.2), fibred and cofibred, whose fibres are the opposites of the usual categories of sheaves of modules on a site. One denotes by \(K(\mathcal{S})\) the category \(K(\mathcal{M})\) (2.2.8) and by \(K^+(\mathcal{S})\) (resp. \(K^-(\mathcal{S})\)) the full subcategory of \(K(\mathcal{S})\) whose fibre categories are the opposites of the categories \(K^+(S)\) (resp. \(K^-(S)\)) for \(S \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{S}\). The categories \(K(\mathcal{S})\), \(K^+(\mathcal{S})\) and \(K^-(\mathcal{S})\) are triangulated over \(\mathcal{S}\), fibred and cofibred.

Let \(f : S \longrightarrow S'\) be an arrow of \(\mathcal{S}\). Every injective is acyclic (1.2.3) for the functor \(Rf_*\), and every sheaf of flat modules is acyclic for the functor \(Lf^*\) (4.1.1 and 1.2.6), whence derived functors (1.2.7)
\[(4.1.2.1) \qquad Rf_* : D^+(S) \longrightarrow D^+(S')\] \[(4.1.2.2) \qquad Lf^* : D^-(S) \longrightarrow D^-(S') \, .\]
If \(Rf_*\) (resp. \(Lf^*\)) is of finite dimension, one may in 4.1.2.1 (resp. 4.1.2.2) replace the exponent \(+\) (resp. \(-\)) by \(b\), by \(-\) (resp. \(+\)), or suppress it (1.2.10).

One denotes by \(D(\mathcal{S})\) (resp. \(D^+(\mathcal{S})\), resp. \(D^-(\mathcal{S})\)) the category deduced from \(K(\mathcal{S})\) (resp. \(K^+(\mathcal{S})\), resp. \(K^-(\mathcal{S})\)) by inverting the quasi-isomorphisms.

blocks.title: Scholium
blocks.html:
Scholium 4.1.3

("Trivial duality theorem").

(a) Suppose that all the functors \(Rf_*\) (resp. \(Lf^*\)) are of finite dimension. Then :

(i) The formation of \(D(\mathcal{S})\) commutes with every change of base category \(\mathcal{S}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{S}\). The category \(D(\mathcal{S})\) is triangulated over \(\mathcal{S}\) (2.2.3), and its fibres are identified with the opposites of the categories \(D(S)\) for \(S \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{S}\).

(ii) The category \(D(\mathcal{S})\) is cofibred (resp. fibred) over \(\mathcal{S}\). Let \(f : S \longrightarrow S'\) ; if \(Lf^*\) (resp. \(Rf_*\)) is of finite dimension, then every object of \(D(S')\) (resp. \(D(S)\)) has an inverse image (resp. direct image) under \(f\) in the sense of the category \(D(\mathcal{S})\) over \(\mathcal{S}\). The inverse-image and direct-image functors are identified with \(Lf^*\) and \(Rf_*\).

(iii) Every object of \(D^-(S')\) (resp. \(D^+(S)\)) has an inverse image (resp. direct image) in the sense of \(D(\mathcal{S})\) and the inverse-image (resp. direct-image) functor is identified with \(Lf^*\) (resp. \(Rf_*\)).

(b) (i) The formation of \(D^-(\mathcal{S})\) (resp. \(D^+(\mathcal{S})\)) commutes with every change of base category \(\mathcal{S}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{S}\). The category \(D^-(\mathcal{S})\) (resp. \(D^+(\mathcal{S})\)) is triangulated over \(\mathcal{S}\), and its fibres are identified with the opposites of the categories \(D^-(S)\) (resp. \(D^+(S)\)).

(ii) The category \(D^-(\mathcal{S})\) (resp. \(D^+(\mathcal{S})\)) is fibred (resp. cofibred) over \(\mathcal{S}\) ; the "inverse image" (resp. "direct image") functors are identified with the derived functors \(Lf^*\) (resp. \(Rf_*\)).

(iii) If \(f : S \longrightarrow S'\) is such that \(Rf_*\) (resp. \(Lf^*\)) is of finite dimension, every object of \(D^-(S)\) (resp. \(D^+(S')\)) has a direct image in the sense of \(D^-(\mathcal{S})\) (resp. an inverse image in the sense of \(D^+(\mathcal{S})\)), and the "direct image" (resp. "inverse image") functor is identified with \(Rf_*\) (resp. \(Lf^*\)).

It will suffice to verify that in each case the hypotheses of 2.4.1 or 2.4.3 are fulfilled, the other assertions being deduced, after a base change \(\{S\} \longrightarrow \mathcal{S}\), or \(I \longrightarrow \mathcal{S}\), from 2.3.5 and 1.2.10. In case (b), the complexes of flat (resp. flasque) sheaves satisfy the hypotheses of 2.4.1. In case (a), one uses 2.4.3 so as to have to consider only those \(f\) such that the dimension of \(Rf_*\) (resp. \(Lf^*\)) is bounded above by a fixed \(N\). Let us prove that there exist "enough" complexes \(K\) whose components have their direct (resp. inverse) images all acyclic for the direct (inverse) image functors under consideration. Let \(K\) be a complex and \(K^*\) (resp. \(K_*\)) a Cartan-Eilenberg resolution of \(K\) by complexes with flasque (resp. flat) components. If \(n > N\), one sees that \(f_* \tau''_{\leq n}(K^*) = \tau''_{\leq n} f_*(K^*)\) (resp. \(f^* \tau''_{\geq n}(K_*) = \tau''_{\geq n} f^*(K_*)\)), where \(\tau''\) denotes a truncation relative to the second differential. For \(n > 2N\), one deduces that \(\tau''_{\leq n}(K^*)\) (resp. \(\tau''_{\geq n}(K_*)\)) satisfies the hypothesis of 2.4.3, and every complex \(K\) is the source (resp. the target) of a quasi-isomorphism whose target (resp. source) is such a complex.
4.1.4. Consider a commutative square of ringed sites (4.1.4.1) (cf. 0.11)
\[(4.1.4.1) \qquad \xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ X' \ar[r]^{g'} \ar[d]_{f'} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ S' \ar[r]_{g} & S } \qquad .\]

One may consider the subcategory of the category of sites reduced to this diagram; one then uses 2.1.2 to define a "base change morphism" from \(Lg^* Rf_*\) into \(Rf'_* Lg'^*\) when 4.1.3 is applicable:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.1.5

The base change arrow 2.1.2, from \(Lg^* Rf_*\) into \(Rf'_* Lg'^*\), is defined in each of the following cases :

(i) One works in the categories \(D^+\), and \(Lg^*\), \(Lg'^*\) are of finite dimension.

(ii) One works in the categories \(D^-\), and \(Rf_*\), \(Rf'_*\) are of finite dimension.

(iii) One works in the whole derived categories, and \(Rf_*\), \(Rf'_*\), \(Lg^*\), \(Lg'^*\) are of finite dimension, as are \(Lf^*\) and \(Lf'^*\) (or: as are \(Rg_*\) and \(Rg'_*\)).

It will be noted that the last hypothesis of (iii) seems like a hoax. The author does not know how to get rid of it except when the sites under consideration have enough points (4.2.12). The functorial properties of this base change arrow are obtained at once from the description 2.1.2.
4.1.6. Let \((S, \mathcal{A})\) be a ringed site, and consider the "tensor product" functor
\[\otimes : \operatorname{Mod}_d(S, \mathcal{A}^o) \times \operatorname{Mod}_g(S, \mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Mod}(S, C)\]
where \(C\) is the centre of \(\mathcal{A}\).

The recipe of 1.1.6, for the application of which one will define the simple complex associated with a double complex by a sum, allows one to extend this functor to a functor still denoted \(\otimes\) :
\[\otimes : K(S, \mathcal{A}^o) \times K(S, \mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow K(S, C) \, .\]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.1.7

With the preceding notation :

(i) The tensor product functor is left derivable (1.2.1) to a "total tensor product" functor

\[\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} : D^-(S, \mathcal{A}^o) \times D^-(S, \mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D^-(S, C) \; ;\]

(ii) a pair \((K,L)\) of complexes bounded above is split for \(\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}\) as soon as \(K\) or \(L\) has flat components.
The proof is standard.

blocks.title: Notation
blocks.html:
Notation 4.1.8

If \(K \in D^-(S, \mathcal{A}^o)\) and \(L \in D^-(S, \mathcal{A})\), one denotes by \(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} L\) the total tensor product of \(K\) and \(L\). The sheaf \(H_k(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} L) = H^{-k}(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} L)\) is denoted by \(\operatorname{Tor}_k(K,L)\) and is called the \(k^{\text{th}}\) local hypertor of \(K\) and \(L\).

Let \(K \in D^-(S, \mathcal{A}^o)\) and \(L \in D^-(S, \mathcal{A})\). If \(H^i(K) = 0\) for \(i > k\) and \(H^i(L) = 0\) for \(i > \ell\), one verifies that \(H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} L) = 0\) for \(i > k + \ell\) and that \(H^{k+\ell}(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} L) = H^k(K) \otimes H^\ell(L)\). Let us fix \(K\) and regard \(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} L\) as a functor in \(L\). If one applies the definition 1.2.9 of cohomological amplitude as an interval of \(\mathbb{Z}\), the upper bound of this interval is of a trivial nature. It is the largest integer \(i\) such that \(H^i(K) \neq 0\). The lower bound is more interesting:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.1.9

A complex \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(S, \mathcal{A}^o)\) is said to be of Tor-dimension \(\leq n\) if the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:

(i) For every \(\mathcal{A}\)-module \(L\), \(\operatorname{Tor}_k(K,L) = 0\) for \(k > n\).

(ii) For every complex of \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules \(L\) such that \(H^i(L) = 0\) for \(i < \ell\), \(H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} L) = 0\) for \(i < \ell-n\).

(iii) There exists a quasi-isomorphism with target \(K\) and source a complex \(K'\) with flat components, vanishing for \(i < -n\).
4.1.10. Here are some possible variations:

(i) If \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^b(S, \mathcal{A}^o)\) is of finite tor-dimension and if \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D(S, \mathcal{A})\), then the functor \(\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}\) is defined (1.2.1) at \((K,L)\).
(ii) If \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} K^b(S, \mathcal{A}^o)\) has components of finite Tor-dimension, the functor \(L \longmapsto K \otimes L\) \((L \in K(S, \mathcal{A}))\) is left derivable.
(iii) If every Module is of finite Tor-dimension, the functor \(\otimes\) is derived to a functor
\[\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} : D(S, \mathcal{A}^o) \times D(S, \mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D(S, C) \, .\]
4.2. Godement flasque resolutions.

4.2.1. Let \(S\) be a topos and \(X\) a set. It amounts to the same thing to give a family of points of \(S\) indexed by \(X\) or to give a morphism \(k : \operatorname{Top}(X) \longrightarrow S\) from the topos defined by the discrete topological space \(X\) into \(S\). For the said family to be conservative (IV 6.4.1), it is necessary and sufficient that for every sheaf \(F\) of \(S\), the adjunction arrow from \(F\) into \(k_* k^*F\) be a monomorphism (cf. IV 6.4.0).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.2.2

Let \(k : \operatorname{Top}(X) \longrightarrow S\) be a conservative family of points of a topos \(S\). One calls Godement resolution or canonical flasque resolution (relative to \(X\)) of an abelian sheaf \(F\) of \(S\), and one denotes by \(\mathscr{C}^*_X(F)\) (or simply \(\mathscr{C}^*(F)\)), the following right resolution of \(F\):

1) \(\mathscr{C}^0(F) = k_* k^*F\) and \(\varepsilon : F \longrightarrow \mathscr{C}^0(F)\) is the adjunction arrow.

2) Set \(d^{-1} = \varepsilon\); one defines by recursion, for \(n \geq 0\)

\[\mathscr{C}^{n+1}(F) = \mathscr{C}^0(\operatorname{coker} d^{n-1}), \quad \text{and } d^n \text{ as composite arrow}\]

\[d^n : \mathscr{C}^n(F) \longrightarrow \operatorname{coker}(d^{n-1}) \longrightarrow \mathscr{C}^0(\operatorname{coker}(d^{n-1})) \, .\]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.3

Under the hypotheses of 4.2.2,

(i) \(\mathscr{C}^n(F)\) is a flasque sheaf (V 3.7),

(ii) \(\mathscr{C}^n(F)\) is an exact functor in \(F\),

(iii) the stalk at a point \(x \in X\) of the complex \(\mathscr{C}^*(F)\) is a canonically split resolution of \(F_x\).
The sheaves \(\mathscr{C}^n(F)\) are flasque, being the direct image of sheaves (automatically flasque) on the discrete topological space \(X\).

The functors \(k^*\) and \(k_*\) are exact. The functor \(\mathscr{C}^0\) is therefore exact. Let us prove by recursion on \(n \geq 0\) that the functor \(\mathscr{Z}^n(F) = \operatorname{coker}(d^{n-1})\) is exact, hence so is \(\mathscr{C}^{n+1} = \mathscr{C}^0 \mathscr{Z}^n\). Set \(\mathscr{Z}^{-1}(F) = F\). An exact sequence of sheaves
\[0 \longrightarrow F' \longrightarrow F \longrightarrow F'' \longrightarrow 0\]
defines for \(n \geq 0\) a diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=1.4em@R=1.4em{ & 0 \ar[d] & 0 \ar[d] & 0 \ar[d] & \\ 0 \ar[r] & \mathscr{Z}^{n-1}(F') \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathscr{Z}^{n-1}(F) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathscr{Z}^{n-1}(F'') \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & \mathscr{C}^n(F') \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathscr{C}^n(F) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathscr{C}^n(F'') \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & \mathscr{Z}^n(F') \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathscr{Z}^n(F) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathscr{Z}^n(F'') \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ & 0 & 0 & 0 & }\]
whose columns are exact, as are, by the recursion hypothesis, the first 2 rows. The 3rd row is therefore exact, and (ii) is proved.
The short exact sequences
\[0 \longrightarrow \mathscr{Z}^{n-1}(F) \longrightarrow \mathscr{C}^n(F) \longrightarrow \mathscr{Z}^n(F) \longrightarrow 0\]
are special cases of the short exact sequence
\[(4.2.3.1) \qquad 0 \longrightarrow F \xrightarrow{\;\varepsilon\;} \mathscr{C}^0(F) \longrightarrow \mathscr{Z}^0(F) \longrightarrow 0\]
(make the substitution \(F \longmapsto \mathscr{Z}^{n-1}(F)\)). To prove (iii), it remains to prove that the inverse-image sequence of (4.2.3.1) under \(k\) is canonically split. The composite arrow
\[k^*F \xrightarrow{\;k^*(\varepsilon)\;} k^*\mathscr{C}^0 F = k^*(k_* k^*)F = (k^* k_*)k^*F \longrightarrow k^*F\]
is indeed the identity.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.2.4

If \((x_i)_{i \in X}\) is a conservative family of points of a site, to this family there corresponds a conservative family of points of the generated topos, which again allows one to define the canonical flasque resolutions.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.2.5

If \(S\) is a ringed topos, the functors \(\mathscr{C}^n\) carry Modules to Modules.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.2.6

Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a category formed of sites. Suppose given, for each \(S \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{S}\), a set \(S^d\) and a conservative family \(k_S : \operatorname{Top}(S^d) \longrightarrow S\) of points of \(S\) indexed by \(S^d\). Suppose that \(S^d\) is functorial in \(S\) and that the diagrams

\[\xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ \operatorname{Top}(S^d) \ar[r]^{f^d} \ar[d]_{k_S} & \operatorname{Top}(T^d) \ar[d]^{k_T} \\ S \ar[r]_{f} & T }\]

are commutative. The corresponding canonical flasque resolutions are then "functorial in \(S\)".
If \(\mathcal{S}\) is the category of topological spaces, one may take \(S^d\) = the underlying set.

If \(\mathcal{S}\) is the category of étale sites of schemes \(S\) locally of finite type over a scheme \(S_0\), and if for each \(s \in S_0\), \(\overline{k(s)}\) is an algebraic closure of \(k(s)\), one may take for \(S^d\) the set of points of \(S\) with values in one of the \(\overline{k(s)}\).
One may replace the condition "of finite type" by a cardinality condition if the algebraic closures \(\overline{k(s)}\) are replaced by sufficiently large algebraically closed extensions.

4.2.7. One of the interests of canonical flasque resolutions is that they allow one to construct complexes split simultaneously for functors of "tensor product" type and for functors of "direct image" type. They thereby permit a perhaps more comprehensible construction of the base change morphisms (4.1.5).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.2.8

Let \(f : (S, \mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow (S', \mathcal{B})\) be a morphism of ringed sites, \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} K(S, \mathcal{A}^o)\) and \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} K(S', \mathcal{B})\) complexes, and \(k : \operatorname{Top}(X) \longrightarrow S\) a conservative set of points of \(S\). Suppose that one of the following conditions is fulfilled :

(a) The cohomologies of \(K\) and \(L\) are bounded above ;

(b) \(\mathcal{A}\) is of finite Tor-dimension over \(f^*\mathcal{B}\) and \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^b(S, \mathcal{A}^o)\) is of finite Tor-dimension ;

(c) \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D^b(S', \mathcal{B})\) is of finite Tor-dimension.

Then the functor \((K,L) \longmapsto K \otimes f^*L\) is derivable (1.2.1) at \((K,L)\) ; let \(\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lf^*\) be its derived functor.

(i) If \(x\) is a point of \(S\), then \((K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lf^*L)_x \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} K_x \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{B}_{f(x)}} L_{f(x)}\).

(ii) The pair \((K,L)\) is left split for \(\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lf^*\) (1.2.1) if and only if, for every \(x \in X\), the pair \((K_x, L_{f(x)})\) is left split for the functor \(\otimes_{\mathcal{B}_{f(x)}}\).

(iii) Under hypotheses (a) or (b), the functor \(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lf^*L\) in \(L\) is of cohomological amplitude \(\subset d\) (1.2.9) if and only if, \(\forall x \in X\), the complex \(K_x\) of \(\mathcal{B}_{f(x)}\)-modules is of Tor-amplitude \(\subset d\).
This lemma, whose proof is standard, expresses the "pointwise nature" of the functor under consideration.

4.2.9. Let \(L\) be a complex. One calls Godement resolution (relative to \(X\)) of \(L\) the simple complex (defined in terms of sums) associated with the double complex \(\mathscr{C}^*L\) (1.1.4). One calls Godement resolution truncated at order \(n\) \(\tau''_{\leq n} \mathscr{C}^*L\) the simple complex associated with the double complex deduced from \(\mathscr{C}^*L\) by truncation (1.1.15) in the direction of the Godement differential. By 4.2.3 (iii), \(L\) is, point of \(X\) by point of \(X\), homotopic to the complexes \(\tau''_{\leq n} \mathscr{C}^*L\) and \(\mathscr{C}^*L\); these complexes are therefore "as good as \(L\)" with respect to functors of "tensor product" type (4.2.8).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.10

Let \((S, \mathcal{A})\) be a ringed site, \(X\) a conservative set of points of \(S\) and \(N,M \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}\) with \(N\) or \(M < \infty\). Let \(A\) be the subcategory of \(K(S)\) formed of the complexes \(L\) such that

(a) If \(N = \infty\), then \(H^i(L) = 0\) for \(i\) large enough ; if \(M = \infty\), then \(H^i(L) = 0\) for \(i\) small enough.

(b) For all \(x \in X\) and every \(\mathcal{A}_x\)-module \(Q\) of Tor-dimension \(\leq N\), the complex \(L_x\) is left split for the functor \(* \otimes_{\mathcal{A}_x} Q\).

(c) For every morphism of topoi \(f : \widetilde{X} \longrightarrow E\) of cohomological dimension \(\leq M\), the complex \(L\) is right split for the functor \(f_*\).

Then the inclusion of \(A\) into \(K(S)\) induces an equivalence between the category deduced from \(A\) by inverting the quasi-isomorphisms and the category \(D^*(S)\), \(* = +\) if \(N < M = \infty\), \(* = -\) if \(M < N = \infty\) and \(* =\) blank if \(N,M < \infty\).

Let \(K\) be a complex satisfying (a). If \(N = \infty\), then the canonical arrow \(a : K_1 = \tau_{\leq i} K \longrightarrow K\) is a quasi-isomorphism for \(i\) large enough. If \(N < \infty\), one sets \(K_1 = K\). Let \(K_1^*\) be a flat Cartan-Eilenberg resolution and set \(K_2 = \tau''_{\leq 2N} K_1\) (truncation in the direction of the new differential). The composite arrow from \(K_2\) into \(K\) is a quasi-isomorphism, and \(K_2\) satisfies (b).

Let \(K\) be a complex satisfying (a) and (b). If \(M = \infty\), then \(N < \infty\); for \(i\) large enough, \(b : K \longrightarrow \tau_{\geq i} K_1 = K_3\) is a quasi-isomorphism, and \(K_3\) still satisfies (a) and (b). If \(M < \infty\), one sets \(K = K_3\). Let \(K_4 = \tau''_{\leq M} \mathscr{C}^*K_3\). Then \(K_4\) satisfies (a), (c), and (b) by 4.2.3 (iii).
The proposition therefore follows from two successive applications of [CD I 2.4.2].

blocks.title: Variants
blocks.html:
Variants 4.2.11

If \(N < \infty\) (resp. if \(M < \infty\), resp. if \(N, M < \infty\)), then one could have worked similarly with complexes bounded below (resp. above, resp. bounded).
4.2.12. Here is how to use these constructions to define the base change morphism 4.1.4 under more general hypotheses than those of loc. cit., when the sites under consideration have enough points.
Let a commutative diagram (cf. (0.11)) of sites
\[(4.2.12.1) \qquad \xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ X' \ar[r]^{g'} \ar[d]_{f'} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ S' \ar[r]_{g} & S } \qquad ,\]
\(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of rings on \(S\), \(\mathcal{A}'\) a sheaf of rings on \(S'\) and \(L\) a complex of \((\mathcal{A}', g^*\mathcal{A})\)-bimodules on \(S'\). One supposes that:
(i) the sites \(X\) and \(X'\) admit conservative families of points, \(k : Q \longrightarrow X\) and \(k' : Q' \longrightarrow X'\), fitting into a commutative diagram
\[(4.2.12.2) \qquad \xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ X' \ar[r]^{g'} \ar[d]_{k'} & X \ar[d]^{k} \\ Q' \ar[r]_{g_0} & Q } \qquad .\]
(ii) One of the following hypotheses is fulfilled:
(a) The functors \(Rf_*\) and \(Rf'_*\) are of finite cohomological dimension, and \(L\) is bounded above. One sets \(s = -\).
(b) \(L\) is bounded below, with components of uniformly bounded Tor-dimension (as \(g^*\mathcal{A}\)-modules). One sets \(s = +\).
(c) \(L\) is bounded, and the hypotheses of (a) and (b) are fulfilled. One sets \(s =\) blank.

One denotes by \(L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^* : D^s(S, \mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D^s(S', \mathcal{A}')\) the left derived functor (1.2.1) of the functor \(K \longmapsto L \otimes_{g^*\mathcal{A}} g^*K\) from \(K^s(S, \mathcal{A})\) to \(K^s(S', \mathcal{A}')\).
One proposes to define a base change arrow
\[(4.2.12.3) \qquad \varphi : L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^* Rf_* K \longrightarrow Rf'_*(f'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg'^*K)\]
for \(K\) in \(D^s(X, \mathcal{A})\).
By 4.2.10, it suffices to define it, functorially in \(K\), for the complexes belonging to the category \(A\) of 4.2.10, for
\[N \geq \sup_i (\text{tor dim of } L^i \text{ over } g^*)\] \[M \geq \text{cohomological dimension of } Rf_* \, .\]
Such a complex is split both for the functor \(Rf_*\) and for the functor \(f'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{A}} g'^*\) (4.2.8). The canonical arrows
\[\alpha : f_*K \longrightarrow Rf_*K\] \[\beta : f'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg'^*K \longrightarrow L \otimes g'^*K\]
are therefore quasi-isomorphisms. To compute the left-hand side \(I\) of (4.2.12.3), it therefore suffices to take a left resolution (i.e. a quasi-isomorphism)
\[\gamma : K_1 \longrightarrow f_*K \, ,\]
with \(K_1\) split for \(L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^*\); one has
\[\mathrm{I} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} L \otimes Lg^* K_1 \, .\]
Similarly, to compute the right-hand side \(\mathrm{II}\) of (4.2.12.3), it suffices to take a right resolution
\[\delta : f'^*L \otimes g'^*K \longrightarrow K_2 \, ,\]
with \(K_2\) split for \(Rf'_*\); one has
\[\mathrm{II} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} f'_* K_2 \, .\]
One then defines the base change arrow as the composite

\[\mathrm{I} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} L \otimes g^*K_1 \xrightarrow{\;\gamma\;} L \otimes g^*f_*K \xrightarrow{\;c\;} f'_*(f'^*L \otimes g'^*K) \xrightarrow{\;\alpha\;} f'_* K_2 \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{II} \, ,\]
where the arrow \(c\) is the usual base change arrow, at the level of the actual complexes.
This base change arrow has the following characteristic property, which in principle makes it easy to verify its compatibility properties.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.13

Under the preceding hypotheses, let \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} C^s(X, \mathcal{A})\), \(K_1 \in \operatorname{Ob} C^s(S, \mathcal{A})\) and \(K_2 \in \operatorname{Ob} C^s(X', \mathcal{A}')\). Let moreover \(u\) be an \(f\)-morphism from \(K\) to \(K_1\), i.e. \(u \in \operatorname{Hom}(K_1, f_*K) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}(f^*K_1, K)\), and \(v\) a morphism from \(f'^*L \otimes g'^*K\) to \(K_2\). From \(u,v\) and the usual base change arrow one deduces a morphism of complexes \(c_{u,v} : L \otimes g^*K_1 \longrightarrow f'_* K_2\). Let \(u'\), \(v'\) and \(c'_{uv}\) be the composite arrows

\[u' : K_1 \xrightarrow{\;u\;} f_*K \longrightarrow Rf_*K\]

\[v' : L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg'^*K \longrightarrow L \otimes g'^*K \xrightarrow{\;v\;} K_2\]

\[c'_{u,v} : L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^*K_1 \longrightarrow L \otimes g^*K_1 \xrightarrow{\;c_{uv}\;} f'_* K_2 \longrightarrow Rf'_*K_2 \, .\]
The following diagram is commutative

\[(4.2.13.1) \qquad \xymatrix@C=4em@R=2.6em{ L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^*Rf_*K \ar[r]^-{\varphi} \ar[d]_{L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^*(u')} & Rf'_*(f'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg'^*K) \ar[d]^{Rf'_*(v')} \\ L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^*K_1 \ar[r]_-{c'_{uv}} & Rf'_* K_2 } \qquad .\]
Suppose first that \(K_1 = f_*K\) and that \(K_2 = f'^*L \otimes g'^*K\), and let a commutative diagram of complexes
\[\xymatrix@C=2.6em@R=2em{ K^a \ar[r] \ar[d] & K \ar[d] \\ K^c \ar[r] & K^b }\]

such that \(K^a\) is split for \(Lf'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg'^*\), \(K^b\) is split for \(Rf_*\), and \(K^c\) is split for these two functors: to construct this diagram, one begins by constructing \(K^a\), then applies a canonical flasque resolution (possibly truncated) to \(K^a\) and \(K\).

Let us apply the functor \(f_*\) (resp. \(L \otimes g'^*\)) to this diagram, and resolve the complexes of the diagram \((K_1, K_1^a, K_1^b, K_1^c)\) (resp. \((K_2, K_2^a, K_2^b, K_2^c)\)) so as to obtain a commutative cube, where \(\approx\) denotes a quasi-isomorphism (the two cubes below are approximate reconstructions of the three-dimensional diagrams of the original) :

\[\xymatrix@!0@C=3em@R=2.4em{ & K_1^{a} \ar[rr] \ar[dd] & & K_1 \ar[dd] \\ K_1^{a'} \ar[ur]^{\approx} \ar[rr] \ar[dd] & & K_1' \ar[ur]_(0.35){\approx} \ar[dd] & \\ & K_1^{c} \ar[rr] & & K_1^{b} \\ K_1^{c'} \ar[ur]^{\approx} \ar[rr] & & K_1^{b'} \ar[ur]_(0.35){\approx} & }\]
with \(K_1'\), \(K_1^{a'}\), \(K_1^{b'}\), \(K_1^{c'}\) split for the functor \(L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^*\) (resp.

\[\xymatrix@!0@C=3em@R=2.4em{ & K_2^{a} \ar[rr] \ar[dd] & & K_2 \ar[dd] \\ K_2^{a'} \ar[ur]^{\approx} \ar[rr] \ar[dd] & & K_2' \ar[ur]_(0.35){\approx} \ar[dd] & \\ & K_2^{c} \ar[rr] & & K_2^{b} \\ K_2^{c'} \ar[ur]^{\approx} \ar[rr] & & K_2^{b'} \ar[ur]_(0.35){\approx} & }\]

with \(K_2'\), \(K_2^a\), \(K_2^b\), \(K_2^c\) split for the functor \(Rf'_*\)). Using the usual base change morphisms, one obtains a commutative prism of complexes over \(S'\) (approximate reconstruction) :
and one concludes by noting that the arrows of the diagram (4.2.13.1) are identified with the following composite arrows:
for \(\varphi\) : the composite of the arrows (1) ;
for \(L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^*(u')\) : the composite of the arrows (2), one of which is the inverse of a quasi-isomorphism ;
for \(Rf'_*(v')\) : the composite of the arrows (3), one of which is the inverse of a quasi-isomorphism ;
for \(c'_{uv}\) : the composite of the arrows (4).
In the general case, set \(K_1' = f_*K\) and \(K_2' = f'^*L \otimes g'^*K\). One then has a diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=3em{ & L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^*Rf_*K \ar[rr]^-{\varphi} & & Rf'_*(f'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg'^*K) & \\ L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^*K_1 \ar[ur] \ar[r] & L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^*K_1' \ar[u] \ar[rr] & & Rf'_* K_2' \ar[u] \ar[r] & Rf'_* K_2 \ar[ul] } \, ,\]
whose triangles are commutative, as is the inner rectangle by what precedes. The contour is therefore commutative, and this proves 4.2.13.
4.3. The base change theorem.
One proposes to reformulate, in terms of derived categories, the base change theorem for proper morphisms XII 5.1 (iii).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.3.1

Let a cartesian diagram of schemes

\[\xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ X' \ar[r]^{g'} \ar[d]_{f'} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ S' \ar[r]_{g} & S }\]

with \(f\) proper. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{A}'\) be torsion sheaves of rings on \(S\) and \(S'\) and \(L\) a complex, bounded above, of \((\mathcal{A}', g^*\mathcal{A})\)-bimodules. One supposes that the dimension of the fibres of \(f\) is bounded. Hypothesis 4.2.12 (a) is then fulfilled, and the base change arrow (4.2.12.3), between functors from \(D^-(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\) to \(D^-(S', \mathcal{A}')\) :

\[\varphi_K : L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg^* Rf_*K \longrightarrow Rf'_*(f'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Lg'^* K) \, ,\]

is an isomorphism.

The functors under consideration are triangulated and "way-out" [RD I 7], so that, to verify that \(\varphi_K\) is an isomorphism, it suffices to verify that the \(\varphi_{\underline{H}^i(K)}\) are isomorphisms. One may therefore suppose that \(K\) is reduced to a (torsion) sheaf of \(f^*\mathcal{A}\)-modules placed in degree 0.

To verify that \(\varphi_K\) is an isomorphism, it suffices to verify it after applying the forgetful functor from the category of \(\mathcal{A}'\)-Modules to that of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)-Modules, where \(n\mathcal{A} = n\mathcal{A}' = 0\).

This allows one to reduce to the case where \(\mathcal{A}' = \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\), with \(n\mathcal{A} = 0\). One may then replace \(L\) by a complex isomorphic to it in the derived category, with flat components over \(g^*\mathcal{A}\), and bounded above. Since the functors under consideration are triangulated and "way out" in \(L\), it suffices to verify that \(\varphi_K\) is an isomorphism after replacing \(L\) by one of its components. One may therefore suppose that \(L\) is reduced to a sheaf of flat \(g^*\mathcal{A}\)-modules placed in degree 0. It must be proved that the arrows
\[\varphi^q : L \otimes g^*R^q f_*K \longrightarrow R^q f'_*(f'^*L \otimes g'^*K)\]

are isomorphisms. Let \(s\) be a geometric point of \(S'\), \(X_s\) the fibre of \(X'\) at \(s\) and \(K_s\) the inverse image of \(K\) on \(X_s\). By XII 5.1 (iii), the fibre at \(s\) of \(\varphi^q\) is the arrow
\[\varphi^q_s : L_s \otimes H^q(X_s, K) \longrightarrow H^q(X_s, L_s \otimes K) \, .\]

By D. Lazard's theorem [1], the flat \(\mathcal{A}_s\)-module \(L_s\) is a filtering inductive limit of free \(\mathcal{A}_s\)-modules \(L_{s,i}\); the functor \(H^q(X_s, *)\) commutes with filtering inductive limits. The arrow \(\varphi^q\) is therefore the inductive limit of the arrows
\[\varphi^q_i : L_{s,i} \otimes H^q(X_s, K) \longrightarrow H^q(X_s, L_{s,i} \otimes K) \, .\]
These last are obviously isomorphisms, hence so is \(\varphi^q_s\), and \(\varphi\) is an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Variants
blocks.html:
Variants 4.3.2

(i) When \(L\) is a bounded complex with components of finite Tor-dimension over \(g^*\mathcal{A}\), the hypotheses (c) of 4.2.12 are fulfilled, and one may work in the whole derived category.

(ii) If \(L\) is bounded below, with components of finite Tor-dimension over \(g^*\mathcal{A}\), the hypotheses (b) of 4.2.12 are fulfilled, even if \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{A}'\) are not torsion; the base change arrow \(\varphi_K\) (\(K \in D^+(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\)) will be an isomorphism if the sheaves \(\underline{H}^i(K)\) are torsion.

pages.title: 5. The direct image functors with proper support.

blocks.html: 5. The direct image functors with proper support.
5.1. The fundamental construction.

One proposes to follow the program indicated in 3.1 and to define the functor \(Rf_!\) for \(f\) a compactifiable morphism (3.2). It will be shown in an appendix how to treat the case of an arbitrary separated morphism of finite type.

5.1.1. Let \(X\) be a topos, \(U\) an open of \(X\) (IV 8.3) and \(j\) the inclusion morphism of \(U\) into \(X\). One defined in IV 5.2 an "extension by the empty set" functor from the category of sheaves of sets on \(U\) to that of sheaves of sets on \(X\). This functor \(j_!\) is left adjoint to the restriction functor \(j^*\).

One also denotes by \(j_!\) the functor from the category of sheaves of pointed sets on \(U\) (resp. of sheaves of groups, resp. of sheaves of \(j^*\mathcal{A}\)-modules for \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of rings on \(X\)) to the analogous category on \(X\), left adjoint to the restriction functor \(j^*\) (IV ). These three functors \(j_!\) are compatible with the forgetful functors, from the category of Modules to that of Groups, and from the category of Groups to that of pointed Sets (∗). If \(i : F \longrightarrow X\) is the inclusion of the closed complement of \(U\), then \(j^*j_!\) is (canonically isomorphic to) the identity and \(i^*j_!\) is the constant functor with value the initial object (or final, which here amounts to the same thing). This moreover characterizes \(j_!\). One deduces that the three functors \(j_!\) considered are exact and inject into the corresponding functors \(j_*\). They are called extension by zero functors. The formula \((j_1 j_2)^* = j_2^* j_1^*\) transposes into a transitivity isomorphism
The functors \(j_!\) are compatible with base changes:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.1.2

Let \(f : X \longrightarrow Y\) be a morphism of topoi, \(V\) an open of \(Y\) and \(U\) its inverse image in \(X\) :

\[\xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ U \ar[r]^{f'} \ar[d]_{j'} & V \ar[d]^{j} \\ X \ar[r]_{f} & Y }\]

There then exists one and only one base change isomorphism \(f^*j_! \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} j'_! f'^*\) making the diagram

\[(5.1.2.1) \qquad \xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2.4em{ f^*j_! \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d] & j'_! f'^* \ar[d] \\ f^*j_* \ar[r]_-{\alpha} & j'_* f'^* } \, ,\]

commutative, where \(\alpha\) is the base change arrow.

Proof. The base change arrow \(\varphi : j^*f_* \longrightarrow f'_*j'^*\) is trivially an isomorphism. It transposes into a base change isomorphism \(\varphi' : j'_! f'^* \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} f^*j_!\). To verify that the diagram (5.1.2.1) is commutative, it suffices to see that its restriction to \(U\) is, which is trivial.

5.1.3. Under the hypotheses of 5.1.1, with \(X\) ringed by a sheaf of rings \(\mathcal{A}\), the functor \(j_!\) on Modules is exact, hence passes trivially to the derived categories and defines a functor, still denoted \(j_!\), from \(D(U, j^*\mathcal{A})\) to \(D(X, \mathcal{A})\). One again has transitivity isomorphisms
One again has, at the level of the derived categories, an adjunction formula
\[(5.1.3.2) \qquad \operatorname{Hom}_{D(X)}(j_! K, L) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Hom}_{D(U)}(K, j^*L) \, .\]

5.1.4. Let \(f : X \longrightarrow Y\) be a proper morphism, \(\mathcal{A}\) a torsion sheaf of rings on \(Y\), and let us ring \(X\) by the inverse-image sheaf of rings of \(\mathcal{A}\). Suppose that the dimension of the fibres of \(f\) is bounded above by an integer \(n\) (which is the case if \(Y\) is quasi-compact). One then knows that for each sheaf of \(f^*\mathcal{A}\)-modules \(F\) on \(X\), the sheaves \(R^q f_* F\) vanish for \(q > 2n\) (XII 5.3 bis). The functor \(f_*\) therefore admits a derived functor (1.2.10)
\[Rf_* : D(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D(Y, \mathcal{A}) \, .\]
If \(f\) is the composite \(g\, h\) of two proper morphisms, one has a transitivity formula \(Rf_* = Rg_* Rh_*\), which one may, as usual, express in terms of cofibred categories (Scholium 5.1.3).
5.1.5. Let a commutative diagram of schemes

in which \(j_1\) and \(j_2\) are open immersions and \(f\), \(g\) proper morphisms whose fibre dimension is bounded above by an integer \(n\). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a torsion sheaf of rings on \(Y\), and let us ring \(U\), \(V\) and \(X\) by the inverse images of \(\mathcal{A}\). By 5.1.3.2, if \(K \in D(U)\), to define an arrow
\[(5.1.5.2) \qquad d : j_{2!}\, Rg_* K \longrightarrow Rf_* j_{1!}\, K\]
amounts to defining an arrow
\[d' : Rg_* K \longrightarrow j_2^* Rf_* j_{1!}\, K \, .\]
The fibre product \(X' = V \times_Y X\) fits into a commutative diagram
and, trivially, one has \(j_2^* Rf_* j_{1!}\, K \simeq Rf'_*(j'^*_2 j_{1!}\, K) \simeq Rf'_* k_! K\).

The arrow \(k\) is a proper open immersion; one therefore has \(k_! = k_*\), whence an isomorphism \(Rf'_* k_! K \simeq Rf'_* k_* K \simeq Rg_* K\), which provides us with the sought isomorphism \(d'\) and the morphism \(d\). One sees moreover that the restriction of \(d\) to \(V\) is an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.1.6

The morphism 5.1.5.2 is an isomorphism.

It remains to verify that the restriction of \(d\) to \(Y - V = F\) is an isomorphism. Let \(X'' = X \times_Y F\) and let us apply the base change theorem for a proper morphism (4.3.1) to the cartesian square
\[\xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ X'' \ar[r]^{i'} \ar[d]_{f''} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ F \ar[r]_{i} & Y } \, ,\]
for \(\mathcal{A}' = i^*\mathcal{A}\) and \(L = \mathcal{A}'[0]\). One finds:
so that both sides of (5.1.5.2) vanish outside \(U\) and \(d\) is an isomorphism.

5.1.7. Let \(S\) be a scheme ringed by a torsion sheaf of rings \(\mathcal{A}\). For every \(S\)-scheme \(\varphi : X \longrightarrow S\), one sets \(\mathcal{A}_X = \varphi^*\mathcal{A}\). Let us place ourselves in the category \((S)\) of quasi-compact quasi-separated \(S\)-schemes and \(S\)-compactifiable morphisms (3.2). By 3.2.3, this category, the subcategory \((S,i)\) of open immersions, and the subcategory \((S,p)\) of proper morphisms satisfy hypotheses 3.2.4.
One proposes to apply the theory 3.3.2 to the following data (notation of 3.3.1)
\(\alpha\)) \(F(X) = D(X, \mathcal{A}_X)\) for \(\varphi : X \longrightarrow S\) in \(S\) :
(i) For \(p : X \longrightarrow Y\) proper, one takes for the functor \(p_*\) the functor \(Rp_*\).
(ii) One uses the usual transitivity isomorphisms \(R(pq)_* = Rp_* Rq_*\).
(i') For an open immersion \(i : X \longrightarrow Y\), one takes for the functor \(i_*\) the functor \(i_!\).
(ii') One uses the transitivity isomorphisms (5.1.3.1).
(iii) For every commutative diagram (5.1.5.1) one takes for the isomorphism \(d\) the isomorphism (5.1.5.2).
One verifies conditions (a) (b) (c) (a') (b') (c') of 3.3.2, which proves point (a) of the:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.1.8

(a) In the category \((S)\) defined in 5.1.7, one can, in one and essentially only one way, define for every arrow \(f : X \longrightarrow Y\) a functor

\[Rf_! : D(X, \mathcal{A}_X) \longrightarrow D(Y, \mathcal{A}_Y) \, ,\]

and for every composite morphism \(f = g h : X \xrightarrow{\;h\;} Y \xrightarrow{\;g\;} Z\) transitivity isomorphisms \(c_{f,g}\) between \(Rf_!\) and \(Rg_! Rh_!\) such that

(i) The \(c_{f,g}\) satisfy the "cocycle condition"

\[(c_{f,g} * Rh_!) \circ c_{fg,h} = (Rf_! * c_{g,h}) \circ c_{f,gh} \, .\]

(ii) When one restricts to the proper morphisms (resp. to the open immersions) one recovers the variance theory 5.1.4 (resp. 5.1.3).

(iii) For every diagram (5.1.5.1), the isomorphism \(d\) (5.1.5.2) is the composite isomorphism \(c_{f,j'} \circ c_{j,f'}^{-1}\).

(b) The functors \(Rf_!\) are "way out" [RD I 7] and triangulated.

Every functor \(Rf_!\) is composed of a functor \(Rg_*\), for \(g\) proper with quasi-compact target, hence with fibres of bounded dimension, and a functor \(j_!\), for \(j\) an open immersion. These functors are way out and triangulated, hence so is \(Rf_!\).
5.1.8.1. The transitivity isomorphisms 5.1.8 (a) are often used via the "composite functors" spectral sequence deduced from them, valid for \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D(X, \mathcal{A}_X)\) :
\[(5.1.8.2) \qquad E_2^{pq} = R^p g_! R^q h_!(K) \Longrightarrow R^{p+q} f_!(K) \, .\]
To obtain it, one notes that, by 5.1.8 b) and [VERDIER 2], for every \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D(Y, \mathcal{A}_Y)\), one has a spectral sequence
\[(5.1.8.3) \qquad E_2^{pq} = R^p g_! (\underline{H}^q(L)) \Longrightarrow R^{p+q} g_!(L) \, ,\]
and (5.1.8.2) is the special case of (5.1.8.3) for \(L = Rh_!\, K\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.1.9

(i) One calls "total direct image functors with proper support" the functors constructed in 5.1.8. One will omit the adjective "total" when there is no risk of confusion.

(ii) One calls \(q^{\text{th}}\) direct image functor with proper support, and denotes by \(R^q f_!\), the composite functor \(\mathscr{H}^q \circ Rf_!\).

(iii) If \(X\) is a scheme over a separably closed field \(k\), embeddable in a scheme proper over \(k\), one identifies sheaves of modules on \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\) with usual modules, and one denotes the functor \(R^q f_!\) by one of the notations \(H^q_c(X, \ )\), \(H^q_!(X, \ )\), or simply \(H^q_c(\ )\) if there is no danger of confusion. It is then called the "\(q^{\text{th}}\) hypercohomology group with proper support", or "\(q^{\text{th}}\) cohomology group with proper support" if it is applied to a complex reduced to degree \(0\).
5.1.9.1. The notation \(Rf_!\) is abusive in that the functor \(Rf_!\) is not the right derived functor of the functor \(f_!\) that will be defined in 6.1.2. Some prefer the notation \(R_! f\).

5.1.10. The ingredients in the proof of 5.1.8 are the proper base change theorem and the identity between \(j_*\) and \(j_!\) when \(j\) is a proper open immersion. This allows one to state various variants of 5.1.8; we leave it to the reader to give them a precise meaning and to verify them.

blocks.title: Variant
blocks.html:
Variant 5.1.11

In the category \((S)\), one can, in one and essentially only one way, define for every arrow \(f : X \longrightarrow Y\) a functor \(f_!\) from the category of sheaves of pointed sets on \(X\) to the category of sheaves of pointed sets on \(Y\) and, for every composite morphism \(f = g h\), transitivity isomorphisms satisfying conditions (i), (ii) (iii) analogous to those of 5.1.4.
See 6.1.2 for a direct description of this functor.

blocks.title: Variant
blocks.html:
Variant 5.1.12

For every compactifiable morphism \(f : X \longrightarrow Y\), one can define a functor \(R^1 f_!\) from the category of sheaves of Ind-finite groups on \(X\) to the category of sheaves of pointed sets on \(Y\), with, for every compactification \(f = \bar{f} j\) of \(f\), an isomorphism \(R^1 f_! \simeq R^1 \bar{f}_* \circ j_!\).

One postulates here no transitivity formula; the only problem is to show that the functor \(R^1 f_!\) does not depend on the chosen compactification of \(f\). Let \(p : (\bar{f}_1, i_1) \longrightarrow (\bar{f}_2, i_2)\) be a morphism of compactifications, i.e. a diagram
\[(5.1.12.1) \qquad \xymatrix@C=3.5em@R=2.5em{ X \ar[r]^{i_1} \ar[dr]^{i_2} \ar[dd]_{f} & \bar{X}_1 \ar[d]^{p} \\ & \bar{X}_2 \ar[dl]^{\bar{f}_2} \\ Y & } \, ,\]
where \(\bar{f}_1 = \bar{f}_2 \circ p\), \(p\) being proper. If \(G\) is a sheaf of groups on \(X\), one has an exact sequence of pointed sets (with \(\alpha\) injective)
\[0 \longrightarrow R^1 \bar{f}_{2*}(p_* i_{1!}\, G) \xrightarrow{\;\alpha\;} R^1 \bar{f}_{1*}(i_{1!}\, G) \longrightarrow \bar{f}_{2*} R^1 p_*(i_{1!}\, G) \, ,\]

and an arrow from \(i_{2!}\, G\) into \(p_* i_{1!}\, G\), whence by composition an arrow \(\beta\) from \(R^1 \bar{f}_{2*} i_{2!}\, G\) into \(R^1 \bar{f}_{1*} i_{1!}\, G\). Arguing as in 3.3.2.1, one sees that the problem is to prove that this arrow is always an isomorphism when \(G\) is Ind-finite.
If one applies the proper base change theorem to \(p\) and to the sheaf of sets \(i_{1!}\, G\), one verifies that \(p_* i_{1!}\, G = i_{2!}\, G\), whence the exact sequence
\[0 \longrightarrow R^1 \bar{f}_{2*}(i_{2!}\, G) \xrightarrow{\;\beta\;} R^1 \bar{f}_{1*}(i_{1!}\, G) \longrightarrow \bar{f}_{2*} R^1 p_* i_{1!}\, G \, .\]

The arrow \(\beta\) is injective (since \(\alpha\) is). If one applies the proper base change theorem to \(p\) and to the sheaf of groups \(G\), assumed Ind-finite, one finds that \(R^1 p_* i_{1!}\, G = 0\). Hence \(\beta\) is an epimorphism, which completes the proof of 5.1.12.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.1.13

For every site \(X\), one denotes by \(D_{\mathrm{tors}}(X)\) the full subcategory of the derived category of the category of abelian sheaves on \(X\), formed of the complexes whose cohomology sheaves are torsion.

blocks.title: Variant
blocks.html:
Variant 5.1.14

In the category \((S)\), one can, in one and essentially only one way, define for every arrow \(f : X \longrightarrow Y\) a triangulated and "way out" functor [RD, I 7]

\[Rf_! : D^+_{\mathrm{tors}}(X) \longrightarrow D^+_{\mathrm{tors}}(Y)\]

and for every composite morphism \(f = g h\) transitivity isomorphisms satisfying conditions (i) (ii) (iii) analogous to those of 5.1.4.

blocks.title: Variant
blocks.html:
Variant 5.1.15

Let us place ourselves in the category of \(S\)-schemes ringed by torsion sheaves, the arrows being the morphisms of ringed schemes inducing (0.8) an \(S\)-compactifiable morphism of schemes. For every arrow \(f : (X, \mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow (Y, \mathcal{B})\), let \(Rf_!\) be the composite of the forgetful functor from the category of \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules to that of \(f^*\mathcal{B}\)-modules, and of \(Rf_!\). These functors enjoy the variance properties of the usual functors \(Rf_!\).

It will be noted, however, that the notation \(Rf_!\) is reasonable here only if \(\mathcal{A}\) is finite over \(f^*\mathcal{B}\), as one realizes by taking \(X = Y = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(k\) algebraically closed.

5.1.16. Let \(f : X \longrightarrow S\) be a compactifiable morphism, \(j : U \longrightarrow X\) an open of \(X\), \(i : F \longrightarrow X\) the closed complement, \(\mathcal{A}_S\) a torsion sheaf of rings on \(S\), \(\mathcal{A}_X\) its inverse image on \(X\) and \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D(X, \mathcal{A}_X)\).
The exact sequence of complexes
\[0 \longrightarrow j_! j^*K \longrightarrow K \longrightarrow i_* i^*K \longrightarrow 0\]
gives rise to a distinguished triangle in \(D(X, \mathcal{A}_X)\) [VERDIER C.D. I 2.4]. Its image under \(Rf_!\) is a distinguished triangle (5.1.8 (b))
\[(5.1.16.1) \qquad R(fj)_! j^*K \longrightarrow Rf_! K \longrightarrow R(fi)_! i^*K \longrightarrow R(fj)_! j^*K[1] \cdots\]
which defines a long exact cohomology sequence
\[(5.1.16.2) \qquad \cdots R^q(fj)_! j^*K \longrightarrow R^q f_! K \longrightarrow R^q(fi)_! i^*K \xrightarrow{\;\partial\;} R^{q+1}(fj)_! j^*K \longrightarrow \cdots\]
In the special case where \(S\) is the spectrum of a separably closed field and \(K\) is reduced to a sheaf \(\underline{G}\) placed in degree 0, the sequence (5.1.16.2) is written
\[(5.1.16.3) \qquad \cdots H^q_c(U, \underline{G}) \longrightarrow H^q_c(X, \underline{G}) \longrightarrow H^q_c(F, \underline{G}) \xrightarrow{\;\partial\;} H^{q+1}_c(U, \underline{G}) \cdots\]
5.1.17. Let a diagram of \(S\)-compactifiable schemes
\[\xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ X \ar[rr]^{u} \ar[dr]_{f} & & Y \ar[dl]^{g} \\ & S & } \, ,\]

with \(u\) proper. One rings \(X\) and \(Y\) by the inverse image of a torsion sheaf of rings \(\mathcal{A}_S\) on \(S\). For \(K \in D(Y, \mathcal{A}_Y)\), the obvious (adjunction) arrow \(K \longrightarrow Ru_* u^*K\) defines, by application of the functor \(Rg_!\), an arrow
\[(5.1.17.1) \qquad u^* : Rg_! K \longrightarrow Rg_! Ru_* u^*K = Rg_! Ru_! u^*K \simeq Rf_! u^*K\]
(contravariance of cohomology with proper support with respect to proper morphisms).
For \(S\) the spectrum of an algebraically closed field and \(K\) reduced to a sheaf \(\underline{G}\) placed in degree 0, this arrow is written
\[(5.1.17.2) \qquad u^* : H^q_c(Y, \underline{G}) \longrightarrow H^q_c(X, \underline{G}) \, .\]
5.2. The base change theorem.

5.2.1. Let \(f : X \longrightarrow Y\) be a morphism of topoi, \(V\) an open of \(Y\), \(U = f^{-1}(V)\) its inverse image in \(X\), \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of rings on \(Y\), \(\mathcal{A}'\) a sheaf of rings on \(X\) and \(L\) a complex, bounded above, of \((\mathcal{A}', f^*\mathcal{A})\)-bimodules:
\[(5.2.1.1) \qquad \xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ U \ar[r]^{f'} \ar[d]_{j'} & V \ar[d]^{j} \\ X \ar[r]_{f} & Y } \, .\]
One then has a base change isomorphism (5.1.2.1) between functors from \(D(V, \mathcal{A})\) to \(D(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\) : \(f^*j_! \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} j'_! f'^*\).

Moreover, one has an obvious isomorphism between functors from \(D^-(U, f'^*\mathcal{A})\) to \(D^-(X, \mathcal{A}')\) : \(L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{f^*\mathcal{A}} j'_! K \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} j'_!(j'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{f'^*\mathcal{A}} K)\). To construct it, it suffices to note that if a complex \(K\) is split for the functor \(j'^*L \otimes_{f'^*\mathcal{A}} {\ }\), then the complex \(j'_! K\) is split for the functor \(L \otimes_{f^*\mathcal{A}} {\ }\), and that one has an isomorphism of the preceding type at the level of complexes. Composing these two isomorphisms, one obtains a base change isomorphism between functors from \(D^-(V, \mathcal{A})\) to \(D^-(X, \mathcal{A}')\) :
\[(5.2.1.2) \qquad L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{f^*\mathcal{A}} f^* j_! K \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} j'_!(j'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{f'^*\mathcal{A}} f'^*K) \, .\]
If \(L\) is bounded with components of finite tor-dimension over \(f^*\mathcal{A}\), this isomorphism is still defined for \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D(V, \mathcal{A})\).

5.2.2. Let \(f : X \longrightarrow S\) and \(g : S' \longrightarrow S\) be morphisms of schemes, and suppose that \(f\) is the composite of an open immersion \(j\) and a proper morphism \(p\), whose fibre dimension is bounded by an integer \(n\) (automatic for \(S\) quasi-compact). These morphisms fit into a diagram with cartesian squares

\[\xymatrix@C=2.5em@R=2em{ X' \ar[rr]^{g'} \ar[dr]^{j'} \ar[dddr]_{f'} & & X \ar[dr]^{j} & \\ & \bar{X}' \ar[rr]^(0.32){\bar{g}} \ar[dd]^(0.35){p'} & & \bar{X} \ar[dd]^{p} \\ & & & \\ & S' \ar[rr]_{g} & & S }\]

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a torsion sheaf of rings on \(S\), \(\mathcal{A}'\) a torsion sheaf of rings on \(S'\) and \(L\) a complex, bounded above, of \((\mathcal{A}', g^*\mathcal{A})\)-bimodules. One rings \(X\) and \(\bar{X}\) (resp. \(X'\) and \(\bar{X}'\)) by the inverse images \(\mathcal{A}_X\) and \(\mathcal{A}_{\bar{X}}\) (resp. \(\mathcal{A}'_{X'}\) and \(\mathcal{A}'_{\bar{X}'}\)) of \(\mathcal{A}\) (resp. \(\mathcal{A}'\)) on \(X\) and \(\bar{X}\) (resp. \(X'\) and \(\bar{X}'\)). One then has base change isomorphisms (5.2.1.2) between the functors \(p'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} \bar{g}^* j_! K\) and \(j'_!(f'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} g'^*K)\) from \(D^-(X, \mathcal{A}_X)\) to \(D^-(\bar{X}', \mathcal{A}'_{\bar{X}'})\), and base change isomorphisms (4.3.1) between the functors \(L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} g^* Rp_* K\) and \(Rp'_*(p'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} \bar{g}^*K)\) from \(D^-(\bar{X}, \mathcal{A}_{\bar{X}})\) to \(D^-(S', \mathcal{A}')\). By composition, one deduces a base change isomorphism between functors from \(D^-(X, \mathcal{A}_X)\) to \(D^-(S', \mathcal{A}')\) :
\[(5.2.2.1) \qquad L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} g^* Rp_* j_! K \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} Rp'_* j'_!(f'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} g'^*K) \, .\]

When \(L\) is bounded with components of finite tor-dimension, the preceding arguments and 4.3.2 (i) allow one to define the base change isomorphism for \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D(X, \mathcal{A}_X)\).

In order to be able to refer to 5.1.8, suppose that \(S\) is quasi-compact quasi-separated. The functors \(Rp_* j_! = Rf_!\) and \(Rp'_* j'_! = Rf'_!\) then depend only on \(f\) and \(f'\), which gives a meaning to the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.2.3

The base change isomorphism (5.2.2.1) does not depend on the chosen compactification \(f = p j\) of \(X\).
Let a morphism of compactifications \(q : \bar{X}_1 \longrightarrow \bar{X}_2\)

The base change isomorphism \(c_1\) relative to \(\bar{X}_1\) is obtained by "composing" those relative to \(j_1\) and \(p_1\), or again by composing those relative to \(j_1\), \(q\) and \(p_2\). The isomorphism \(c_2\) relative to \(\bar{X}_2\) is obtained by composing those relative to \(j_2\) and \(p_2\). To verify that \(c_1 = c_2\), it suffices to verify that the isomorphism \(c'_1\) relative to \(j_2\) is obtained as the composite \(c'_2\) of those relative to \(j_1\) and \(q\). Let us denote by a \('\) the arrows deduced by the base change \(g\) from the arrows (5.2.3.1); \(c'_1\) and \(c'_2\) are isomorphisms
\[c'_1, c'_2 : L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} \bar{g}_2^* j_{2!} K \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} j'_{2!}(j'^*_2 L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} g'^*K) \, .\]
By (5.1.3.2), to verify that \(c'_1 = c'_2\), it suffices to verify it after restricting to \(X'_2\), which is trivial.
The base change isomorphisms relative to two compactifications between which there exists a morphism are therefore equal, and one concludes by 3.2.6 (ii).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.2.4

Let \(f = u v : X \longrightarrow Y \longrightarrow S\) be a composite of \(S\)-compactifiable morphisms. The base change isomorphisms (5.2.2.1) relative to \(u\), \(v\) and \(f\) give rise to a commutative diagram (notation of (5.2.4.1) below) :

\[\xymatrix@C=2em@R=3em{ L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} g^* R(uv)_! K \ar[rr]^-{\sim} \ar@{=}[d] & & R(u'v')_!((u'v')^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} g''^*K) \ar@{=}[d] \\ L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} g^* Ru_! Rv_! K \ar[r]^-{\sim} & Ru'_!(u'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} g'^* Rv_! K) \ar[r]^-{\sim} & Ru'_! Rv'_!(v'^*u'^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} g''^*K) } \, .\]
Let us choose a compactification of \((u,v)\) (3.2.5):

Lemma 5.2.4 expresses that the base change isomorphism \(c_1\) relative to \(f\) is the composite \(c_2\) of those relative to \(u\) and \(v\). The isomorphism \(c_1\) is obtained by composing the base change isomorphisms relative to \(j_1\), \(j_2\), \(p_3\) and \(p_2\). For \(c_2\), one composes those relative to \(j_1\), \(p_1\), \(j_3\), \(p_2\). It therefore suffices to compare the isomorphisms \(c'_1\), the composite of those relative to \(p_3\) and \(j_2\), and \(c'_2\), the composite of those relative to \(j_3\) and \(p_1\).
Consider the cartesian diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=1.6em@R=2em{ \bar{X}' \ar[rrr]^{\bar{g}''} \ar[dr]^{j'_2} \ar[dd]_{p'_1} & & & \bar{X} \ar[dr]^{j_2} & \\ & \bar{\bar{X}}' \ar[rrr]^(0.3){\bar{\bar{g}}} \ar[drr]_(0.4){p'_3} & & & \bar{\bar{X}} \\ Y' \ar[rrr]^(0.25){g'} \ar[dr]^{j'_3} \ar[dd]_{v'} & & & Y \ar[dr]^{j_3} \ar[dd]^(0.3){v} & \\ & \bar{Y}' \ar[rrr]^(0.3){\bar{g}'} \ar[dl]_{p'_2} & & & \bar{Y} \ar[dl]^{p_2} \\ S' \ar[rrr]_{g} & & & S & \\ }\]
\[c'_1, c'_2 : L' \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} \bar{g}'^* R(j_3 p_1)_! K \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} R(j'_3 p'_1)_!((j'_3 p'_1)^*L' \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} \bar{g}''^*K) \, .\]
By (5.1.3.2), to verify that \(c'_1 = c'_2\), it suffices to verify that \(j'^*_3(c'_1) = j'^*_3(c'_2)\), which is trivial.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.2.5

Let morphisms of schemes ringed by torsion sheaves of rings

\[(S'', \mathcal{A}'') \xrightarrow{\;g_2\;} (S', \mathcal{A}') \xrightarrow{\;g_1\;} (S, \mathcal{A}) \, ,\]

and \(f : X \longrightarrow S\) a compactifiable morphism, whence a diagram :
One rings \(X\), \(X'\), \(X''\) by \(f^*\mathcal{A}\), \(f'^*\mathcal{A}'\) and \(f''^*\mathcal{A}''\). Then, the diagram
is commutative.
This lemma follows immediately from the analogous results for the functors \(j_!\) and \(Rp_*\) for \(p\) proper. We leave to the reader the task of adapting it.
We summarize the preceding statements in the

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.2.6

The functor \(Rf_!\) commutes with base change.

blocks.title: Variants
blocks.html:
Variants 5.2.7

(i) The functors \(f_!\) (for sheaves of pointed sets: 5.1.11) and the functors \(R^1 f_!\) (for sheaves of groups: 5.1.12) commute with base change.

(ii) The functors \(Rf_!\) (5.1.14) commute with base change.

(iii) Under the hypotheses (5.2.2), if \(L\) is bounded and has components of finite tor-dimension, the functors \(Rf_! : D(X) \longrightarrow D(S)\), commute with base change.
Theorem 5.2.6 is essentially equivalent to the conjunction of the following two corollaries 5.2.8 and 5.2.9.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2.8

Let \(f : X \longrightarrow S\) be a compactifiable morphism, and \(\mathfrak{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). For every geometric point \(s\) of \(S\), let \(X_s\) be the geometric fibre of \(X\) at \(s\) and \(\mathfrak{F}_s\) the induced sheaf. We have canonically

\[(R^q f_!(\mathfrak{F}))_s = H^q_c(X_s, \mathfrak{F}_s) \, .\]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.2.8.1

If the fibres of \(f\) are of dimension \(\leq d\), the functor \(Rf_!\) is of cohomological dimension \(\leq 2d\) (1.2.9): for every torsion sheaf \(F\), we have \(R^i f_! F = 0\) for \(i > 2d\). The functor \(R^{2d} f_!\) is therefore right exact on the category of torsion sheaves.

By base change (5.2.8) we reduce to the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field. If then \(\bar{X}\) is a proper scheme over \(S\) containing \(X\) as a dense Zariski open, \(j : X \longrightarrow \bar{X}\), we have \(\dim(\bar{X}) = \dim(X) \leq d\). For \(\underline{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\) and \(i > 2d\), we thus have, by X 4.3, 5.2
\[H^i_c(X, \underline{F}) = H^i(\bar{X}, j_! \underline{F}) = 0 \, .\]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2.9
