Let \(f : X \longrightarrow S\) be a compactifiable morphism, \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of torsion rings on \(S\), \(K\) a bounded above complex of left \(f^*\mathcal{A}\)-modules and \(L\) a bounded above complex of right \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules. We have canonically

\[L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{A}} Rf_!(K) = Rf_!(f^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{f^*\mathcal{A}} K) \, .\]
This proposition formally implies the following result:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.2.10

Let \(f : X \longrightarrow S\) be a compactifiable morphism, \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of torsion rings on \(S\), \(K \in D^-(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\) and \(d \in \mathbb{Z}\). If \(K\) is of finite Tor-dimension \(\leq d\) (4.1.9), then \(Rf_! K\) is of finite Tor-dimension \(\leq d\).
It suffices to verify that for every sheaf of right \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules \(L\) on \(S\), we have
\[H^{-i}(L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Rf_! K) = 0 \quad \text{for } i > d \, .\]
By 5.2.9, we know that
\[H^{-i}(L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Rf_! K) = R^{-i} f_!(f^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} K) \, ,\]
moreover, by hypothesis,
\[H^{-i}(f^*L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} K) = 0 \quad \text{for } i > d \, ,\]
and we conclude by remarking that if a complex \(M\) of sheaves of modules on \(X\) satisfies \(H^{-i}(M) = 0\) for \(i > d\), then we still have \(H^{-i}(Rf_! M) = 0\) for \(i > d\).
In the special case of constant noetherian sheaves of rings, we have the more general result:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.2.11

Let \(f : X \longrightarrow S\) be a morphism of sites, \(A\) a ring, \(C\) its centre and \(d \in \mathbb{Z}\). We assume that

(i) the functor \(Rf_* : D^+(X,C) \longrightarrow D^+(S,C)\) is of finite cohomological dimension.

(ii) \(A\) is right noetherian.

(iii) \(S\) has enough points.

For every complex \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(X,A)\) of sheaves of left \(A\)-modules, if \(K\) is of finite Tor-dimension \(\leq d\), then the complex \(Rf_* K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(S,A)\) is of Tor-dimension \(\leq d\).
Proof. By virtue of (i), the functor \(f_*\) is derivable into functors
\[Rf_* : D(X,A) \longrightarrow D(S,A)\]
and
\[Rf_* : D(X,C) \longrightarrow D(S,C)\]

By 4.2.8, it suffices to verify that for every point \(s\) of \(S\), the complex \((Rf_* K)_s\) of \(A\)-modules is of Tor-dimension \(\leq d\); for this it suffices that for every right \(A\)-module \(L\) of finite type we have
\[H^{-i}(L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Rf_* K) = 0 \quad \text{for } i > d \, .\]
Reasoning as in 5.2.10, we see that for this it suffices that the "base change arrow"
\[(5.2.11.1) \qquad L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} Rf_* K \longrightarrow Rf_*(L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} K)\]
be an isomorphism.

Let \(L^*\) be a resolution of \(L\) by free \(A\)-modules of finite type. Since the functors under consideration are way-out on the right, it suffices to prove that (5.2.11.1) is an isomorphism after replacing \(L\) by any component of \(L_*\), and we are reduced to the trivial case where \(L\) is free of finite type.

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 5.2.12

(i) Hypothesis (iii) of 5.2.11 is probably unnecessary.

(ii) If we omit the noetherian hypothesis on \(A\), 5.2.11 remains valid when the functors \(R^i f_*\) commute with filtered inductive limits.

(iii) The hypothesis that \(S\) be ringed by a constant sheaf of rings is essential. One would obtain a counterexample by taking for \(S\) the spectrum of a strictly local discrete valuation ring, for \(f\) the inclusion of the generic point \(\eta\), for sheaf of rings \(\mathcal{A}\) the sheaf equal to \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) at the generic point and \(\mathbb{Z}/n^2\mathbb{Z}\) at the closed point \(s\) (\(n > 1\) prime to the residue characteristics) and for sheaf the module \(f^*\mathcal{A}\).
5.3. Comparison theorem and finiteness theorem.
5.3.1. To a scheme \(X\) of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\) are associated its étale site \(X_{\mathrm{ét}}\), its transcendental site \(X_{\mathrm{cl}}\) and a morphism of sites (XI 4)
\[\varepsilon : X_{\mathrm{cl}} \longrightarrow X_{\mathrm{ét}} \, .\]
If \(j : U \longrightarrow X\) is an open immersion, the commutative diagram
\[\xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ U_{\mathrm{cl}} \ar[r] \ar[d] & U_{\mathrm{ét}} \ar[d] \\ X_{\mathrm{cl}} \ar[r] & X_{\mathrm{ét}} }\]

identifies \(\widetilde{U_{\mathrm{cl}}}\) with the open subset of \(\widetilde{X_{\mathrm{cl}}}\) that is the inverse image of the open subset \(\widetilde{U_{\mathrm{ét}}}\) of \(\widetilde{X_{\mathrm{ét}}}\). If \(p : Y \longrightarrow X\) is a proper morphism, the continuous map \(p^{\mathrm{an}} : Y^{\mathrm{an}} \longrightarrow X^{\mathrm{an}}\) is proper and separated. To see this, we reduce by Chow's lemma to the case \(p\) projective.
Let \(f : X \longrightarrow S\) be a compactifiable morphism of schemes of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\), and let \(f = p j\) be a compactification of \(f\).

\[(5.3.1.1) \qquad \xymatrix@C=2em@R=2em{ X_{\mathrm{cl}} \ar[rrr]^{\varepsilon} \ar[dr]^{j_{\mathrm{cl}}} \ar[dddr]_{f_{\mathrm{cl}}} & & & X \ar[dr]^{j} & \\ & \bar{X}_{\mathrm{cl}} \ar[rrr]^(0.35){\varepsilon} \ar[dd]^(0.35){p_{\mathrm{cl}}} & & & \bar{X} \ar[dd]^{p} \\ & & & & \\ & S_{\mathrm{cl}} \ar[rrr]_{\varepsilon} & & & S }\]

The functor \(p_{\mathrm{cl}*} j_{\mathrm{cl}!}\) is none other than the direct image with proper support functor \(f_{\mathrm{cl}!}\) (see VERDIER [3]). If \(S_{\mathrm{cl}}\), hence \(X_{\mathrm{cl}}\), is separated, the functor \(j_{\mathrm{cl}!}\) transforms soft sheaves on \(X_{\mathrm{cl}}\) into a soft sheaf on \(\bar{X}_{\mathrm{cl}}\) [TF II 3.5.5]. Since the question is local on \(S\), it in any case transforms flabby sheaves on \(X_{\mathrm{cl}}\) into sheaves on \(X_{\mathrm{cl}}\) that are acyclic for the functor \(p_{\mathrm{cl}*}\). We thus have (cf. VERDIER [3])
\[Rf_{\mathrm{cl}*} = Rp_{\mathrm{cl}*} j_{\mathrm{cl}!} \, .\]
5.3.2. By 5.1.2, we have a base change isomorphism, between functors from \(D(X)\) to \(D(\bar{X}_{\mathrm{cl}})\)
\[\varepsilon^*j_! \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} j_{\mathrm{cl}!} \varepsilon^* \, .\]
By 4.2.12 or 4.1.5, we have a base change morphism between functors from \(D^+(\bar{X})\) to \(D^+(S_{\mathrm{cl}})\):
\[\varepsilon^*Rp_* \longrightarrow Rp_{\mathrm{cl}*} \varepsilon^* \, .\]
By composition, we deduce a base change morphism, between functors from \(D^+_{\mathrm{tors}}(X)\) to \(D^+_{\mathrm{tors}}(S_{\mathrm{cl}})\) (5.1.13)
\[(5.3.2.1) \qquad \varepsilon^*Rf_! \longrightarrow Rf_{\mathrm{cl}!} \varepsilon^* \, .\]
One verifies as in 5.2.3 that it does not depend on the chosen compactification of \(f\); it satisfies a transitivity formula of the type 5.2.4.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.3.3

(Comparison theorem). The morphism (5.3.2.1) is an isomorphism.

By construction, it suffices to treat the case where \(f\) is proper. The functors under consideration are triangulated and "way-out" [RD I 7]. It therefore suffices to treat the case where \(K\) reduces to a torsion sheaf placed in degree 0, and we conclude by XVI 4.1 (i).

blocks.title: Variants
blocks.html:
Variants 5.3.4

(i) If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a sheaf of torsion rings on \(S_{\mathrm{ét}}\), we likewise obtain an isomorphism (5.3.2.1) between functors from \(D(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\) to \(D(S, \varepsilon^*\mathcal{A})\).

(ii) In low degree, we find the usual variants for sheaves of pointed sets and sheaves of Ind-finite groups.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.5

Let \(X\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\), which can be compactified into a proper scheme over \(\mathbb{C}\), and \(F\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). We then have

\[H^q_c(X, F) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} H^q_c(X_{\mathrm{cl}}, \varepsilon^*F) \, .\]

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.3.6

Let \(f : X \longrightarrow S\) be a compactifiable morphism of finite presentation and \(A\) a left noetherian torsion ring. The functor \(Rf_! : D(X,A) \longrightarrow D(S,A)\) transforms complexes with constructible cohomology into complexes with constructible cohomology.

The assertion is local on \(S\), which we may assume affine. By passage to the limit, we reduce to the case \(S\) noetherian. The complexes with constructible cohomology form a triangulated subcategory of \(D(S,A)\). Since the functor \(Rf_!\) is "way-out", we reduce to verifying that if \(\mathfrak{F}\) is a constructible sheaf of \(A\)-modules, the sheaves \(R^q f_! \mathfrak{F}\) are constructible. Let \(f = pj\), with \(p\) proper and \(j\) an open immersion. We have \(R^q f_! \mathfrak{F} = R^q p_*(j_! \mathfrak{F})\). The sheaf \(j_! \mathfrak{F}\) is constructible and we conclude by XIV 1.1.
5.3.7. In low degrees, we have analogous statements for the direct images with proper support of a constructible sheaf of sets or of Ind-finite groups.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.8

Let \(X\) be a separated scheme of finite type over a separably closed field \(k\) and \(\mathfrak{F}\) a constructible torsion sheaf on \(X\). We assume that \(X\) can be compactified into a proper scheme over \(k\). Then the groups \(H^q_c(X, \mathfrak{F})\) are finite.
5.4. Künneth formula.
5.4.1. Let a commutative diagram (0.11) of sites be given

\[(5.4.1.1) \qquad \xymatrix@C=1.6em@R=2em{ & & Z' \ar[dll]_{p'} \ar[d]^{h} \ar[drr]^{q'} & & \\ X' \ar[dr]_{f} & & Z \ar[dl]_(0.4){p} \ar[dr]^(0.4){q} & & Y' \ar[dl]^{g} \\ & X \ar[dr] & & Y \ar[dl] & \\ & & S & & }\]

We assume \(S\) ringed by a sheaf of rings \(\mathcal{A}\), with centre \(\mathcal{C}\); we shall again denote by \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{C}\) the inverse images of these sheaves on the sites of (5.4.1.1).
If \(K\) is a sheaf of right \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules on \(X\) and \(L\) a sheaf of left \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules on \(Y\), we set
\[K \boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}} L = p^*K \otimes_{\mathcal{A}} q^*L\]

(external tensor product). Likewise for \(K\) (resp. \(L\)) on \(X'\) (resp. \(Y'\)). Let then \(K\) be a sheaf of right \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules on \(X'\) and \(L\) a sheaf of left \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules on \(Y'\). The base change arrows (XII 4.1) define
\[(5.4.1.2) \qquad \begin{cases} p^*f_* K \longrightarrow h_* p'^*K \\[4pt] q^*g_* L \longrightarrow h_* q'^*L \, , \end{cases}\]
whence, by tensor product, an arrow
\[(5.4.1.3) \qquad f_*K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} g_*L \longrightarrow h_* p'^*K \otimes_{\mathcal{A}} h_* q'^*L \longrightarrow h_*(K \boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}} L) \, .\]
Suppose that the functors

\[\begin{aligned} Rf_* &: D^+(X', \mathcal{A}^o) \longrightarrow D^+(X, \mathcal{A}^o) \\ Rg_* &: D^+(Y', \mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D^+(Y, \mathcal{A}) \\ Rh_* &: D^+(Z', \mathcal{C}) \longrightarrow D^+(Z, \mathcal{C}) \end{aligned}\]

are of finite cohomological dimension, and hence extend to the entire derived categories. It is then natural, for \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(X', \mathcal{A}^o)\) and \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(Y', \mathcal{A})\), to define a Künneth arrow
\[(5.4.1.4) \qquad Rf_* K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} Rg_* L \longrightarrow Rh_*(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} L) \, .\]

We shall define it only if the sites under consideration have enough points, so as to be able to use 4.2.10 and 4.2.8. By virtue of 4.2.10, it suffices to define it for a pair \((K,L)\) that is split on the left for the functor \((K,L) \longmapsto K \boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}} L\), with \(K\) and \(L\) split on the right for the functors \(f_*\) and \(g_*\) and bounded above.

Let \(K_1\) be a flat resolution of \(f_* K\), \(L_1\) a flat resolution of \(g_*L\) and \(u : K \boxtimes L \longrightarrow M\) a resolution of \(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} L\), split for the functor \(Rh_*\). We have morphisms

\[Rf_*K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} Rg_*L \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} K_1 \boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}} L_1 \longrightarrow f_*K \boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}} g_*L \longrightarrow h_*(K \boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}} L) \longrightarrow h_*M \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} Rh_*(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} L)\]
and we define (5.4.1.4) as their composite.
This arrow has the following characteristic property, whose proof is entirely analogous to that of 4.2.13:

5.4.1.5. Let \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} C^-(X', \mathcal{A}^o)\) and \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} C^-(Y', \mathcal{A})\). Set \(K_1 = f_*K\), \(L_1 = g_*L\), and \(M_2 = K \boxtimes L\). The following diagram is then commutative

\[\xymatrix@C=2.6em@R=3em{ Rf_*K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} Rg_* L \ar[rrr] & & & Rh_*(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} L) \ar[dd] \\ & & & \\ K_1 \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} L_1 \ar[uu] \ar[r] & K_1 \boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}} L_1 \ar[r] & h_* M_2 \ar[r] & Rh_* M_2 } \, .\]
We have an analogous commutativity (cf. 4.2.13) starting instead from morphisms \(K_1 \longrightarrow f_*K\), \(L_1 \longrightarrow g_*L\) and \(K \boxtimes L \longrightarrow M_2\).
The commutativity 5.4.1.5 makes the verification of the compatibility properties of the Künneth morphism easy in principle.

5.4.2. Let a commutative diagram (5.4.1.1) of schemes and \(\mathcal{A}\) a torsion sheaf on \(S\) be given. Suppose that \(f\) and \(g\) are compactifiable (3.2.1), that \(Z = X \times_S Y\) and that \(Z' = X' \times_S Y'\). Let us factor \(f\) and \(g\) into a proper morphism and an open immersion; we obtain a diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=2.2em@R=2.2em{ X' \ar[d]_{j_1} \ar@/_2.6em/[dd]_{f} & Z' \ar[l]_{p'} \ar[r]^{q'} \ar[d]^{j_3} & Y' \ar[d]^{j_2} \ar@/^2.6em/[dd]^{g} \\ \bar{X}' \ar[d]_{\bar{f}} & \bar{Z}' \ar[l]_(0.45){\bar{p}} \ar[r]^(0.45){\bar{q}} \ar[d]^{\bar{h}} & \bar{Y}' \ar[d]^{\bar{g}} \\ X & Z \ar[l]^{p} \ar[r]_{q} & Y }\]
in which we have set \(\bar{Z}' = \bar{X}' \times_S \bar{Y}'\). We have an isomorphism of trivial nature, for \(K\) and \(L\) complexes on \(X'\) and \(Y'\)
\[(5.4.2.1) \qquad j_{3!}(K \boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}} L) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} j_{1!} K \boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}} j_{2!} L \, .\]

By "composing" the inverse of this isomorphism with the Künneth arrow (5.4.1.4) relative to \((\bar{f}, \bar{g}, \bar{h}, j_{1!} K, j_{2!} L)\), we obtain, for \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(X', \mathcal{A})\) and \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(Y', \mathcal{A})\), a Künneth arrow
\[(5.4.2.2) \qquad Rf_! K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} Rg_! L \longrightarrow Rh_!(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} L) \, ,\]
which one verifies does not depend on the chosen compactifications.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.4.3

Under the hypotheses of 5.4.2, the Künneth arrow in cohomology with proper supports (5.4.2.2) is an isomorphism.
Proof. (a) By construction, it suffices to verify this result when \(f\) and \(g\) (and hence also \(h\)) are proper.
(b) Let a commutative diagram be given
\[(5.4.3.1) \qquad \xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ X_1 \ar[r]^{p_1} \ar[d] & S_1 \ar[d] & Y_1 \ar[l]_{q_1} \ar[d] \\ X \ar[r]_{p} & S & Y \ar[l]^{q} }\]
and let \(Z_1 = X_1 \times_{S_1} Y_1\), \(X'_1 = X' \times_X X_1\), \(Y'_1 = Y' \times_Y Y_1\) and \(Z'_1 = X'_1 \times_{S_1} Y'_1 = Z' \times_Z Z_1\), so that we have a morphism of diagrams (5.4.1),
whose arrows will be uniformly denoted by \(C\).
We shall admit that:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.4.3.2

The following diagram is commutative:

\[\xymatrix@C=1.4em@R=3.5em{ C^*(Rf_! K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} Rg_! L) \ar@{=}[r] \ar[d] & C^*Rf_!K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} C^* Rg_! L \ar[r]^-{\sim} & Rf_{1!} C^*K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} Rg_{1!} C^* L \ar[d] \\ C^*(Rh_!(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} L)) \ar[r]^-{\sim} & Rh_!(C^*(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} L)) \ar@{=}[r] & Rh_!(C^*K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} C^* L) } \, .\]
In this diagram, the horizontal arrows are base change arrows and the vertical arrows the Künneth arrows for the two diagrams (5.4.1.1) under consideration.

To prove 5.4.3, it suffices to prove that the Künneth arrow is an isomorphism at every geometric point of \(Z\). By 5.4.3.2, it suffices to verify this after any base change (5.4.3.1) such that \(S_1\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field and \(p_1\), \(q_1\) are isomorphisms.
After such a base change, the diagram (5.4.1.1) reduces to a diagram
\[(5.4.3.3) \qquad \xymatrix@C=1.8em@R=2em{ & X \times_S Y \ar[dl]_{p} \ar[dd]^(0.32){f \times g} \ar[dr]^{q} & \\ X \ar[dr]_{f} & & Y \ar[dl]^{g} \\ & S & }\]
and the Künneth arrow to an arrow
\[(5.4.3.4) \qquad k : Rf_! K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} Rg_! L \longrightarrow R(f\times g)_!(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} L) \, .\]
(c) Let a diagram (5.4.3.3) be given in which \(f\) and \(g\) are proper. We shall admit that:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.4.3.5

The following diagram is commutative

\[\xymatrix@C=3em@R=3em{ Rf_! K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} Rg_! L \ar[r] \ar[d] & R(f\times g)_!(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes}_{\mathcal{A}} L) \ar@{=}[d] \\ Rf_!(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{A}} f^* Rg_! L) \ar[r] & Rf_!(Rp_!(p^*K \otimes q^*L)) } \, .\]

In this diagram, the horizontal arrows are the Künneth arrows and the base change arrow. The vertical arrows are a base change arrow by \(f\) and a transitivity isomorphism. Theorem 5.4.3 is a consequence of this lemma and of 4.3.1.
The courageous reader may verify that this lemma remains valid if \(f\) and \(g\) are not necessarily proper.

5.4.4. Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(f_i : X'_i \longrightarrow X_i\) (\(i \in I\)) a finite family of compactifiable morphisms of \(S\)-schemes, \(X\) the product over \(S\) of the \(X_i\), \(X'\) the product over \(S\) of the \(X'_i\) and \(f : X' \longrightarrow X\) the product of the \(f_i\). If \(S\) is ringed by \(\mathcal{A}\), as in 5.4.1, and if we ring the \(X_i\) and \(X'_i\) by the inverse image of \(\mathcal{A}\), we have more generally an isomorphism
\[(5.4.4.1) \qquad \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\underset{i \in I}{\boxtimes}}\, Rf_{i!}(K_i) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} Rf_!\Bigl(\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\underset{i \in I}{\boxtimes}}\, K_i\Bigr) \, ,\]
for \(K_i \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(X'_i, \mathcal{A})\). The definition of this isomorphism, as well as that of the two sides of (5.4.4.1), does not require the choice of a total order on \(I\).
5.5. Cohomology of symmetric powers.

The principal result of this n° is Theorem 5.5.21, giving in particular the cohomology with proper supports of a symmetric power of a scheme \(X\) over an algebraically closed field \(k\), for suitable coefficients (for example \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)) in terms of the cohomology with proper supports of \(X\). The analogue of this theorem in semi-simplicial topology is well known, at least for cohomology with coefficients in a commutative ring \(A\); it is verified at the level of semi-simplicial cochains. Indeed, if \(X_\bullet\) is a semi-simplicial set, there exists a canonical continuous bijection from the geometric realization of the \(n\)th symmetric power \((X_\bullet)^n/\mathfrak{S}_n\) of \(X_\bullet\) to the \(n^{\text{th}}\) symmetric power of the geometric realization of \(X_\bullet\), and this bijection induces an isomorphism on cohomology.

5.5.1. Let us recall some properties (due to D. LAZARD) of flat modules, some properties (due to ROBY) of the functors \(\mathrm{TS}^n\) and \(\Gamma^n\), and some properties (due to DOLD and PUPPE) of the derived functors of non-additive functors.
5.5.1.1. Every flat module over a ring \(A\) is a filtered inductive limit of free modules of finite type (LAZARD [1, I 1.2]). This result implies the following ones:

5.5.1.2. The functor \(\varinjlim\) is an equivalence of the category of Ind-objects (I 8.1) of the category of free \(A\)-modules of finite type (resp. projective of finite type) with the category of flat \(A\)-modules.

5.5.1.3. If \(A\) and \(B\) are two rings, every functor \(T : \operatorname{Mod}(A) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Mod}(B)\) that transforms a free module of finite type into a flat module and commutes with filtered inductive limits transforms a flat module into a flat module (LAZARD [1, I 1.5]).
5.5.1.4. Every exact sequence of \(A\)-modules, with \(L''\) flat,
\[0 \longrightarrow L' \longrightarrow L \longrightarrow L'' \longrightarrow 0\]
is an inductive limit of split exact sequences (LAZARD [1, I 2.3]).
5.5.2. Let \(A\) be a commutative ring and \(M\) an \(A\)-module.

5.5.2.1. For every integer \(n\), we denote by \(\mathrm{TS}^n(M)\) (or \(\mathrm{TS}^n_A(M)\)) the module of symmetric tensors of degree \(n\) of \(M\). Denoting by \(\mathfrak{S}_n\) the symmetric group of degree \(n\), we have by definition
\[\mathrm{TS}^n(M) = (\otimes^n M)^{\mathfrak{S}_n} \, .\]

If \(B\) is an \(A\)-algebra, then \(\mathrm{TS}^n(B)\) is a subalgebra of \(\otimes^n B\). If moreover \(B\) is commutative, then \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathrm{TS}^n(B))\) is by definition the \(n^{\text{th}}\) symmetric power of \(\operatorname{Spec}(B)\) over \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\):

\[\operatorname{Spec}(\mathrm{TS}^n_A(B)) = \operatorname{Sym}^n_{\operatorname{Spec}(A)}(\operatorname{Spec}(B)) \underset{\mathrm{dfn}}{=} (\operatorname{Spec}(B)/\operatorname{Spec}(A))^n/\mathfrak{S}_n \, .\]

5.5.2.2. Let us recall (ROBY [1, I 1 pg.226]) that a polynomial law \(f\) from an \(A\)-module \(M\) to an \(A\)-module \(N\) is the datum, for every commutative \(A\)-algebra \(A'\), of a map \(f_{A'} : M \otimes_A A' \longrightarrow N \otimes_A A'\), these maps being such that for every homomorphism of \(A\)-algebras \(u : A' \longrightarrow A''\), the diagram
\[\xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ M \otimes_A A' \ar[r]^{f_{A'}} \ar[d]_{u} & N \otimes_A A' \ar[d]^{u} \\ M \otimes_A A'' \ar[r]_{f_{A''}} & N \otimes_A A'' }\]
is commutative.
A polynomial law \(f\) is said to be homogeneous of degree \(n\) (ROBY [1, I 1 pg.226]) if, for every \(a' \in A'\), we have identically
Such a polynomial law will also be called a map that is \(n^{\text{ic}}\) (quadratic, cubic, ...); we shall denote the set of these by
\[\operatorname{Hom} n^{\text{ic}}(M,N) \, .\]

More generally, if \((M_i)_{i \in I}\) is a finite family of \(A\)-modules and \(\underline{n} = (n_i)_{i \in I}\) a family of integers, a multihomogeneous polynomial law of multidegree \(\underline{n}\) from the modules \(M_i\) to \(N\) is a polynomial law from \(\sum M_i\) to \(N\) satisfying identically, for \(a_i \in A'\),
\[f_{A'}((a_i x_i)_{i \in I}) = \prod_{i \in I} a_i^{n_i} \cdot f_{A'}((x_i)_{i \in I}) \, .\]
We shall denote by \(\operatorname{Hom} \underline{n}^{\text{ic}}((M_i),N)\) the set of these polynomial laws.
5.5.2.3. For every module \(M\), the covariant functor from \(A\)-modules to sets
\[N \longmapsto \operatorname{Hom} n^{\text{ic}}(M,N)\]

is representable by an \(A\)-module \(\Gamma^n(M)\) (or \(\Gamma^n_A(M)\)), endowed with a universal \(n^{\text{ic}}\) map \(\gamma^n : M \longrightarrow \Gamma^n(M)\) (ROBY [1, IV 1 pg.226]). Given \((M_i)_{i \in I}\) and \(\underline{n}\) as in 5.5.2.2, the covariant functor
\[N \longmapsto \operatorname{Hom} \underline{n}^{\text{ic}}((M_i),N)\]

is represented by the module \(\bigotimes_{i \in I} \Gamma^{n_i}(M_i)\), endowed with the universal (of multidegree \(\underline{n}\)) multihomogeneous polynomial law \((m_i) \longmapsto \bigotimes_{i \in I} \gamma^{n_i}(m_i)\).

5.5.2.4. The functors \(\mathrm{TS}^n\) and \(\Gamma^n\) commute with filtered inductive limits (for the second, (ROBY [1, IV 6 pg.275])). They transform free modules into free modules, hence flat modules into flat modules (5.5.1.2).

5.5.2.5. The \(n^{\text{ic}}\) map from \(M\) to \(\mathrm{TS}^n(M)\) given by \(m \longmapsto \otimes^n m\) defines a map \(\varphi\), called canonical, from \(\Gamma^n(M)\) to \(\mathrm{TS}^n(M)\), satisfying
\[\varphi(\gamma^n(m)) = \otimes^n m \, .\]
This map is an isomorphism for \(M\) free of finite type (ROBY [1,IV pg.272]) hence also for \(M\) flat (5.5.2.4 and 5.5.1.1).
Let \(M\) be an \(A\)-module and \(P\) an exact sequence
\[P : P_1 \xrightarrow{\;d\;} P_0 \xrightarrow{\;\varepsilon\;} M \longrightarrow 0 \, .\]
Let \(P'_1 = P_1 \times P_0\), and let \(j_0\) and \(j_1\) be the morphisms from \(P'_1\) to \(P_0\) of coordinates \((d, \operatorname{Id})\) and \((0, \operatorname{Id})\). The sequence
\[\Gamma^n(P'_1) \mathrel{\overset{\Gamma^n(j_0)}{\underset{\Gamma^n(j_1)}{\rightrightarrows}}} \Gamma^n(P_0) \longrightarrow \Gamma^n(M) \longrightarrow 0\]
is then exact (ROBY [1 pg.284]). For \(P\) a flat presentation of \(M\), we deduce from it a description of the functor \(\Gamma^n\) via the functor \(\mathrm{TS}^n\)
\[(5.5.2.5.1) \qquad \mathrm{TS}^n(P'_1) \rightrightarrows \mathrm{TS}^n(P_0) \longrightarrow \Gamma^n(M) \longrightarrow 0 \, .\]
5.5.2.6. If \(M = M' \oplus M''\), the \(n^{\text{ic}}\) map
\[m \longmapsto (\gamma^{n'} m \otimes \gamma^{n''} m)_{n'+n''=n}\]
defines an isomorphism, called canonical (ROBY [1, III 4])
\[(5.5.2.6.1) \qquad \Gamma^n(M) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \sum_{n'+n''=n} \Gamma^{n'}(M') \otimes \Gamma^{n''}(M'') \, .\]
If \(\Sigma\) is an exact sequence
\[\Sigma : 0 \longrightarrow M' \longrightarrow M \longrightarrow M'' \longrightarrow 0 \, ,\]
the module \(\Gamma^n(M)\) is endowed with a canonical (decreasing) filtration and with morphisms
\[(5.5.2.6.2) \qquad \Gamma^i(M') \otimes \Gamma^{n-i}(M'') \longrightarrow \operatorname{Gr}^i(\Gamma^n(M)) \, .\]

These data are characterized by the properties of being functorial in \(\Sigma\) and of satisfying an evident compatibility with (5.5.2.6.1) for \(\Sigma\) split. The arrows (5.5.2.6.2) are isomorphisms for \(\Sigma\) split, hence also for \(M'\) flat (5.5.1.4).
5.5.2.7. The functor \(\Gamma^n\) commutes with extension of scalars (ROBY [1, III 3 pg.262]) (the analogous property for \(\mathrm{TS}^n\) is in general false).
5.5.2.8. If \(u : M_1 \times M_2 \longrightarrow N\) is a bilinear map, then \(\gamma^n \circ u\) is a bihomogeneous polynomial law of bidegree \((n,n)\) and hence defines
\[(5.5.2.3') \qquad u^n : \Gamma^n(M_1) \otimes \Gamma^n(M_2) \longrightarrow \Gamma^n(N) \quad \text{satisfying} \quad u^n(\gamma^n x \otimes \gamma^n y) = \gamma^n u(x,y) \, .\]

In particular, if \(B\) is an \(A\)-algebra, the product \(B \times B \longrightarrow B\) induces a product on \(\Gamma^n(B)\). This product makes \(\Gamma^n(B)\) into an \(A\)-algebra, and the canonical map from \(\Gamma^n(B)\) to \(\mathrm{TS}^n(B)\) is an algebra homomorphism.

5.5.3. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category. We denote by \(\operatorname{ssimpl}^+(\mathcal{A})\) the category of co-semi-simplicial objects of \(\mathcal{A}\), by \(C^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\) the category of differential complexes \(K\) with \(K^i = 0\) for \(i < 0\), and by \(K^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\) the image of \(C^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\) in \(K(\mathcal{A})\). If \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} \operatorname{ssimpl}^+(\mathcal{A})\), the associated normalized complex \(N(K) \in \operatorname{Ob} C^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\) is defined by
\[(5.5.3.1) \qquad \begin{cases} N(K)^n = \text{intersection of the kernels of the degeneracy operators of } K^n \text{ in } K^{n-1} \\[4pt] d = \sum (-1)^i \partial_i \end{cases}\]

If we again denote by \(K\) the complex with components \(K^n\), and differential \(d = \sum (-1)^i \partial_i\), then \(N(K)\) is a direct factor subcomplex in \(K\), and \(K/N(K)\) is homotopic to zero.
According to DOLD-PUPPE [1], the functor \(N\) is an equivalence of categories
\[N : \operatorname{ssimpl}^+(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow C^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}) \, .\]

This equivalence and its inverse transform homotopic morphisms into homotopic morphisms. Moreover, for every \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} \operatorname{ssimpl}^+(\mathcal{A})\), \(K^n\) is a sum of copies of \(N(K)^i\) (\(i \leq n\)); if \(\mathbb{P}\) is a property of objects of \(\mathcal{A}\), stable under finite sums and direct factors, we deduce that the \(K^i\) have the property \(\mathbb{P}\) for \(i \leq n\) if and only if the \(N(K)^i\) have this property for \(i \leq n\).

The equivalence \(N\) is used by DOLD and PUPPE to extend every functor (not necessarily additive) \(T : \mathcal{A} \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) from \(\mathcal{A}\) to an arbitrary category \(\mathcal{B}\) into a functor \(C^{\geq 0}(T)\) (or simply \(T\)) from \(C^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\) to \(C^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{B})\)
The functor \(C^{\geq 0}(T)\) passes to the quotient to define
\[(5.5.3.3) \qquad T \text{ or } K^{\geq 0}(T) : K^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow K^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{B}) \, .\]

5.5.3.4. If \(T\) is of degree \(\leq n\), i.e. if the \((n+1)^{\text{th}}\) "cross effect" is zero (DOLD-PUPPE [1, 4.18 pg.232]) then, for every \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} C^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\) such that \(K^i = 0\) for \(i > m\), we have \([T(K)]^i = 0\) for \(i > nm\) (DOLD-PUPPE [1, 4.2.3 pg.233]).

5.5.3.5. In particular, if \(T\) is a functor of finite degree from the category of \(A\)-modules to that of \(B\)-modules, which transforms a flat object into a flat object, then a bounded flat complex has as image a bounded flat complex.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.4

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category.

(i) The quasi-isomorphisms in \(K^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\) allow a calculus of fractions on the left and on the right.

(ii) The evident functor is an equivalence between the category deduced from \(K^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\) by inverting the quasi-isomorphisms and the category \(D^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\).

The functor \(\tau_{\geq 0} : C(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow C^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\) (1.1.13) passes to the quotient to define a functor \(\tau_{\geq 0} : K(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow K^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\), left adjoint to the inclusion of \(K^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A})\) into \(K(\mathcal{A})\). The functor \(\tau_{\geq 0}\) transforms quasi-isomorphisms into quasi-isomorphisms, and the adjunction arrow \(X \longrightarrow \tau_{\geq 0}(X)\) is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if \(H^i(X) = 0\) for \(i < 0\). Lemma 5.5.4 thus follows from VERDIER [CD] and from points (i) and (ii) of the following lemma, whose proof is left to the reader:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.4.1

Let \(K\) be a category, \(K'\) a full subcategory, \(S\) a set of morphisms of \(K\) equal to the inverse image of the set of isomorphisms of \(K(S^{-1})\) (cf. [GAB.ZIS 1, chap 1]) and \(S'\) its trace in \(K'\). We assume that the inclusion \(i\) of \(K'\) into \(K\) admits a left adjoint \(\tau\), and that \(\tau(S) \subset S'\).

(i) The evident functor from \(K'(S'^{-1})\) to \(K(S^{-1})\) is fully faithful, and admits \(\tau\) as left adjoint.

(ii) If \(K(S^{-1})\) can be calculated by a calculus of fractions on the left (resp. on the right), then \(K'(S'^{-1})\) has the same property.

If the inclusion \(i\) does not necessarily have a left adjoint, and if \(\tau\) denotes the not-everywhere-defined functor that is left adjoint to \(i\), we have:

(iii) If \(K(S^{-1})\) can be calculated by a calculus of fractions on the left (resp. on the right) and if for every \(u \in S\), with target (resp. source) in \(K'\), \(\tau(u)\) is defined and in \(S'\), then \(K'(S'^{-1})\) admits a calculus of fractions on the left (resp. on the right) and the functor \(K'(S'^{-1}) \longrightarrow K(S^{-1})\) is fully faithful.
5.5.5. Let \(T : \mathcal{A} \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) be a functor between abelian categories. As in 1.2.1, we define the derived functors of \(T\)

\[\begin{aligned} LT &: D^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Pro}(D^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{B})) \\ RT &: D^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Ind}(D^{\geq 0}(\mathcal{B})) \end{aligned}\]
by the formulas
\[LT(K) = \varprojlim_{s : K' \to K} T(K') \, , \qquad RT(K) = \varinjlim_{s : K \to K'} T(K') \, ,\]
where \(s\) runs through the filtered category of quasi-isomorphisms with target (resp. source) \(K\).

We say that \(T\) is left derivable (resp. right) at \(K\) if \(LT(K)\) (\(RT(K)\)) is representable. We say that \(K\) is left split (resp. right) for \(T\) (or, by abuse of language, split for \(LT\) (resp. \(RT\))) if the following canonical arrow is an isomorphism:
\[LT\, K \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} TK \qquad (\text{resp. } TK \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} RT\, K) \, .\]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.5.6

Let \(F\) be a functor from the category of modules over a ring \(A\) to an abelian category \(\mathcal{B}\). Suppose that the filtered inductive limits in \(\mathcal{B}\) are representable and exact, and that \(F\) commutes with filtered inductive limits. Then every bounded complex \(M^\bullet \in \operatorname{Ob} K^{\geq 0}(A)\) of flat modules is split for \(LF\).

The proposition follows immediately from the definitions, from the following lemma, which will be proved in 5.5.6.4, and from the fact that the quasi-isomorphisms \(u : N^\bullet \longrightarrow M^\bullet\), with \(N^\bullet \in C^{b,\geq 0}(A)\) having flat components, form a cofinal set in the category of quasi-isomorphisms with target \(M^\bullet\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.6.1

Let \(u : N^\bullet \longrightarrow M^\bullet\) be a quasi-isomorphism between flat complexes, objects of \(C^{b,\geq 0}(A)\). Then \(F(u)\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.6.2

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an additive category and \(d\) a bounded-above interval of \(\mathbb{Z}\). We denote by \(C^d\) (resp. \(C^{d,b}\), resp. \(K^d\), resp. \(K^{d,b}\)) the category of complexes that are zero in degrees \(i \notin d\) (resp. and bounded, resp. up to homotopy). We have an equivalence

\[\ell : \operatorname{Ind}(C^{d,b}(\mathcal{A})) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} C^d(\operatorname{Ind} \mathcal{A}) \, ;\]

the inverse of this equivalence induces a functor

\[\ell' : K^d(\operatorname{Ind} \mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Ind}(K^{d,b}(\mathcal{A})) \, .\]
A) Let us prove that \(\ell\) is fully faithful. So let \(K\) be a bounded complex of objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(L = \varinjlim L_\alpha\) an Ind-complex. We have

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}(K,L) &\underset{\mathrm{dfn}}{=} \varinjlim \operatorname{Hom}(K,L_\alpha) = \varinjlim Z^0(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(K,L_\alpha)) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} Z^0 \varinjlim_\alpha \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(K,L_\alpha) \\ &\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} Z^0 \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(K, \ell L) = \operatorname{Hom}(K, \ell L) \, , \end{aligned}\]
the second-to-last isomorphism coming from the fact that \(K\) is finite, so that \(\varinjlim\) commutes with the passage from the double to the simple complex. This proves the assertion.

B) We leave to the reader the (rather tedious) task of verifying that \(\ell\) is essentially surjective by constructing, from left to right, starting from an arbitrarily chosen degree, "enough" bounded complexes mapping into a bounded-above complex of Ind-objects \(K\); and of developing likewise the following point:

C) If \(\ell f : \ell \varinjlim K_\alpha \longrightarrow \ell \varinjlim L_\beta\) is homotopic to zero: \(f = d H + Hd\), then, for every \(\alpha\), \(H\) lifts to \(H^i_\alpha : K^i_\alpha \longrightarrow L^i_{\beta(\alpha)}\) which, for \(\beta\) large enough, defines a null-homotopy of \(f_\alpha : K_\alpha \longrightarrow L_{\beta(\alpha)}\).

5.5.6.3. Let \(A\) be a ring, \(d\) a bounded-above interval of \(\mathbb{Z}\), \(P(A)\) the category of finitely generated projective \(A\)-modules, \(P\ell(A)\) the category of flat \(A\)-modules. We denote by \(D^{\mathrm{Tor} \subset d}(A)\) the image of \(C^d(P\ell(A))\) in \(D(A)\) and by \(D^{\mathrm{parf} \subset d}(A)\) the image of \(C^{d,b}(P(A))\) in \(D(A)\). By 5.5.1.2, we have \(P\ell(A) \simeq \operatorname{Ind} P(A)\). We also have \(K^{d,b}(P(A)) \simeq D^{\mathrm{parf} \subset d}(A)\). We then deduce from 5.5.6.2, and from the fact that \(H^i\) commutes with filtered inductive limits, that there exists a commutative diagram of functors

\[\xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ C^d(P\ell(A)) \ar[d] & \operatorname{Ind} C^{d,b}(P(A)) \ar[l]_-{\varinjlim} \ar[d] \\ K^d(P\ell(A)) \ar[r]^-{\ell'} \ar[d] & \operatorname{Ind} K^{d,b}(P(A)) \ar[d] \\ D^{\mathrm{Tor} \subset d}(A) \ar[r]_-{\ell''} & \operatorname{Ind} D^{\mathrm{parf} \subset d}(A) }\]
5.5.6.4. Let us prove 5.5.6.1. With the notations of 5.5.6.3, if \(d\) is an interval \([0,k]\), we have (since \(F\) commutes with \(\varinjlim\)) commutative diagrams

\[\xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ K^d(P\ell(A)) \ar[r]^-{\ell'} \ar[d]_{K^{\geq 0}(F)} & \operatorname{Ind} K^d(P(A)) \ar[d]^{\operatorname{Ind}(K^{\geq 0}(F))} \\ K^+(\mathcal{B}) \ar[r] \ar[d]_{H^i} & \operatorname{Ind} K^+(\mathcal{B}) \ar[d]^{\operatorname{Ind}(H^i)} \\ \mathcal{B} & \operatorname{Ind} \mathcal{B} \ar[l]^-{\varinjlim} }\]
If \(u\) is as in 5.5.6.1, then, by 5.5.6.3, \(\ell'(u)\) is an isomorphism, and hence \(H^i K^{\geq 0}(F)(u)\) is an isomorphism, which is what we had to prove.

5.5.7. Let \(X\) be a scheme over a scheme \(S\) and \(k\) an integer. We assume that the symmetric power \(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X)\) is defined. A reader who does not wish to make this assumption may work in the category of algebraic spaces (ARTIN [1]). We ring \(S\) with a sheaf of commutative rings \(\mathcal{A}\). From 5.5.19 onward, \(\mathcal{A}\) will be assumed torsion. By abuse of notation, we will again denote by \(\mathcal{A}\) the inverse image of \(\mathcal{A}\) on an arbitrary \(S\)-scheme.

Let \(\underline{F}\) be a sheaf of modules on \(X\); the sheaf \(\boxtimes^k \underline{F}\), the external tensor product of \(k\) copies of \(\underline{F}\), is a sheaf on \(X^k/S\), equivariant under the action of the symmetric group \(\mathfrak{S}_k\) on \(X^k/S\). By passing to invariants, it defines a sheaf \(\mathrm{TS}^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(\underline{F})\) on \(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X)\), called the external symmetric tensor power of \(\underline{F}\).
In order to reason "point by point", it is useful to work with the points of \(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X)\) described as follows.

5.5.7.1. Let \(s\) be a geometric point of \(S\). A point \(x\) of \(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X)\) with values in \(k(s)\) defines a geometric point of \(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X)\). We will denote by \((x_1 \ldots x_k)\) a point of \((X/S)^k\) with values in \(k(s)\) having image \(x\), by \(y_1 \ldots y_\ell\) the distinct elements of the sequence \(x_1 \ldots x_k\), and by \(n_i\) (\(1 \leq i \leq \ell\)) the multiplicity of \(y_i\) in this sequence (\(\sum n_i = k\)).
With the notations of 5.5.7.1, and denoting by \(\mathfrak{S}\) a symmetric group, we have
\[(5.5.7.2) \qquad \mathrm{TS}^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F)_x \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \Bigl( \bigotimes_1^\ell \bigl( \otimes_1^{n_i} F_{y_i} \bigr) \Bigr)^{\prod_1^\ell \mathfrak{S}_{n_i}} \, ,\]
the tensor products being taken over \(\mathcal{A}_S\). In particular, for \(F\) flat, we have, thanks to 5.5.2.5,
\[(5.5.7.3) \qquad \mathrm{TS}^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F)_x \xleftarrow{\;\sim\;} \bigotimes_1^\ell \Gamma^{n_i}(F_{y_i}) \, ,\]

using an argument by induction on \(\ell\), using the flatness of the \(\Gamma^{n_i}(F_{y_i})\) (5.5.2.4) and the following fact: if \(G\) (resp. \(H\)) is a finite group acting on an \(A\)-module \(M\) (resp. \(N\)), and if \(M\) and \(N^H\) are flat, then
\[M^G \otimes_A N^H \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} (M \otimes_A N)^{G \times H} \, .\]
5.5.8. Let \(F\) be a Module on \(X\), and \(P\) a flat presentation of \(F\)
\[P : P_1 \longrightarrow P_0 \longrightarrow F \longrightarrow 0 \, .\]

We define \(P'_1\), \(j_0\) and \(j_1\) as in 5.5.2.5, and we define \(\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F)\) (external \(\Gamma\) functor) as the cokernel of the double arrow \((\mathrm{TS}^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(j_0), \mathrm{TS}^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(j_1))\). With the notations of 5.5.7.1, we deduce from 5.5.7.3 and 5.5.2.5 isomorphisms
\[(5.5.8.1) \qquad \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F)_x \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \bigotimes_1^\ell \Gamma^{n_i}(F_{y_i}) \, .\]
From this formula, we deduce that \(\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F)\), which a priori depends functorially on \(F\), depends, up to unique isomorphism, only on \(F\).
5.5.9. We have a functorial morphism
\[\alpha : \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{TS}^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F) \, .\]
The pair \((\Gamma, \alpha)\) is characterized by the two properties:
(i) For \(F\) flat, \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism
(ii) With the notations of 5.5.2.5, for every presentation
\[P_1 \xrightarrow{\;d\;} P_0 \xrightarrow{\;\varepsilon\;} F \longrightarrow 0\]
of \(F\), the sequence
\[\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(P'_1) \rightrightarrows \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(P_0) \longrightarrow \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F) \longrightarrow 0\]
is exact.
We have moreover:
(iii) The functors \(\mathrm{TS}^k\) and \(\Gamma^k\) commute with filtered inductive limits (by 5.5.7.2, 5.5.8.1, 5.5.2.4).
(iv) The functor \(\Gamma^k\) commutes with every extension \(\mathcal{A} \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}'\) of the base ring.
(v) The functor \(\Gamma^k\) commutes with every base change \(S' \longrightarrow S\): for every cartesian square
\[\xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ X' \ar[r]^{g'} \ar[d]_{f'} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ S' \ar[r]_{g} & S } \, ,\]
we have
\[\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(g')^* \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}} g'^* \, .\]
(vi) The functor \(\Gamma^k\) commutes with inverse images under every radicial morphism \(i : X' \longrightarrow X\) (for example a closed immersion): We have
\[\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(i)^* \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}} i^*\]
(vii) For \(j : X' \longrightarrow X\) an immersion, we have
\[\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(j)_! \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}} j_!\]
5.5.10. Let \(k_1\), \(k_2\) and \(k = k_1 + k_2\) be three integers \(\geq 0\). We then have a finite morphism ( ):
\[\vee_{k_1 k_2} : \operatorname{Sym}^{k_1}_S(X) \times_S \operatorname{Sym}^{k_2}_S(X) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X) \, .\]
If \(F_i\) (\(i = 1,2\)) is a Module on \(\operatorname{Sym}^{k_i}_S(X)\), we denote by \(F_1 \vee F_2\) the sheaf on \(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X)\)
5.5.11. Let there be an exact sequence of Modules on \(X\)
\[\Sigma : 0 \longrightarrow F' \longrightarrow F \longrightarrow F'' \longrightarrow 0 \, .\]
With the notations 5.5.7.1, we have, thanks to 5.5.8.1 and 5.5.2.6, a filtration on \(\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F)_x\), and morphisms:

\[\bigotimes_{\substack{1 \leq \alpha \leq \ell \\ \sum i_\alpha = i}} \Gamma^{i_\alpha}(F'_{y_\alpha}) \otimes \bigotimes_{1 \leq \alpha \leq \ell} \Gamma^{n_\alpha - i_\alpha}(F''_{y_\alpha}) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Gr}^i(\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F)_x) \, .\]

The left-hand side is nothing other than \((\Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}}(F') \vee \Gamma^{k-i}_{\mathrm{ext}}(F''))_x\). One verifies easily that these data, constructed point by point, come from a (unique) filtration with \(k+1\) steps of \(\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F)\), and from (unique) morphisms
\[(5.5.11.1) \qquad \Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}}(F') \vee \Gamma^{k-i}_{\mathrm{ext}}(F'') \longrightarrow \operatorname{Gr}^i(\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F)) \, .\]
If the exact sequence \(\Sigma\) is split, we have more precisely (verification point by point from 5.5.2.6.2).
\[(5.5.11.2) \qquad \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(F' \oplus F'') \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \sum_{k_1+k_2=k} \Gamma^{k_1}_{\mathrm{ext}}(F') \vee \Gamma^{k_2}_{\mathrm{ext}}(F'') \, .\]
If the exact sequence \(\Sigma\) is splittable point by point, or if \(F''\) is flat, the morphisms (5.5.11.1) are isomorphisms (cf. 5.5.1.4).

5.5.12. Let \(u : X \longrightarrow Y\) be a morphism of \(S\)-schemes. We assume that the symmetric powers \(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(Y)\) exist. Let \(F\) be a Module on \(X\), \(G\) a Module on \(Y\) and \(v \in \operatorname{Hom}(u^*G, F) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Hom}(G, u_* F)\) a \(u\)-homomorphism from \(F\) to \(G\) (0.2). If \(\prod^n u\) is the \(n^{\text{th}}\) cartesian power of \(u\), the homomorphism \(v\) induces a \(\prod^n u\)-homomorphism \(\boxtimes^n v\) from \(\boxtimes^n F\) to \(\boxtimes^n G\).
By passing to invariants, this defines
\[\mathrm{TS}^n(v) : \mathrm{TS}^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(F) \xrightarrow[\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)]{} \mathrm{TS}^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(G) \, .\]
We deduce from Definition 5.5.8 that there exists one and only one \(\operatorname{Sym}^n(u)\)-homomorphism \(\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(v)\), functorial in \((F, G, v)\),
\[(5.5.12.0) \qquad \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(v) : \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(F) \xrightarrow[\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)]{} \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(G)\]
making the following diagram commute (cf. (0.2) for the (unusual) direction of the arrows):

\[\xymatrix@C=5em@R=4em{ \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(F) \ar[r]^-{\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(v)}_-{\text{over } \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)} \ar[d]_{\alpha \text{ over Id}} & \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(G) \ar[d]^{\alpha \text{ over Id}} \\ \mathrm{TS}^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(F) \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{TS}^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(v)}_-{\text{over } \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)} & \mathrm{TS}^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(G) }\]
We will use this arrow mainly as a "symmetric Künneth arrow": for \(G = u_*F\), and \(v\) the canonical arrow, the arrow \(\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(v)\) is identified with a homomorphism of Modules
\[(5.5.12.1) \qquad k^n : \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(u_*F) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Sym}^n(u)_* \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(F) \, .\]
5.5.13. Consider the condition:

(5.5.13.1). \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} K^{b,\geq 0}(X, \mathcal{A})\) and, for every geometric point \(x\) of \(X\), the complex \(K_x\) is homotopic to a complex of flat modules \(L_x \in \operatorname{Ob} C^{b,\geq 0}(\mathcal{A}_x)\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.13.2

The subcategory \(D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X,\mathcal{A})\) of \(D^b(X,\mathcal{A})\) formed by the complexes of Tor-dimension \(\leq 0\) is equivalent to the category obtained from the category of complexes \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} K^{b,\geq 0}(X,\mathcal{A})\) satisfying (5.5.13.1) by inverting the quasi-isomorphisms. This construction may be carried out equally well by a left or a right calculus of fractions.

Let \(P\) be the subcategory of \(K^-(X,\mathcal{A})\) formed by the complexes that are pointwise homotopic to a complex of flat modules. It is known (VERDIER [C.D.]) that \(D^-(X,\mathcal{A})\) is obtained from \(P\) by inverting the quasi-isomorphisms, by a right or left calculus of fractions. We then apply 5.5.4.1 to the inclusion of \(K^{b,\geq 0}(X,\mathcal{A}) \cap P\) in \(P\). Indeed, if \(K\) is of Tor-dimension \(\leq 0\), and pointwise homotopic to complexes of flat modules \(L_x\), then \(\tau_{\geq 0}(K)\) is pointwise homotopic to the \(\tau_{\geq 0}(L_x)\), and these are again complexes of flat modules, so that \(\tau_{\geq 0}(K)\) satisfies 5.5.13.1.
5.5.14. By 5.5.6.1, 5.5.7.2 or 5.5.8.1 and 5.5.2.4, every quasi-isomorphism \(v : K' \longrightarrow K\) between complexes satisfying (5.5.13.1) induces quasi-isomorphisms

\[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{TS}^k(v) &: \mathrm{TS}^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(K') \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{TS}^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(K) \\ \Gamma^k(v) &: \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(K') \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(K) \end{aligned}\]

It follows that the functors \(\Gamma^k\) and \(\mathrm{TS}^k\) are derivable (5.5.5) on the subcategory \(D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X,\mathcal{A})\) of \(D^b(X,\mathcal{A})\), and that the complexes satisfying (5.5.13.1) are left split for these functors. By 5.5.2.4, \(\Gamma^k\) and \(\mathrm{TS}^k\) induce functors

\[(5.5.14.1) \qquad L\mathrm{TS}^k : D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X,\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X), \mathcal{A})\] \[(5.5.14.2) \qquad L\Gamma^k : D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X,\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X), \mathcal{A}) \, .\]
Moreover, the canonical morphism \(\alpha\) (5.5.9) induces, by 5.5.9 (i), an isomorphism between the functors 5.5.14.1 and 5.5.14.2
\[(5.5.14.3) \qquad \alpha : L\Gamma^k \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} L\mathrm{TS}^k \, .\]
5.5.14.4. The isomorphisms of 5.5.9 (iv) (v) (vi) (vii) pass to the derived category and define isomorphisms:
(iv') For \(\mathcal{A}'\) an \(\mathcal{A}\)-algebra, we have

\[L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(K) \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathcal{A}' \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathcal{A}') \, .\]
(v') For every base change \(g : S' \longrightarrow S\), we have
\[\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(g')^* L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}} K \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(g'^*K) \, .\]
(vi') For every radicial morphism \(i : X' \longrightarrow X\), we have
\[\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(i)^* L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}} K \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}} i^*K \, .\]
(vii') For \(j : X' \longrightarrow X\) an immersion, we have:
\[\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(j)_! L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}} j_! \, .\]
5.5.15. Let there be an exact sequence of flat complexes of \(C^{\geq 0}(X,\mathcal{A})\),
\[0 \longrightarrow K' \longrightarrow K \longrightarrow K'' \longrightarrow 0 \, ,\]

and let us apply the functor \(\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}\) (5.5.3). We find (as in 5.5.11) that the semi-simplicial Module \(\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(N^{-1}K)\) on \(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X)\) admits a filtration whose successive quotients are the semi-simplicial Modules
\[\Gamma^{k'}_{\mathrm{ext}}(N^{-1}K') \vee \Gamma^{k''}_{\mathrm{ext}}(N^{-1}K'') \qquad (k'+k'' = k) \, .\]

Passing to the derived category, we find that \(L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(K)\) is represented by a filtered complex whose successive quotients represent the objects \(L\Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}}(K') \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\vee} L\Gamma^{k-i}_{\mathrm{ext}}(K'')\) of the derived category (apply 5.5.2.4 and the EILENBERG-ZILBER-CARTIER theorem (isomorphism in \(\mathcal{K}\) of a double semi-simplicial object and its diagonal: DOLD PUPPE [1.2.9 pg.213]).
In the derived category, this construction can already be carried out starting from an exact sequence of complexes satisfying 5.5.13.1.

∗ In more intrinsic terms, let \(\Delta\) be a "true triangle" of objects of \(D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X,\mathcal{A})\), i.e. an object of the "filtered derived category" with \(\operatorname{Gr}^i(\Delta) = 0\) for \(i \neq 0,1\) and \(\operatorname{Gr}^i(\Delta) \in \operatorname{Ob} D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X,\mathcal{A})\) (DELIGNE, in Appendice à VERDIER [2], or VI B n° 2.5.1, 2.5.2).
The preceding construction then yields an object \(L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(\Delta)\) of the filtered derived category of \(\operatorname{Sym}^k_S(X)\), isomorphisms

\[\operatorname{Gr}^i(L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(\Delta)) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} L\Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}}(\operatorname{Gr}^1(\Delta)) \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\vee} L\Gamma^{k-i}_{\mathrm{ext}}(\operatorname{Gr}^0(\Delta))\]
and, denoting by \(|\ \ |\) the complex underlying a filtered complex, an isomorphism
\[|\, L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(\Delta)\, | \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} L\Gamma^k_{\mathrm{ext}}(|\Delta|) \, . \qquad *\]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.16

Let \(N\) be an integer. The category \(D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X,\mathcal{A})\) is obtained from the category of complexes \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} K^{b,\geq 0}(X,\mathcal{A})\) satisfying the conditions (i) and (ii) below by inverting the quasi-isomorphisms:

(i) Condition (5.5.13.1).

(ii) The complex \(K\) is split for every direct image functor of cohomological dimension \(\leq N\), relative to an isomorphism of topoi \(f : \widetilde{X}_{\mathrm{ét}} \longrightarrow T\).

That there is a right calculus of fractions follows from 5.5.13 and from the fact that, via the truncated canonical flasque resolutions (4.2.9), every complex \(K\) satisfying (i) maps into a complex satisfying (i) and (ii).

5.5.17. Let \(u : X \longrightarrow Y\) be a morphism of \(S\)-schemes. We assume that \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(Y)\) exist, that there exists an integer \(N\) such that the functor \(u_*\) is of dimension \(\leq N\) on the category of \(\mathcal{A}\)-Modules, and that the functor \(Ru_*\) transforms bounded complexes of Tor-dimension \(\leq 0\) into complexes of Tor-dimension \(\leq 0\). These last two conditions are automatic if \(u\) is proper, \(\mathcal{A}\) torsion, and \(Y\) coherent (i.e. quasi-compact, quasi-separated) (5.2.8.1, 5.2.10).
Let \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} K^{b,\geq 0}(X, \mathcal{A})\) be a complex satisfying the conditions (i) and (ii) of 5.5.16, with \(N\) as above. By 5.5.14, the arrow
\[\beta : L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K)\]
is a quasi-isomorphism. Likewise, the arrow
\[\gamma : u_*K \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} Ru_*K\]
is a quasi-isomorphism.
We define the symmetric Künneth arrow from \(L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_*(K)\) to \(R\operatorname{Sym}^n(u)_* L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K)\) as the composite

\[(5.5.17.1) \qquad \begin{aligned} k^n : L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_*K &\xleftarrow[\gamma]{\;\sim\;} L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} u_*K \longrightarrow \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} u_*K \xrightarrow{(5.5.12.1)} \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_* \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K) \\ &\longrightarrow R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_* \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K) \xleftarrow[\beta]{\;\sim\;} R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_* L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K) \, . \end{aligned}\]
It follows from 5.5.16 that the morphisms (5.5.17.1) define a morphism between functors from \(D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X, \mathcal{A})\) to \(D^+(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(Y), \mathcal{A})\)
\[(5.5.17.2) \qquad k^n : L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_* \longrightarrow R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S u_* L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} \, ,\]
also called the symmetric Künneth morphism.
This morphism is characterized by property 5.5.18 below.

5.5.17.3. Let \(S\), \(X\), \(Y\) and \(u\) be as above, \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} C^{b,\geq 0}(X, \mathcal{A})\) a complex of Tor-dimension \(\leq 0\), \(K_1 \in \operatorname{Ob} C^{b,\geq 0}(Y, \mathcal{A})\) and \(K_2 \in \operatorname{Ob} C^b(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(X), \mathcal{A})\). Let \(v\) be a \(u\)-homomorphism (0.2) from \(K\) to \(K_1\), and let \(t\) be a homomorphism (in the ordinary sense, like all those that follow) from \(\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K)\) to \(K_2\). We have morphisms
a) \(\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(v) : \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K_1) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_* \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K)\) (5.5.12.0)
b) \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_*(t) : \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_* \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_* K_2\),
with composite
\[\varphi' : \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K_1) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_* K_2 \, ,\]
defining, by composition
\[\varphi : L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K_1) \longrightarrow R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_* K_2 \, .\]
Moreover, \(v\) and \(t\) induce:
\[\begin{cases} v' : K_1 \longrightarrow Ru_*K \\[4pt] t' : L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} K \longrightarrow K_2 \end{cases} \, .\]
We then have:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.5.18

Under the hypotheses 5.5.17.3, the following diagram is commutative in \(D^+(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(Y), \mathcal{A})\):

\[\xymatrix@C=5em@R=4em{ L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_*K \ar[r]^-{k^n}_-{\text{(symmetric Künneth)}} & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_* L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} K \ar[d]^{R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_*(t')} \\ L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} K_1 \ar[u]^{L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(v')} \ar[r]_-{\varphi} & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_* K_2 }\]
The proof is entirely similar to that of 5.4.1.5 and is left to the reader.
5.5.19. From now on we assume \(\mathcal{A}\) torsion.
Let \(u : X \longrightarrow Y\) be a compactifiable morphism of \(S\)-schemes:
\[\xymatrix@C=2.5em@R=2em{ X \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{j} \ar[dr] \ar@/_1.6em/[rr]_{u} & \bar{X} \ar[r]^{\bar{u}} & Y \ar[dl] \\ & S & }\]
We assume that \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(X)\), \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(\bar{X})\) and \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(Y)\) exist. For every Module \(F\) on \(X\), we then have
\[(5.5.19.1) \qquad \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(j_!F) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(j)_! \Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(F) \, ,\]
and this isomorphism passes trivially to the derived categories.
We define the symmetric Künneth morphism between functors from \(D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X, \mathcal{A})\) to \(D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(Y), \mathcal{A})\)
\[(5.5.19.2) \qquad k^n_u \text{ or } k^n : L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_! \longrightarrow R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}\]
as being the composite

\[\begin{aligned} L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_! &\underset{\mathrm{dfn}}{=} L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} R\bar{u}_* j_! \xrightarrow{(5.5.17.2)} R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(\bar{u})_* L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} j_! \\ &\xrightarrow[\sim]{(5.5.19.1)} R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(\bar{u})_* \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(j)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} \\ &\xrightarrow{\text{(5.5.14.4 (vii'))}} R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} \, . \end{aligned}\]
5.5.20. We leave to the reader the task of carrying out the following verifications, easy in principle using 5.5.18.
5.5.20.1 (Intrinsic character). The morphism (5.5.19.2) is independent of the choice of the compactification \(\bar{u}\) of \(u\).
5.5.20.2 (Transitivity). Let there be a diagram of \(S\)-schemes
\[X \xrightarrow{\;u\;} Y \xrightarrow{\;v\;} Z \, ,\]

with \(u\) and \(v\) quasi-projective; we assume that \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(Z)\) exists (hence also \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(Y)\) and \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(X)\)) (SGA 1 V 1.7, EGA II 4.5.4). The following diagram of functors is then commutative

\[\xymatrix@C=1.6em@R=3.5em{ L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} R(vu)_! \ar[rr]^-{k^n_{vu}} \ar@{=}[d] & & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(vu)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} \ar@{=}[d] \\ L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Rv_! Ru_! \ar[r]^-{k^n_v} & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(v)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_! \ar[r]^-{k^n_u} & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(v)_! R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} }\]

5.5.20.3. The symmetric Künneth morphism is compatible with the changes of base or of space of the type 5.5.9 (iv) (v) (vi). More precisely, we have the following compatibilities with the morphisms 5.5.14.4 (iv') (v') (vi').
(iv") For every \(\mathcal{A}\)-algebra \(\mathcal{A}'\), and every quasi-projective \(S\)-morphism \(u : X \longrightarrow Y\) the diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=1.2em@R=3.5em{ L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_!(K) \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathcal{A}' \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_{k^n_u} & L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(Ru_!(K) \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathcal{A}') \ar[r]^-{\sim} & L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_!(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathcal{A}') \ar[d]^{k^n_u} \\ R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K) \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathcal{A}' \ar[r]^-{\sim} & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_! \bigl(L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K) \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathcal{A}'\bigr) \ar[r]^-{\sim} & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathcal{A}') }\]
is commutative.
(v") For every base change \(g : S' \longrightarrow S\), giving rise to a cartesian diagram
\[\xymatrix@C=1.8em@R=1.8em{ X' \ar[rr]^{g'} \ar[dr]_{u'} \ar[dd] & & X \ar[dr]^{u} \ar[dd] & \\ & Y' \ar[rr]^(0.35){g''} \ar[dl] & & Y \ar[dl] \\ S' \ar[rr]_{g} & & S & }\]
the diagram of functors, entirely analogous to (iv"), is commutative:

\[\xymatrix@C=1.2em@R=3.5em{ \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(g'')^* L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_! \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_{k^n_u} & L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} g''^* Ru_! \ar[r]^-{\sim} & L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru'_! g'^* \ar[d]^{k^n_{u'}} \\ \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(g'')^* R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} \ar[r]^-{\sim} & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u')_! g'^* L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} \ar[r]^-{\sim} & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u')_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} g'^* }\]
(vi") For every radicial base change \(g : Y' \longrightarrow Y\), giving rise to a cartesian diagram of \(S\)-schemes
\[\xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ X' \ar[r]^{g'} \ar[d]_{u'} & X \ar[d]^{u} \\ Y' \ar[r]_{g} & Y } \, ,\]
the following diagram of functors is commutative:

\[\xymatrix@C=1.2em@R=3.5em{ \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(g)^* L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_! \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_{k^n_u} & L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} g^* Ru_! \ar[r]^-{\sim} & L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru'_! g'^* \ar[d]^{k^n_{u'}} \\ \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(g)^* R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} \ar[r]^-{\sim} & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u')_! g'^* L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} \ar[r]^-{\sim} & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u')_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} g'^* } \, .\]

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.5.21

(Symmetric Künneth formula). Let \(S\) be a coherent scheme (= quasi-compact quasi-separated) ringed by a sheaf of commutative torsion rings \(\mathcal{A}\), whose stalks are noetherian rings. We ring each \(S\)-scheme by the inverse image of \(\mathcal{A}\). Let \(u : X \longrightarrow Y\) be a morphism of quasi-projective \(S\)-schemes. For any integer \(n \geq 0\) and \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X, \mathcal{A})\), the symmetric Künneth arrow (5.5.19.2)

\[k^n : L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_!K \longrightarrow R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} K\]

is an isomorphism in \(D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(Y), \mathcal{A})\).
The proof of this theorem will occupy the whole of the remainder of 5.5.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.5.21.1

The quasi-projectivity hypothesis serves only to ensure that \(u\) admits a compactification \(\bar{u}\)

\[X \xrightarrow{\;j\;} \bar{X} \xrightarrow{\;\bar{u}\;} Y\]

such that the schemes \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(X)\), \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(\bar{X})\) and \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(Y)\) exist for every \(n\). The language of algebraic spaces should make it possible to replace this hypothesis by the sole hypothesis that \(u\) is compactifiable.
The first part of the proof consists in reducing 5.5.21 by dévissage to an "irreducible" case:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.22

Theorem 5.5.21 is implied by the following special case:

(*) For every algebraically closed field \(k\), every projective and smooth curve \(X\) over \(k\) and every prime number \(\ell\), the symmetric Künneth arrows (obtained for \(Y = S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(\mathcal{A} = \mathbb{Z}/\ell\), \(K = \mathbb{Z}/\ell\); see explanations below)

\[(5.5.22.1) \qquad L\Gamma^n(R\Gamma(X, \mathbb{Z}/\ell)) \longrightarrow R\Gamma(\operatorname{Sym}^n_k(X), \mathbb{Z}/\ell)\]

are isomorphisms (\(n \geq 0\)).

In 5.5.22.1, the symbol \(\Gamma\) has an unfortunate double use: in the expression \(R\Gamma\), it denotes the "global sections" functor; in the expression \(L\Gamma^n\), it denotes the functor 5.5.2.3. In this formula we use the isomorphism \(\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathbb{Z}/\ell\).
Let \(S\), \(X\), \(Y\), \(u\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) be given as in 5.5.21.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.22.2

Let there be an exact sequence of complexes in \(C^{b,\geq 0}(X, \mathcal{A})\), of tor-dimension \(\leq 0\):

\[0 \longrightarrow K' \longrightarrow K \longrightarrow K'' \longrightarrow 0 \, .\]

If the Künneth arrows \(k^n\) (\(n \geq 0\)) relative to two of the complexes \(K'\), \(K\) and \(K''\) are all isomorphisms, then the Künneth arrows relative to the third are also isomorphisms.

We reduce to the case where \(u\) is projective, and where the complexes \(K'\), \(K\), \(K''\) satisfy the conditions (i) and (ii) of 5.5.16, for \(N\) at least equal to twice the dimension of the arrows of \(u\). The symmetric Künneth arrows are then given by 5.5.17.1.

Let us show by induction on \(n\) that if, for \(i \leq n\) and two of the complexes \(K'\), \(K\), \(K''\), the arrows \(k^i\) are isomorphisms, then the arrows \(k^i\) (\(i \leq n\)) are isomorphisms for the third.
To see this, we note that, thanks to 5.5.14, the morphism
\[(a) \qquad k^n : L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_*K \longrightarrow R\operatorname{Sym}^n(u)_* L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} K\]
can be represented by a morphism of filtered complexes
\[k'^n : K_0 \longrightarrow K_1\]
of finite filtration, this morphism inducing on the successive quotients arrows isomorphic to the composite arrows

\[(b_i) \qquad L\Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_*K' \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\vee} L\Gamma^{n-i}_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_*K'' \longrightarrow R\operatorname{Sym}^i(u)_*(L\Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}} K' \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\vee} L\Gamma^{n-i}_{\mathrm{ext}} K'')\]
below:

\[\begin{aligned} L\Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_*K' \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\vee} L\Gamma^{n-i}_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_*K'' &\xrightarrow{k^i_v\, k^{n-i}} R\operatorname{Sym}^i(u)_* L\Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}} K' \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\vee} R\operatorname{Sym}^{n-i}(u)_* L\Gamma^{n-i}_{\mathrm{ext}}(K'') \\ &\underset{\mathrm{dfn}}{=} \vee_{i,n-i\, *}\bigl(R\operatorname{Sym}^i(u)_* \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes} R\operatorname{Sym}^{n-i}(u)_*\bigr)(L\Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}} K' \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes} L\Gamma^{n-i}_{\mathrm{ext}} K'') \\ &\xrightarrow[\sim]{5.4.3} \vee_{i,n-i\, *}\bigl(R\operatorname{Sym}^i(u)_* \times R\operatorname{Sym}^{n-i}(u)_*\bigr)(L\Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}} K' \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes} L\Gamma^{n-i}_{\mathrm{ext}} K'') \\ &= R\operatorname{Sym}^n(u)_* \vee_{i,n-i\, *}(L\Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}} K' \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\boxtimes} L\Gamma^{n-i}_{\mathrm{ext}} K'') \underset{\mathrm{dfn}}{=} R\operatorname{Sym}^n(u)_*(L\Gamma^i_{\mathrm{ext}} K' \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\vee} L\Gamma^{n-i}_{\mathrm{ext}} K'') \end{aligned}\]

By the induction hypothesis (and the Künneth formula), these arrows are quasi-isomorphisms for \(i \neq 0,n\). Any two of the following assertions therefore imply the third: \((a)\) is a quasi-isomorphism; \((b_0)\) is a quasi-isomorphism; \((b_n)\) is a quasi-isomorphism. These are precisely the three arrows in question, qed.

5.5.22.3. Suppose that the assertion (*) considered in 5.5.22 is true, and let us prove 5.5.21. Let \(S\), \(X\), \(Y\), \(\mathcal{A}\), \(K\) and \(u\) be as in 5.5.21. The problem is local on \(S\), which we may assume to be affine. Every complex \(K\) is a successive extension of complexes of the form \(i_! i^*K\) for \(i\) the inclusion into \(X\) of a locally closed affine subset. By dévissage (5.5.22.2), we may therefore assume \(K\) to be of the form \(i_! K_1\), for an immersion \(i : X_1 \longrightarrow X\) with affine source. The compatibility 5.5.20.2 allows us to replace \(X\) by \(X_1\), \(K\) by \(K_1\), and hence to assume \(u\) affine. Let us factor \(u\) as a composite \(u = u_1 \ldots u_k\) of morphisms whose fibres have dimension \(\leq 1\). The compatibility 5.5.20.2 shows that it suffices to prove that the arrows \(k^n\) relative to the \(u_i\) and to an arbitrary complex \(K\) are isomorphisms. We are thus reduced to the case \(S\) affine, \(u\) of relative dimension \(\leq 1\).

5.5.22.4. For \(k^n\) to be an isomorphism, it suffices that its restrictions to the geometric fibres of \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(Y)\) be so; the compatibility 5.5.20.3 (v") thus reduces us to assuming \(S\) the spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\).

5.5.22.5. For every rational point \(y\) of \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_k(Y)\), there exists a finite reduced subset \(Y'\) of \(Y\) such that \(y\) lies in the image of \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_k(Y')\). The compatibility 5.5.20.3 (vi") therefore allows us to assume that \(Y\) is a sum of finitely many copies of \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\).

5.5.22.6. If \(Y = \coprod Y_i\), then every complex \(K\) on \(X\) is a sum of complexes concentrated on one of the schemes \(X_i = u^{-1}(Y_i)\). By dévissage (5.5.22.2) and by the compatibility 5.5.20.3 (vi), it suffices to prove 5.5.21 for each of the morphisms \(u_i : X_i \longrightarrow Y_i\). By 5.5.22.5, this reduces us to the case where
\[Y = S = \operatorname{Spec}(k) \, , \quad k \text{ algebraically closed}, \quad \dim X \leq 1 \, .\]
The sheaf \(\mathcal{A}\) now reduces to a noetherian ring \(A\). The following proposition will make it possible to reduce to the case where \(A\) is a field.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.5.23

Let \(A\) be a noetherian ring (commutative), \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(A)\) a bounded-above complex of \(A\)-modules and \(n\) an integer. The following conditions are equivalent

(i) \(K\) is of Tor-dimension \(\leq n\)

(ii) For every \(x \in \operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and every \(i < -n\), \(H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_A k(x)) = 0\).

We have (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) trivially. Suppose (ii). To prove (i), we shall prove by noetherian induction on the closed subset \(F\) of \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) that if a module \(N\) satisfies \(N_x = 0\) for \(x \notin F\), then \(H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_A N) = 0\) for \(i < -n\).

Let \(I\) be the unique ideal defining \(F\) such that \(A/I\) is reduced, and let \(N_k\) be the submodule of \(N\) annihilated by \(I^k\). We have \(N = \varinjlim N_k\). Since the functors Tor commute with filtered inductive limits, we reduce to the case where there exists \(k\) such that \(N = N_k\), so that \(N\) is a successive extension of modules killed by \(I\), and the long exact cohomology sequence reduces us to the case where \(N\) is already an \(A/I\)-module.
Let \(\eta\) be a maximal point of \(F\), and define \(A/I\)-modules \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) by the exact sequence
\[(5.5.23.1) \qquad 0 \longrightarrow M_1 \longrightarrow N \xrightarrow{\;i\;} N \otimes k(\eta) \longrightarrow M_2 \longrightarrow 0 \, .\]

We have \((M_j)_\eta = 0\) (\(j = 1,2\)). If, for each closed subset \(G \subset F\) with \(\eta \notin G\), we denote by \(M_{j,G}\) the submodule of \(M_j\) consisting of the sections of \(M_j\) with support in \(G\), then we have
\[M_j = \varinjlim_{\eta \notin G} M_{j,G} \, .\]
By the induction hypothesis and a passage to the limit, we therefore have
\[H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_A M_j) = 0 \quad \text{for } i < -n \, .\]
The module \(N \otimes k(\eta)\) is a vector space over \(k(\eta)\), hence a sum of copies of \(k(\eta)\). By hypothesis, we have
\[H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_A (N \otimes k(\eta))) = 0 \quad \text{for } i < -n \, .\]
If \(I\) is the image of the arrow \(i\) of (5.5.23.1), we have exact sequences

\[\begin{aligned} H^{i-1}(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} M_2) &\longrightarrow H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} I) \longrightarrow H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} (N \otimes k(\eta))) \\ H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} M_1) &\longrightarrow H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} N) \longrightarrow H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} I) \, , \end{aligned}\]
from which we deduce that \(H^i(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes} N) = 0\) for \(i < -n\), qed.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.5.24

For an arrow \(u : K \longrightarrow L\) in \(D^-(A)\) to be an isomorphism, it suffices that for every \(x \in \operatorname{Spec}(A)\), the arrow

\[u_x : K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_A k(x) \longrightarrow L \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_A k(x)\]

be an isomorphism in \(D^-(k(x))\).

Let \(M\) be the cone (mapping cylinder) of \(u\). By hypothesis, \(M \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_A k(x) = 0\) for every \(x \in \operatorname{Spec}(A)\). By 5.5.23, we therefore have \(M = 0\), and \(u\) is an isomorphism.

5.5.25.1. Let us continue the proof of 5.5.22, interrupted at 5.5.23. By the compatibility 5.5.20.3 (iv") and 5.5.24, the morphism \(k^n\) relative to \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X,A)\) is an isomorphism if and only if the morphisms \(k^n\) relative to the \(K \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_A k(x) \in \operatorname{Ob} D^{b,\mathrm{tor} \leq 0}(X, k(x))\) are isomorphisms, for \(x \in \operatorname{Spec}(A)\). This reduces us to the case where \(A\) is a field of characteristic \(\ell > 0\).
5.5.25.2. The exact sequence (where \(C\) denotes a cone)
\[0 \longrightarrow K[-1] \longrightarrow C K[-1] \longrightarrow K \longrightarrow 0\]
shows that the arrows \(k^n\) are isomorphisms for \(K\) if and only if they are so for \(K[-1]\) (5.5.22.2).
5.5.25.3. The exact sequences
\[0 \longrightarrow \sigma_{\geq n} K \longrightarrow K \longrightarrow \sigma_{\leq n} K \longrightarrow 0\]
show that, for the Künneth arrows to be isomorphisms, for \(K\) a flat complex, it suffices that they be so for the components of \(K\), placed in degree 0 (5.5.22.2) and (5.5.25.2).

5.5.25.4. Let \(F\) then be a sheaf of \(A\)-vector spaces. This sheaf is an inductive limit of constructible sheaves (IX 2.7.2), automatically flat since \(A\) is a field, and by passing to the limit we reduce to the case \(K\) constructible, concentrated in degree zero.

5.5.25.5. If a complex \(K\) is a direct factor of a complex \(L\), the morphism \(k^n\) relative to \(K\) is a direct factor of the morphism \(k^n\) relative to \(L\), hence an isomorphism if the latter is one. The trace method (IX 5.8) thus applies, and it suffices to treat the case where \(F\) is of the form \(j_! A_{X'}\), for \(j : X' \longrightarrow X\) quasi-finite. The compatibility 5.5.20.2 allows us to replace \(X\) by \(X'\), whence the reduction
\[X \text{ is of dimension} \leq 1 \text{ and } K = A_X \, .\]
5.5.25.6. We may assume \(X\) reduced. If \(j : U \longrightarrow X\) is the open subset of smoothness of \(X\), with complement \(i : F \longrightarrow X\), the exact sequence
\[0 \longrightarrow j_! j^* A_X \longrightarrow A_X \longrightarrow i_! i^*A_X \longrightarrow 0\]
reduces us, by dévissage, to the cases where \(X\) is either a smooth curve or a finite set. Moreover, the formula
\[A_X = A \overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}/\ell} (\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_X\]
reduces, by 5.5.20.3 (iv"), to the case where \(A_X = \mathbb{Z}/\ell\).
If \(X\) is a curve, we embed \(X\) in the corresponding smooth projective curve, and a further dévissage reduces to one of the two following cases
(i) \(X\) is a smooth projective curve, \(Y = S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) with \(k\) algebraically closed, \(\mathcal{A} = \mathbb{Z}/\ell\), \(K = \mathbb{Z}/\ell\).
(ii) \(X\) is a sum of finitely many copies of \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(Y = S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) (\(k\) algebraically closed), \(\mathcal{A} = \mathbb{Z}/\ell\), \(K = \mathbb{Z}/\ell\).

A final dévissage of \((\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_X\) into the sheaves \((\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_{X'}\), for \(X'\) a connected component of \(X\), reduces, in (i) and (ii), to assuming \(X\) connected. Case (ii) is then trivial. This proves 5.5.22.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.26

Theorem 5.5.21 is a consequence of the two following special cases of assertion (*) of 5.5.22 :

Case 1. We assume that \(k = \mathbb{C}\).

Case 2. We assume that \(k\) is of characteristic \(p > 0\) and that \(\ell = p\).

With the notation of 5.5.22, denote by \(p\) the characteristic of \(k\). If \(p = 0\), the Lefschetz principle (relying here on the compatibility 5.5.20.3 (v"), and on XII 5.4) allows us to reduce to the case where \(k = \mathbb{C}\).

It remains to treat the case where \(p > 0\) and \(\ell \neq p\). The curve \(X\) lifts to a curve \(X'\) over the ring \(W(k)\) of Witt vectors over \(k\) (SGA 1 III 7.4). Set \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(W(k))\); consider the diagram
\[\xymatrix@C=2.4em@R=2em{ X'_\eta \ar[r] \ar[d]_{f_\eta} & X' \ar[d]^{f'} & X \ar[l] \ar[d]^{f} \\ \eta \ar[r] & S & \operatorname{Spec}(k) \ar[l] } \, ,\]

and let \(f_n\), \(f'_n\) and \(f_{\eta,n}\) be the respective projections of \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_k(X)\), \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(X')\) and \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_\eta(X'_\eta)\) onto \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(S\) and \(\eta\). It is known that \(f'_n\) is a smooth projective morphism (projectivity is obvious; for smoothness, the simplest thing is to reduce to the case where \(X' = \mathbb{P}^1_S\), in which case \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(X') \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathbb{P}^n\) as follows from the theorem on elementary symmetric functions). By the specialization theorem XVI 2.2, the sheaves \(R^i f_{n*}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)\) are locally constant on \(S\). The same holds for the sheaves \(L^i \Gamma^n(Rf'_{n!} \mathbb{Z}/\ell)\). To verify that the arrow of (5.5.22.1) relative to \(X\) over \(k\) is an isomorphism, it therefore suffices, by 5.5.20.3 (v"), to prove the analogous statement for the geometric generic fibre \(X_{\bar{\eta}}\) of \(X\) over \(S\). The field \(k(\bar{\eta})\) is of characteristic 0, and, in view of the first reduction, this proves 5.5.26.

To prove 5.5.21 in these two special cases 5.5.26, we shall compare the symmetric Künneth morphism, on the one hand with its transcendental analogue (5.5.27 and 5.5.28), on the other hand with its coherent analogue (5.5.29 to 5.5.37).

5.5.27. If \(p : X \longrightarrow S\) is a continuous map between topological spaces, with \(S\) ringed by a sheaf of commutative rings \(\mathcal{A}\), the constructions 5.5.7, 5.5.8 apply as they stand to define a functor \(\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}}\) from modules on \(X\) to modules on \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(X) = X^n/\mathfrak{S}_n\). The sorites 5.5.7 to 5.5.18 carry over. Likewise, if \(S\), \(X\) and \(Y\) are locally compact Hausdorff topological spaces
\[\xymatrix@C=2em@R=2em{ X \ar[rr]^{u} \ar[dr] & & Y \ar[dl] \\ & S & } \, ,\]
and if the fibres of \(u\) are of bounded cohomological dimension, the sorites 5.5.19, 5.5.20 of the symmetric Künneth morphism in cohomology with proper support carry over.

If \(p : X \longrightarrow S\) is a morphism of schemes of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\), the functors \(\Gamma^n\) and \(L\Gamma^n\) commute with the "passage to the transcendental" functors. Finally, if \(X\), \(Y\), \(S\), \(\mathcal{A}\), \(K\) are as in 5.5.21, with \(S\) separated of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\), and if we denote generically by \(\varepsilon\) the morphisms of sites of the form \(\varepsilon : X_{\mathrm{cl}} \longrightarrow X_{\mathrm{ét}}\), the following diagram is commutative:

\[(5.5.27.1) \qquad \xymatrix@C=4em@R=3.5em{ \varepsilon^* L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} Ru_! K \ar[r]^-{k^n} \ar[d] & \varepsilon^* R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u)_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} K \ar[d] \\ L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} R u^{\mathrm{an}}_! \varepsilon^*K \ar[r]_-{k^{u^{\mathrm{an}}}} & R\operatorname{Sym}^n_S(u^{\mathrm{an}})_! L\Gamma^n_{\mathrm{ext}} \varepsilon^* K }\]

5.5.28. By the compatibility 5.5.27.1, and an elementary case of the comparison theorem (XI 4.4 or XVI 4.1), in order to treat case 1 of 5.5.26, it suffices to verify that if \(X\) is a complex nonsingular projective curve, then the topological analogue of 5.5.22.1 is an isomorphism.

The topological space \(X^{\mathrm{an}}\) is triangulable (this fact is here trivial, since \(X\) is a ramified covering of the Riemann sphere). The topological analogue of the dévissage lemma 5.5.22.2 then reduces us to proving
(*) If \(D\) is a closed simplex (of dimension 0, 1 or 2), the topological symmetric Künneth arrow
\[(5.5.28.1) \qquad k^n : L\Gamma^n R\Gamma(D, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) \longrightarrow R\Gamma(\operatorname{Sym}^n(D), \mathbb{Z}/\ell)\]
is an isomorphism.
We have
\[R\Gamma(D, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = \mathbb{Z}/\ell \text{ placed in degree 0} \, ,\]
and therefore
\[L\Gamma^n R\Gamma(D, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = \mathbb{Z}/\ell \text{ placed in degree 0} \, .\]
On the other hand, \(\operatorname{Sym}^n(D)\) is contractible, and we again have
